Oṃ,
salutations to the illustrious Śiva and Śivā.
The Glorious Makuṭāgama (The Tradition of the Crown)
The Chapter on the Introduction to the Tantra.
On the glorious Mahendra mountain, which brings delight to the eyes of the worlds,
there are bilva trees, śamī trees, banyan trees, campaka trees, and pippala trees.
In a great golden assembly hall, adorned with all precious materials and surrounded by sandalwood trees together with *plakṣa* and *punnāga*, [he sat]. || 1-2 ||
Seated upon a lion-throne adorned with great jewels, a dwelling of auspiciousness,
was the Supreme Lord, who transcends the reach of speech and mind.
[He meditated upon] the Lord of the universe, free from beginningless impurity, a treasure-house of compassion,
the ordainer of all sciences, accompanied by Gaurī on his left side.
It was served by Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, the Sun, Indra, sages, and Gandharvas,
while being praised with hymns, musical instruments, and auspicious recitations.
To the tranquil and serene Supreme Lord, whose noble crown is the moon,
Maheśvara, with a gracious soul, [approached] out of a desire to grasp the knowledge of Śiva.
Having bowed down with devotion and respect, he spoke words for the welfare of the world.
Maheśvara said:
"O God of gods, Lord of the universe, destroyer of the afflictions of your devotees!"
(2) You are intent upon creation, preservation, withdrawal, concealment, and grace;
you are the illuminator of the jewel of knowledge situated within the ocean of the Śiva Āgamas. 1.8.
O ocean of compassion, skilled in severing the bonds of bound souls,
and endowed with the supreme power whose nature is supreme consciousness.
O Omniscient One, O All-doer, O Ambiguous One, O Soul of All, O You whose face is turned in every direction!
[This is] for the benefit of practitioners, meritorious, and the means to liberation for yogins. (1-10)
"O Supreme Lord, please speak of the supreme, pure knowledge of Śiva.
Thus questioned by Maheśa, the Blessed Supreme Lord [replied].
With a voice that was profound and capable of benefiting the entire world, the illustrious Supreme Lord said:
"I shall explain, in a concise manner, according to your question and as you desire. (1.12)
O illustrious Maheśvara, listen with a concentrated mind to the supreme and most secret knowledge of Śiva, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This work, which removes all sins, is meritorious, and explains the meaning of all tantras; it is composed of one hundred thousand verses and accomplishes all goals. (1-14)
O Maheśvara, I shall now briefly proclaim to you that great *ūrdhvaśaiva* tantra known as the *Makuṭa*. (1.15)
Now, hear in brief and in sequence the ninefold Śaiva [tradition]:
first is the Ūrdhvaśaiva, and the second is the Ādiśaiva.
The third is Mahāśaiva, the fourth is Anuśaiva, the fifth is Avāntara, and the sixth is Miśraśaiva. (1.17)
The seventh is the Bhedaśaiva, and the eighth is the Guṇaśaivaka;
the ninth is the Ājñāśaiva—listen now to the sequence of the divisions of Śaivism.
The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula systems are fourfold;
among them, the Śaiva, which originates from the Upper Stream (ūrdhvasrotas), is the most excellent. (1-19)
Now, the Śaiva [tradition] is remembered as being of two kinds: the gentle (saumya) and the fierce (raudra).
The gentle is said to be of two types: the right-hand (dakṣiṇa) and the mixed (miśrita).
Conduct prescribed by the Vedas is called the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra);
the opposite is the left-hand path (vāmācāra), and their union is the mixed path (saṅkara). || 1-21 ||
This Tantra is the essence of the Vedas; therefore, one who follows the Vedic path should practice it.
This knowledge is the noble culmination of the Vedanta, the supreme and auspicious Siddhānta. 1-22.
The *Ūrdhvasrotas* is the most excellent, consisting of twenty-eight tantras;
it should be known as that which bestows the essential meaning of the Vedas and accomplishes all other purposes. (1.23)

At the beginning of the Tantra, the true nature of the Tantra, endowed with its primary divisions and sub-divisions, shall be declared by means of names such as the *Kāmika* and others; listen as they are explained in sequence. (1.24)
Because it extends vast benefits based upon the reality of mantras and provides protection for persons, it is known as "tantra. (1.25)
Kāmika, Yogaja, Cityaṅkāraṇa, and likewise Ajita;
Dipta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, and Suprabhedaka. || 26 ||
Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyambhuva, Anala, Vīra, Raurava, Makuṭa, and likewise Vimala.
The Candrajñāna, the Bimba, the Prodgīta, the Lalita, as well as the Siddha, the one known as the Santāna, and the Pārameśvara spoken by Śarva. (1–28)
The Kiraṇa and the Vātula, as well as these others numbering twenty-eight—of these, the first ten are proclaimed as the Śiva-bheda. (1–29)
Likewise, there is another group of eighteen known by the name Rudrabheda;
this Tantra, consisting of Śiva and Rudra, is numbered at twenty-eight.
(4) Even if there were but a single speaker, the listeners would be manifold;
yet, in particular, the listeners of the Siddhānta tantras [are many]. (1-31)
Those beginning with Praṇava are proclaimed; listen to this, O Maheśvara.
The listeners of the divisions of Śiva are three times three in their lineage.
Sixty-six pairs of the various forms of Rudra have been proclaimed.
From the Praṇava [arise] Tryakṣa, Sudhākhya, Bhasmaka, and Vibhu, each consisting of three kalās.
Sudīpta, Gopati, Ambikā, Kāraṇa, Śarvarudra, Vrajeśa, Subhrū, Suśiva, and Acyuta. || 1-34 ||
Īśa, named Trimūrti, and Hutāśa, known as Sūkṣma; then indeed Śravaṇa, called Prabhañjana. || 1-35 ||
Kāla, Bhīma, Dharma, Tatogra, the one named Ambu, Ravi, Vighneśvara, and Daśa, who is named Śaśin—these are the ten lords of the months. || 1-36 ||
The presiding deities of the divisions of Śiva are said to be thirty in number, in sequence:
Rudra, Parameśa, Daśārṇa, and Girijātana. (1–37)
Nidhana, Padmasambhūta, the one named Vyoman who is known as Agni, Tejas, Prajāpati, Brahmā, and Nandikeśvara. || 1-38 ||
And Śiva, Mahādeva, the soul of all (Sarvātman), Vīrabhadraka,
Ananta, Bṛhaspati, Praśānta, and Dadhīcaka.
Śūlī, Kavaca, and thereafter Ālaya, Rudrabhairava;
Bindu, Caṇḍeśvara, and Śivaniṣṭha, as well as Ambavāyasa. || 1.40 ||
Somadeva, Nṛsiṃha, Śrīdevī, and Uśanas; Devapitṛ, Saṃvarta, Śiva, and Mahākāla. (1–41)
(5) Indeed, their number, the Rudras who are the presiding deities according to their divisions, and the root-tantras along with their sub-divisions shall be declared in order by name. || 1.42 ||
The Kāmika is said to have three divisions, the Yogaja five divisions,
the Cintya Tantra six divisions, and the Kāraṇa seven divisions.
That which is called Ajita has four divisions; Dīpta has nine divisions;
Sūkṣma is said to be of one kind; and Sahasraka (Sakṣasraka) has ten divisions. (1.44)
Aṃśumat would be Sūryabheda, Suprabheda would be Abhedaka; Vijaya consists of eight divisions, and Niśvāsa likewise has eight divisions.
The Svāyambhuva [Tantra] shall have two divisions, and the Āgneya is its sub-divider;
specifically, there is the Cīra-tantra, and the divisions are thirteen.
Raurava is said to have six divisions, while Makuṭa has two;
Vimala has the division of Kalā, and Candajñāna has fourteen.
The *Tithibheda* and the *Bimbatantra* are proclaimed; sixteen [tantras] are traditionally remembered.
There is the *Lalita*, which concerns the differentiation of qualities (*guṇabheda*), and the *Siddha*, which concerns the differentiation of the ages (*yugabheda*). (1.48)
The *Santāna* would have seven divisions, while that spoken by Śarva would be fivefold;
the *Pārameśa* has seven divisions, and the *Kiraṇa* has nine divisions.
The Vātula and the Ravibheda shall be explained individually, as well as the Nārasiṃha, the Vaktrārambha, and the Bhairavokta. (1.50)
The Kāmika has three divisions: Tāra, Vīṇāśikhottara, and Ātmayoga-sutāra; while Sannati belongs to the Yogaja.

The well-considered, the fortunate, the left, the nectar, the destroyer of evil, and that which arises from another—these are proclaimed as the six divisions of the "to-be-considered" (cintya). || 1.52 ||
The Mahendra, Kāraṇa, Daurga, Pāvana, Bhīmasaṃhitā, Vidveṣa, and Māraṇa—these are the seven divisions within the Kāraṇa [Tantra]. (1.53)
The *Prabhūta*, the *Parodbhūta*, the *Pārvatī*, and the *Padmasaṃhitā*—
these are the four divisions of the *Ajita*, followed by the ninth in number.
Immeasurable, covering the year, innumerable, and of infinite splendor;
it is bliss arising from Mādhava, wonderful and likewise imperishable. (1.55)
And in the *Sūkṣmatantra*, that which is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) alone is proclaimed;
it is transcendent, auspicious, pure, immeasurable, and possesses [all] castes. (1.56)
Prabuddha, Vibudha, Hastālaṅkāra, and Subodhaka—these are declared to be the ten divisions of the Thousand Tantras. (1.57)
The Kāśyapa, the Vāsava, the Indra, the Vāsiṣṭha, and likewise the Gautama; the Bhūtatantra, the Prakaraṇa, the Vidyā, and the Purāṇa as well. || 1-58 ||
Īśāna, Uttara, Nīlalohita, Ātman, Laṅkāraka, and Brāhma—these are the twelve divisions of the Sun. (1.59)
It is well-differentiated yet non-differentiated; it is the source of existence and the source of Kubera;
it is most terrible and yet non-terrible; it is stainless and the destroyer of death.
The eight divisions of the [tantra] named Vijaya are proclaimed as follows:
Niśvāsa, Mantraniśvāsa, and that known as Niśvāsottara; || 1.61 ||
In this [Niśvāsakārikā] are the Niśvāsaguhyam, the Niśvāsaghoram, the Niśvāsakārikā,
the Niśvāsanayana, and the Niśvāsamukhodaya.
The eight divisions of the Niśvāsa, which constitute the Mahātantra, have been proclaimed;
namely, the Prājāpatya and the Padma, these two belonging to the Svāyambhuva.
For the anus, two [seats] are prescribed: the fiery (āgneya) and the void (vyoma), which is well-restrained;
the pure pedestal (prastara) is masculine, awakening, and free from delusion. (1.64)
And the Mōhasamaya, the Śakaṭa, the Śākaṭāthika-bhadraka, the Vileghana, the Vīra, the Hala, and the Bodhabodhaka. || 1-65 ||
O Maheśvara, thirteen divisions have been proclaimed in the Vīra-tantra:
Kāladāha, Kalātīta, Raurava, and Rauravottara; || 1.66 ||
The Mahākālamata, the Aindra, and the six divisions of the Raurava;
two divisions are declared in the Makuṭa, namely the Makuṭa and the Makuṭottara.
The bull, the bull named Piṅga, the one who has ascended, the one spoken of as a bull, the one with beautiful tusks, the one who has become thus, and Raudra, Bhadra, and Vidhantha. (1–68)
The Anantamaṭṭāhāsa, the Arcita, and likewise the Dhāraṇa;
thus, these sixteen divisions of the Vimalatantra have been proclaimed. (1.69)
Ekapāda, Purāṇa, Sthāṇu, Nandikeśvara, Sthira, Śāṅkara, Śrīmukha, and Śivabhadra are proclaimed [as the names of the Liṅgas]. (1.70)
The Kalpabheda, the Ativyāpta, the Mahāvāruṇa, the Devyāmata, the Vāyavya, and that which is known as the Śivaśāsana. (1.71)
In the *Candrajñāna*, fourteen [tantras] are mentioned, beginning with the *Śivaśekhara*:
the *Caturvaktra*, the *Mayoga*, the *Saṃstobha*, and the *Pratibimbaka*. (1.72)
The ornament of meaning (arthālaṅkāra), Aiśāna, Ananta, Auṭika, Tuṭinīraka, that which is called Kuṭṭima, Tulāyoga, and Tulāpratyaya. || 1-73 ||
Mahāvidyā, Mahāsaura, Nairṛta, Paṭṭaśekhara, and Mukhabimba—these fifteen divisions of the Tantra have been proclaimed. (1.74)
The Vārāha, the Pāśabandha, and likewise the Piṅgalāmata;
the Dhanurdhara, the Daṇvadhara, the Śivajñāna, and also the Aṅkuśa. (1.75)
He [taught] the science of consciousness, the science of medicine known as the *Śrī Kālajñāna*, the science of archery, armor, and the piercing of snake fangs. (1.76)
Bharata, Gīta, and Ātodya—these are the sixteen paths in the Proṅgīta; there are three varieties of Lalita: Lalita, Lalitottara, and [the third]. (1.77)
Then [he taught] the Kaumāra, the Śālābheda, that which is called Sāroktarāha, the one known as Auśanottara, and also the Śaśimaṇḍala. || 1.78 ||
The four divisions of the Siddhatantra are proclaimed as follows:
Liṅgādhyakṣa, Surādhyakṣa, Śaṅkara, and Amareśvara. (1.79)
The Asaṃkhyamānila, the Dvaṃdva, the Saptabheda, the Śivayarmottara, the Divya, and the Īśāna—these are proclaimed as the seven [tantras] in the Santāna lineage. (1.80)
The [mantras] proclaimed by Vāyu, those named after Kubera, and the fivefold weapons spoken by Śarva—namely Haṃsa, Padma, Mātaṅga, and the Sāmānya—are considered to be Yakṣiṇīs. (1.81)
In the Pārameśvara [Tantra], there are seven types of *puṣkara* and *suprayoga*:
Gāruḍa, Nairṛta, Rūkṣa, Nīla, Buddha, and Bhānuka. (1.82)
Prabuddha, Dhenuka, Kāla, Kiraṇa, Navakīrtita, Vātulottara, Vātula, and Prarohita. (1-83)
He is the knowledge of time, all-pervading, eternal, and likewise of the nature of dharma;
he is the universe, the most excellent, the pure, the soul of the universe, and the great mouth.
In the Masātantra known as the Vātula, twelve divisions (bhedas) are proclaimed;
the sub-divisions (upabhedas) are stated in sequence to be two hundred and seven.
The [tantras] beginning with Kāmika and ending with Jita originated from the mouth of Sadyojāta;
those beginning with Dīpta and ending with Suprabheda originated from the mouth of Vāmadeva.
Those beginning with Vijayā and ending with Vīrā were born from the mouth of Aghora;
those beginning with Revatī and ending with Mukhasiṃhā were born from the mouth of Puruṣa.
The eight Saṃhitās, beginning with the Prodgīta, are known as originating from the face of Īśāna.
O Maheśvara, listen as I shall declare their number of chapters in due order. (1.88)

That which is produced for the sake of others is declared to be "desirable" (kāmika); that born of yoga is called "lakṣa"; the "cintya" is a hundred thousandfold, while the "kāraṇa" is measured at ten million.
Ajita is said to be a prayuta, while niyuta is called dīpta;
sūkṣma is the number of padmas, and sahasra is the count of śaṅkhas.
The *Aśumān* consists of five hundred thousand verses; the *Suprabheda* has three crores; the *Vijaya* shall likewise have three crores; and one crore is said to be the *Niśvāsa*. (1.91)
The Svāyaṃbhuvakalpa consists of thirty million [years], while the Anala is said to be three hundred thousand; the Vīra is declared to be one million, and the Raurava is eight hundred million.
The *Makuṭa* consists of one hundred thousand [verses], the *Vimala* three hundred thousand;
the *Candrajñāna* shall be three million, and the *Mukhaviṃba* one thousand.
The *prodgīta* consists of three hundred thousand [verses], while the *lalitāṣṭasahasraka* consists of eight thousand;
the *siddha* consists of one and a half crores, and the *santāna* consists of six thousand. (1.94)
The Śarvokta consists of three hundred thousand [verses], as does the Pārameśa;
the Kiraṇa consists of fifty million, and the Vātula consists of one hundred thousand.
O Maheśvara, I shall now briefly describe the form of the Tantra:
the pair of feet is Kāmika, and the pair of calves is Yogaja.
Cintya is said to be the toes of the feet; Kāraṇa is the pair of shanks; Ajita is the region of the knees; and Dīpta is the region of the thighs.
Sūkṣma is the secret region; Sahasra is the surface of the hips;
Aṃśumān is the back part; and Suprabhedaka is the navel. (1.98)
The region of the belly would be Vijaya, the heart would be Niśvāsa;
the pair of breasts is called Svāyaṃbhuva, and the fire is said to be the eye.
One should place Vīra at the region of the ears and Raurava on the two ears;
likewise, one should assign the Makuṭa, the Makuṭatantra, and the Aṅga and Pratyāṅga mantras.
The arms are said to be Vimala, the chest region is Candrajñāna,
the orb of the face is the mouth, and the tongue is called Prodgīta.
The cheeks are called *lalita*, the forehead is *siddha*,
one should know the *kuṇḍala* as *santāna*, and the sacred thread (*upavītaka*) as taught by Śarva.
The Pārameśa, the Hāra, the Kirana, the Ratnabhūṣaṇa, the Kālottara, as well as the Nāḍis; thus the Vāyu [Tantras] shall be twenty-two. (1-103)
The garment is declared to be the wind (vātula), the unguent is the dharma of Śiva; the image is the flower, the garland is the Siddhānta, and the offering is the presentation (nivedana). || 1.104 ||
With his body consisting of the Tantra, the god faces south;
he is the stainless form of bliss, dancing as the partless Śiva.
The Guru should meditate daily for the sake of accomplishment, especially at the time of the twilight rituals (saṃdhyā).
Thus has been described the descent of the tantras up to the end of the Śitikaṇṭha [Tantra]. (1.106)
For others, it is not taught here for fear of excessive expansion of the text;
one should perform everything from the plowing (or tilling) up to the consecration using the root mantra alone.
If it is performed with divisive intent, the performer and the patron both perish;
indeed, sacrifice is said to be rendered useless, especially when accompanied by such divisions.

Furthermore, by means of the sixty-six root mantras that have been taught, the ritual procedure— beginning with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and extending from the plowing (karṣaṇa) up to the final worship (arcanā)— is commenced according to this Tantra.
He should perform everything according to that [tantra] and not act according to another tantra;
the teacher should practice after having extracted from other tantras whatever has not been stated here.
The rites beginning with the plowing [of the site] should be commenced according to the Śivasiddhāntatantra;
one should not perform them according to another tantra, for if one were to do so, it would result in a confusion of tantras (tantrasaṃkara).
Through the fault of mixing tantras, the kingdom and its ruler perish;
however, a follower of Śiva (Śaiva) shall be entitled to authority over all, both his own and that of others.
However, in the case of others, there exists a capacity for agency within their own independent systems. || 113a½ ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Tantra," in the section on Ritual Practice (*kriyāpāda*) of the *Makuṭa-tantra*, the compendium of three thousand verses.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Worship of Śiva.
The Praise of the Worship of Śiva.
I shall describe the meritorious daily worship, which is auspicious, brings about all accomplishments, destroys the taint of great sins, and bestows all sovereign powers. (2-1)
Worship for one's own sake and worship for both one's own sake and the sake of others are said to be twofold:
[performed] upon the body of the Guru, on an auspicious *liṅga*, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and within one's own self. (2-2)
In this momentary maṇḍala, that which is known as sacrifice for one's own sake,
as well as worship for the sake of others, was previously established by gods, sages, or men according to the prescribed rule. (2–3)
A self-manifested linga and an image representing the Lord are declared to yield for all the fruit of ten million times [the merit of] one's own self.
(Regarding the Śiva-dvija, the status of the teacher for the four castes is as follows:
Specifically, in the initiation of the four castes, a Brāhmaṇa is the teacher. 2-5.
(Those who perform worship for their own sake or for the sake of others... the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as those initiated, are the ones who enter. 2-6.

Those who follow the *ūrdhvaśaiva* [tradition] should perform sacrifices for their own sake, not for the sake of others; however, they may also perform sacrifices for the sake of others and for the prosperity of both themselves and others. (2.7)
The teacher who is a Śiva-brāhmaṇa is declared to be an Ūrdhvaśaiva;
he [performs] both for his own sake and for the sake of others for those initiated into Nirvāṇa. (2-8)
For among the Śaiva Āgamas, this is the supreme one;
it is called Caiva-abhiṣeṇa, and its other names are Makuṭa and Paratāṇḍava.
The Tantra concerning the Name-mantra (nāmamantra) is auspicious and consists of that which transcends sound (nādātīta).
However, for one of another caste, it serves for the purpose of malevolent rites (ābhicāra) when used in initiation. (2-10)
The rules for purification.
Having meditated upon Śiva at dawn and having dedicated all his actions to Śiva, he should discharge excrement and other waste in the north-easterly direction of the village. (2.11)
One should avoid [excreting] from a cow-pen, a temple, an anthill, a reservoir of water, or in the presence of Brahmins, cattle, men, or women, except when staying elsewhere. (2.12)
Having wrapped his head and remaining silent, facing northward and covering his right hand, he should enter the reservoir of water.
One should perform purification according to the prescribed rule at a river, a pond, or a well;
this purification consists of the sequential cleansing of the mind and the sequential washing of the feet. (2.14)
The cleaning of the teeth.
One should perform the cleaning of the teeth with branches of the Plakṣa, Udumbara, Nimba, and other such trees;
one should effect the purification of the nose, mouth, and teeth with the Astra-mantra. (2-15)
Having recited the three-syllable mantra, one immediately attains purity of the tongue. Regarding the bath for removing impurities:
having first performed the bath for removing impurities, listen now to the procedure for the mantra-bath. (2-16)
Five types of baths are prescribed for the purification of those who have received initiation:
the watery, the fiery, the divine, the windy, and that of the dust of cows' hooves.
The Varuṇa bath is performed with water; the Āgneya bath occurs with ashes. The Divya bath is by means of rain accompanied by sunshine, and the Vāyavya bath is with the dust raised by cows.
The mental bath is said to be performed with mantras; thus, the baths are fivefold. [One may bathe] in a river, or in a pond, or in a well, or at the sites of holy pilgrimage (tīrtha). (2-19)
Water, whether pure or impure, that flows near the abode of Śiva becomes renowned as the Śivagaṅgā by virtue of being sprinkled from the feet of Śiva. (2.20)
Having gone to one of those [sites], one should especially perform a ritual bath;
one should also construct a circular mandala measuring one cubit in size. (2-21)
The practitioner should take up the clay with the Astra mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*;
he should place it there with the Sadyojāta mantra and purify it with the Vāmadeva mantra. (2.22)
Having touched the clay with the Aghora mantra, one should divide it into three parts; then, one should consecrate each part individually with the Īśāna mantra.
Having recited the six-limbed Brahma-mantra, one should scatter [the earth] starting from the east;
one should scatter a portion of earth consecrated with the Astra-mantra in the ten directions.
One should immediately cast a portion of earth consecrated by recitation into the middle of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha),
properly joining it with the root mantra and the *huṃ phaṭ* syllables.
Having placed the sixteen syllables, one should write [the mantra] beginning with the first letter of one's own name;
then, having recited the weapon-mantra (astra), one should bind the mudrā that delivers one from saṃsāra. (2.26)
Whatever subtle defects exist in the water, their eradication shall occur.
[One should touch] the head, the face, the heart, the secret parts, and the feet on the right side. (2-27)
Having placed a lump of clay as before, one should smear all the limbs [of the image].
Having placed a lump of clay in the north, one should cast it into the middle of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha). || 2-28 ||

The five sacred sites (*pañcatīrthāni*): that at the base of the thumb is the Brāhma; that on the middle of the fingers is the Āgneya; and after that, between the forefinger and the thumb, is the Paitraka. (2.29)
The root of the fingers is declared to be the *devatīrtha*; the tip of the fingers is the *ārṣatīrtha*. One should satisfy the five deities [with water] from the *devatīrtha*.
The tasting [of the water] is performed with the Brahma-tīrtha, the sprinkling with the Vahni-tīrtha,
the touching with the Pitṛ-tīrtha, and the cleansing with the Deva-tīrtha.
One should take [the water] with the *ārṣa* tīrtha and then divide it into five parts.
This is the ritual bath (*vidhisnāna*), accompanied by royal honors, using fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances. (2-32)
One should apply anointment to the limbs with turmeric, saffron, and other such substances.
[At the conclusion of the immersion in water, one should be attended by celestial women.
With the Śiva-mantra recited a hundred times, as well as with the Brahma-mantras, [one should perform the consecration].
And one should pervade the sky with the limbs [of the deity] by means of the mantra beginning with "Tryambaka" and others.
With the mantra "Udutyam Citram Devānām," the one who gazes auspiciously should slowly perform the consecration upon his head using the mouth-mudrā.
The pure sipping of water.
Having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) at the end, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantras;
place the right foot on dry land and the left foot in the water.
Having contracted the hand and adorned it with a purifier (pavitra),
one should consume water here in the measure of a māṣa.
Having thus drunk it three times, one should touch the mouth twice with the thumb;
then, having touched the face with the hand, one should sprinkle the feet.
A wise person should touch the two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger;
one should touch the two nostrils with the thumb and the index finger. (2.40)
Afterwards, one should touch both eyes with the little finger and the thumb;
then, one should again touch the pair of upper arms with the tips of the thumb and middle finger. (2.41)
One should touch the joints with the fingers, as well as the navel, the heart, and the head;
having done this, the knower of mantras should touch each limb in turn. (2.42)
The sipping of water with mantras.
One should again drink the three waters with the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
then, according to the Atharvaveda, there is the touching of the mouth twice with excessive laughter. (2.44)
One should sprinkle water on the head and the feet for the preparation of the assembly of sages;
and on the crown of the head, the eyes, and the ears for the preparation of the Lord of all the gods.
O Indra, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Kṛtaya, [I touch] the arms, the navel, and the heart;
one should likewise perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again with those respective mantras. (2.47)
The special sipping of water.
Immediately thereafter, having drunk it in three portions in succession with fierce mantras, the preceptor should touch it to his heart and indeed to all his limbs. (2.48)
The special sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed for the evening; it is said that midday is [the time for] the Kāmika [tattva]. The pair of feet is indeed the Yogajaṅgha;
the toes of the feet are declared to be the Cintya [tattva], while the pair of shanks is the Kāraṇa [tattva].

The region of the knees should be invincible (*ajita*), the region of the thighs radiant (*dīpta*), the region of the secret parts subtle (*sūkṣma*), and the surface of the hips a thousandfold (*sahasra*). (2.51)
Aṃśumān is the region of the back, while the navel is Suprabhedaka;
Vijaya is the region of the belly, and Niśvāsa would be the heart.
The pair of breasts is said to be the Svāyambhuva [Tīrtha], the eye is Anala,
the region of the throat is Vīra, and the two ears are Raurava.
The crown is Makuṭa; there, the limbs and the minor limbs are likewise [assigned]. The arms are said to be Vimala, and the nose is Candrajñāna.
The face is declared to be called Bimba; the tongue is indeed Prodgīta;
the cheeks are declared to be Lalita; and the forehead is indeed Siddha.
One should know the *santāna* as the earring (*kuṇḍala*), the *upavītaka* as spoken by Śarva, the *hāra* as Pārameśvara, and the *kiraṇa* as the jeweled earring (*ratnakuṇḍala*). (2.56)
The *Kālottara* is likewise [the first], while the *Nāthya* is the wind (*vāyu*) in the twenty-second [tattva].
The *Vātula* is declared to be clothing (*vasana*), and the *Śivadharmā* is ointment (*lepana*). (2-57)
Having meditated with a body consisting of the Tantra upon the incense, flowers, garlands, the Siddhānta, and the offering, [the practitioner] faces the south. (2.58)
Having meditated thus, as before, upon Naṭeśa, whose form is manifold, as Śiva who is of the nature of bliss, stainless, dancing, and partless (niṣkala). (2.59)
Following the foot-imprint, one should perform the consecration with the Śiva-mantras;
having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana) according to the rules, one should recite the name-mantra and chant the Sāvitrī for men one hundred and eight times.

One should then perform the solar worship with the Sūryahṛdaya hymn and the ritual attendance (upasthāna), as well as the five Brahmans, the six limbs, the Vyomavyāpin mantra, and the Tryambaka mantra.
One should recite "udutyaṃ," "citraṃ devānām," and "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad," as well as the Sāvitrī at the twilight, which is Gāyatrī, the deity of all gods. (2.63)

Having uttered the names of the deities ending in the dative case along with the word "kāma" (desire) and "svakariṣīḥ" (you who perform), one should prostrate with the eight limbs while saying, "Gūm, namaḥ, namaḥ. (2.64)

One should perform five circumambulations, and likewise, having sipped water according to the rule, one should worship the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors with the Vāma, Ghora, and Aja-śambara mantras.
One should perform libations in due order: for the gods at the *devatīrtha*, for the sages at the *ṛṣitīrtha*, and for the ancestors at the *pitṛtīrtha* during the sacrificial session.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rule, he stands firm. || 2-67 ||
The Śrī Rudra, the Puruṣasūkta, the Pañcabrahma, and the Ṣaḍaṅga [mantras].
Facing north and observing silence, having recited the syllable *gha* once, one situated within the cage of the *astra* mantra should perform the gathering of the sacred sites (*tīrtha*). (2.69)
The wearing of the purifier (pavitra):
One should perform all ritual acts with the purifier held in hand and observing silence, using either two, three, or five blades of *darbha* grass. (2.70)
Alternatively, one may prepare an auspicious and pure pavitra with seven [strands];
its tip should be four finger-breadths long, and the knot is prescribed to be one finger-breadth. (2.71)
One should attach a cord-loop measuring two finger-breadths to the ring finger;
its knot has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and the cord has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity. (2.72)
The tip [of the blade] has Rudra as its presiding deity; the deities of the purifier [the ring-finger] are the deities for entering the abode of worship.
Having taken kuśa grass and flowers, one should enter the sacrificial hall.
Having washed one's feet and sipped water, one should then perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna). [The Ash-Bath]
I shall now describe the ash-bath, which wards off all suffering.
The Cow-Mothers stood upon the earth for the purpose of bathing Śiva;
they were the embodiment of all the gods, pure, holy, and the destroyer of sins. (2.75)
The gift, the oblation, the food, and all that moves and is stationary exist within cows; now hear the procedure for their specific origin. (2.76)
Having recited the Gosāvitrī once, one should bow down and offer perfume, flowers, incense,
and a lamp at the feet of a cow with her calf.
One should offer a plaster made of *gorocanā* along with milk-rice;
then, having caused betel to be given, one should recite the *Gosāvitrī* mantra one hundred times.
We know him who has sharp horns; we meditate upon him whose feet are the Vedas.
May those cows inspire us.
Having thus propitiated the cow Satī, one should finally take hold of her tail.
With both hands, the Guru should hold a bilva leaf resting upon a lotus petal;
having grasped it with the Sadyojāta mantra, he should place it on the ground without letting it fall.
One should form a mass with the left hand and purify it with the Ghoramantra;
having burned it with the Puruṣamantra, one should enclose it with the Īśāna mantra. (2.81)
The *ketakī*, *mallikā*, *nāga*, *campaka*, and *pāṭala* flowers, as well as the *padma*, *palāśa*, *tulasī*, *apāmārga*, and the tips of *kuśa* grass. (2.82)
Having deposited his caste there, he should take possession of excellent vessels;
he should collect pure ashes produced from the *agnihotra* fire. (2.83)
Taking that ash while recollecting the Śiva-mantra, one should apply the ash with both hands bound in the Brahma-mudrās. (2.84)
Having placed it upon his right knee, he should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times;
[he should consecrate] the head with the Īśa-mantra and the face with the Tatpuruṣa-mantra.
The preceptor should sequentially dust the heart with the Ghora mantra, the secret place with the Vāma mantra, and all the limbs with the Sadyojāta mantra.
Bathing in water performed with these mantras is supremely excellent;
then follows the wearing of the garment.
Having discarded his former garment, he should take up a pure cloth.
Having thoroughly cleansed his hands and feet, the wise man should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
One should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the purification of all ritual actions.
Whatever merit is gained from bathing at all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices—
that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by smearing oneself with holy ashes and wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the dot-lamp (bindudīpa), the trident (triśūla), the half-moon (ardhacandraka),
and the smearing of all limbs with ash are declared to be the insignia of Śiva.
One should also apply a mark on the body with sandalwood mixed with ashes;
for initiated twice-born men, however, the *tripuṇḍra* should be six finger-breadths wide.
Listen as I describe the one hundred thousand characteristics of those who are not initiated but are worthy of description:
for Brāhmaṇas it is six finger-breadths, and for kings (Kṣatriyas) it is four finger-breadths. (2.92)
For Vaiśyas, it is declared to be two finger-breadths; for Śūdras, one finger-breadth.
For all others as well, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be like that of the Śūdras.
Kings and lords should duly apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with sandalwood mixed with ashes; now hear the measurements for its placement in due order.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be four finger-breadths wide on the forehead, the two arms, and the heart; at other locations, it should be one finger-breadth wide.
The teachers should hold pure ashes with both hands;
the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger are employed for the fashioning of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). (2.96)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Agni (Caru) are the presiding deities of the Tripuṇḍra;
it may be applied on the head, the forehead, the neck, or the ears.
One should place [the mantras] in sequence upon the chest, the two arms, the navel, and likewise the back; then on the two thighs, the two knees, and the two feet. (2.98)
Brahmā himself resides in the *brahmarandhra*, Subrahmaṇya on the forehead,
the god Vināyaka in the ear, and Soma and Sūrya in the two eyes.
Rudra and Viṣṇu are in the two arms, and likewise Īśvara is in the heart;
Durgādevī should be in the navel, and the Pitṛs likewise in the back.
On the two thighs are the Nāgas and likewise the Nāga maidens;
and on the pair of knees are the sages and their wives.
The seven oceans and all the sacred fords (tīrthas) reside in the two feet; the various sites of the Tripuṇḍra and the gods are likewise proclaimed [to be there]. (2.102)
One should place the sixteen-syllable mantra in those respective locations;
thus is declared the procedure for the ash-bath, which constitutes the yogic practices.
The first is said to be the seat (āsana), and the second is the rosary (akṣamālā).
The third is the bamboo staff, and the fourth is the yoga-band;
the water-pot shall be the fifth, and the upper garment the sixth.
The seventh is declared to be the uṣṇīṣa, and likewise the eighth is the upavīta;
the ninth is indeed the pavitra, and the tenth is celebrated as the bhasma.
The eleventh is the loincloth, the twelfth is the tooth-stick, and the thirteenth is the taking up of earth; their characteristics shall be described separately. (2.107)
Having fashioned a seat like a tortoise, either from lobha wood or even from dāruṇa, or indeed from khadira, candana, campaka, and bilva. (2-108)
And the four types of trees are described in the Āgama;
they are considered to have a width of two tālas and a height of six aṅgulas.
The feet have a height of two finger-breadths, and the shank is four finger-breadths long; the soles are like the surface of a mirror, and the backs of the feet are level with them. (2.110)
Thus is described the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana), the preliminary practice for yogis;
as well as the rosary before one (japamālā), the frontal garland (puromālā), and likewise the garland upon the head (śiromālā).
Listen now in order to the arm-garland, the hand-garland, and the neck-garland;
it is prescribed for those seeking liberation that they be made of twenty-five Rudrākṣas during recitation. (2-112)
Twenty-six [recitations] are for the sake of Śiva; twenty-seven for the sake of knowledge and the destruction of enemies;
twenty-eight for the sake of enjoyment and nourishment. (2.113)
Thirty beads for those seeking victory, and fifteen for the practice of sorcery;
thus indeed is the rosary for recitation. Now hear the characteristics of others. (2.114)

Starting from the neck and extending to the navel, there should be a necklace reaching the neck; the head-garland should have the same circumference as that, and the arm-garland should be equal to it as well. (2.115)
The *hastamālā* is its measure, and the *karṇamālā* is equal to that;
its sight destroys sin, and its touch bestows all perfections (*siddhi*). (2.116)
The merit from wearing rudrākṣas at all times is greater than that previously mentioned for other dhāraṇās;
whether pure or impure, one should always wear a rudrākṣa. (2-117)
If even a dog dies while wearing a rudrākṣa around its neck, it attains the state of Rudra;
how much more so, then, humans and others? || 2-118 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should always wear a rudrākṣa;
by wearing it, one attains heaven, and there is no further rebirth. (2-119)
He who dies while wearing [them] attains the supreme goal.
Now hear, O Maheśvara, regarding the origin and form of the rudrākṣas. (2-120)
For a thousand divine years, my eyes have been burning;
drops are released from my eyes and have fallen upon the earth.
The *bindus* are the trees of the Guru, and their fruit is said to be the *rudrākṣa*.
Śiva himself is the single face; through its wearing, the fruit is infinite. (2-122)
He who dies while maintaining [this practice] goes to the supreme state. That which has two faces is called Śakti; that which has three faces is called Nāda. (2.123)
The four-faced one is Bindu; Sadāśiva is five-faced;
Īśvara is said to be six-faced; and Rudra is remembered as seven-faced. (2.124)
Viṣṇu has eight faces, nine faces, and four faces;
from the nine-faced up to the one-faced, the deception increases a hundredfold at each stage.
On the hands, neck, crest-lock, ears, and sacred thread, one should always wear [ashes] together with the ash itself for the sake of pacifying all sins. (2.126)
O Lord, even talk of kings, talk of merchants, or talk of the world—especially when used to move a rudrākṣa bead—becomes fruitful as if accompanied by a mantra. (2.127)
He who constantly wears a rosary fashioned from thousands of rudrākṣa beads, which is the very form of Śiva, attains the supreme goal. (2.128)
Therefore, with every effort, one should always perform recitation with rudrākṣas;
[one should also use] a bamboo staff that is straight, smooth, and free from cracks or hollows.
For Brahmins, it should reach the height of the head; for kings (Kṣatriyas), it should be level with the chest;
for Vaiśyas, it should reach the arms; and for Śūdras, it should reach the navel. (2.130)
Thus has the staff been described; now hear about this yogic belt (*yogapaṭṭa*).
The best is made of tiger skin, while the middling is composed of black antelope skin. (2.131)
Alternatively, a threefold yoga-band (yogapaṭṭikā) should be made from threads;
its width should be three finger-breadths, and its measurement should be like that of a sacred thread (upavīta).
The procedure for the yogic belt has been declared; now hear the procedure for the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), [including] the characteristics of the water-pot.
Filled with an *āḍhaka*, it is excellent; filled with three *prasthas*, it is middling. (2-134)
The smallest measurement for a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) is two prasthas;
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
The water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) should be fashioned exactly as described in the treatises on arts and crafts.
One should have the upper garment and the turban made of pure cloth.
The sacred thread (yajñopavīta) should be made of gold or, alternatively, of white woven threads.
One should wear the sacred thread (upavīta) and the upper garment (uttarīya) with the heart-mantra alone;
the purifier (pavitra) has already been described previously—this is the procedure for the ancillaries of worship (arcanāṅga).
Listen to the procedure for the constituent parts of worship:
the seat, the prostration, the water offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, incense, the lamp, and the food offering (naivedya); these are proclaimed as the eight limbs. (2-139)
One should constantly worship Dakṣiṇeśvara with the eightfold offering; at the conclusion of the worship, one should present the oblation as prescribed in the proximity [of the deity]. (2.140)
That which ends with the word "śānta" and that which ends with the word "bali" are said to be the three kinds of worship.
[Now follow] the materials for the foot-washing (pādya).
Uśīra, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and likewise white mustard seeds. || 2-141 ||
That which is endowed with four ingredients is declared to be the water for the feet (pādya).
[Next are] the materials for the sipping-water (ācamana-dravya).
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, nutmeg, and likewise the fruit of the jasmine tree.
Takola, kuṣṭha, candana, and pāṭalī, together with these nine ingredients, are declared to constitute the *ācamanīyaka*. (2.143)
The materials for the *arghya* offering are the tips of *kuśa* grass, milk, water, barley, and likewise half a *siddhārtha* (white mustard seed);
as well as *bilva* leaves, sesame, rice, *tulasī*, and unhusked rice. (2.144)
The *arghya* is said to consist of ten ingredients; these are the fragrant substances:
aloe wood (*agaru*), sandalwood (*candana*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and nutmeg (*koṣṭha*).
These should be combined with camphor (*karpūra*) in either half or one-quarter proportion. (2.146)
The characteristics of flowers are declared to be as follows:
white, reddish, and black correspond to the three qualities of sattva and the rest.
A white flower is sāttvika, while a red flower is rājasa. (2.148)
A black flower is tāmasa, while a yellow flower is auspicious;
one should especially wear flowers that are rājasa and possess leaves.
Flowers appropriate for the season.
One should offer the *nandyāvarta*, *punnāga*, and white *arka* at sunrise;
likewise, the *karavīra*, the lotus (*padma*), *dhurtūra*, and *bṛhatī*. (2.150)
One should especially offer *droṇa* flowers at midday;
and in the evening, one should employ *campaka*, *mallikā*, and *dhūrtūra*.
Having employed the *jātī* and the red lotus at midnight, one should collect all flowers, [but] excluding those flowers that are to be avoided. (2.152)
Overripe, underripe, unopened buds, and likewise those that are defective; || 2-153 ||
One should avoid flowers that are pierced by hair-pins, covered by spider-silk threads, those that have fallen off on their own, or those that have been sprinkled with water. (2.154)
The Flower of Distinction.
Among all varieties of flowers, the mountain flower is preeminent;
among all varieties of leaves, the bilva leaf is preeminent. (2-155)
(Regarding flowers that are not remnants of previous offerings:
Having washed tulasī, bilva leaves, palāśa, and suvarṇaka, one should worship the Supreme Lord again and again. (2.156)
(The leaves: Tulasī, Kṛṣṇatulasī, Sahadevī, Māthavī, Kapāmārga, Śamī, Dalikā, and Āmalākarī. (2-157)
Lakṣmī, Dūrvājaṭī, and especially Hastilakṣaṇī—these are proclaimed as the principal leaves, particularly so. (2.158)
Among all leaves, both the bilva and the two types of tulasī should be gathered;
the leaf is said to be dear to Brahmā, and the bilva is likewise dear to Viṣṇu.
O Rudra, fruit is declared to be dear; indeed, one should avoid all violence.
For the sake of Śiva’s worship, one should collect leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth. (2.160)
There should be no injury to medicinal herbs, nor should one be a harmer of them;
thus has the procedure for flowers been declared [as well as the substances for incense]. (2-161)
Listen to the ritual procedure for incense substances.
Aloe wood, guggulu resin, exudate, sandalwood, molasses, honey, bilva fruit, a cow-pen, uśīra root, and cow’s ghee. (2.162)
The ritual for incense substances has been declared; now the ritual for the lamp is being described:
it consists of cow's ghee or oil combined with a wick made of fragrant cotton. (2.163)
The flame of the lamp is distinguished by a length of four, three, or two finger-breadths;
for the Blessed One, the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, is fond of lamps. (2-164)
Thereafter, O Maheśvara, listen as I shall explain the five purities—
the five purities.
First is the purification of the self, and second is the purification of the site. (2-165)
The third is the purification of substances, the fourth is the purification of the *liṅga*, and the fifth is the purification of mantras; these shall be explained individually. (2-166)
Facing north, silent, firmly established in a bound yogic posture,
and having performed the binding of the ten directions while reciting the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), each consisting of ten measures (mātrā);
this is the procedure for prāṇāyāma.
I shall describe the sequence of breath control (prāṇāyāma); listen thus, O Maheśvara. (2.168)
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka) are considered the threefold [breath control].
Exhalation has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and inhalation has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
The movement of the moon and the sun therein is dependent upon the states of death and birth;
the *iḍā* is to be known as a digit of the moon, and the *piṅgalā* as a portion of the sun.
The filling of the two [nostrils] by the wind constitutes the two mandalas;
exhalation (recaka) is accompanied by emission (sūcaka), while inhalation (pūraka) is based on death (mṛtaka). || 2-171 ||
Upon hearing of birth or death impurity (*sūtaka* or *pretaka*), one should not perform worship or fire oblations (*homa*).
There is no presence [of the deity] in such a state; therefore, now [one must act] according to the prescribed rule. (2-172)
Therefore, O Maheśvara, act with all your ancient power to destroy Candra and Arka; I shall describe the destruction of Candra and Arka—listen thus. (2-173)
The time of the destruction of the moon and the sun.
For one who is devoted to the pervasive *kumbhaka*, constant in silence and action, firm of mind, and always engaged in meditation, there is the destruction of the moon and the sun. (2.174)
Having set aside the impurities of death and birth until the formal decision is announced, one should worship Śiva for as long as the sun and moon endure. (2.175)

The invocation and the seat for him should consist of twelve *mātrās*; the water for the feet (*pādya*) should consist of five *mātrās*, and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) should consist of three *mātrās*. (2.176)
The water for the guest-offering (arghya) should last for one measure; the offering of fragrance for six measures;
the flower for twelve measures; and the incense for fifteen moments. (2.177)

One should perform the offering of a lamp for six measures and the oblation of clarified butter for sixteen measures during the eclipses of the moon and the sun; these constitute the ten duties to be performed.
One should offer the bath, the garment, and the three sacred threads according to the prescribed rule;
this is proclaimed as the ritual of the oblation (homa) accompanied by the twelve measures (mātrā).

Recitation accompanied by one hundred and eight *mātrās* is declared to be the procedure for the ancillaries of worship (*arcanāṅgavidhi*). Listen now to the characteristics of worship (*arcanālakṣaṇa*).

It bestows longevity, wealth, grain, and so forth; it brings about the destruction of enemies and is auspicious; because it causes the gratification of the gods, it is called the means for accomplishing everything. (2-181)
Whether pure or impure, whether in good health or ill, one may perform worship at all times, by day or by night; there is no restriction on that practice. (2.182)
Having performed the destruction of the moon and sun, one should worship at all times;
O God Maheśvara, through the destruction of the moon and sun, there is success in worship.
Having paid obeisance to the Guru-deity, one should bind the foot-seal (pādamudrikā).
The area from the knees up to the navel is said to be the station of the earth. (2-184)

The region of water extends up to the navel; the region of fire extends to the end of the throat; the region of air extends to the end of the forehead; and twelve finger-breadths above that is the region of ether. (2.185)
It has been stated that the five locations, beginning with the earth, are situated in space.
These fivefold locations have been proclaimed; now hear of the mandalas in their proper order. (2-186)
The mandalas of the elements, beginning with earth, are respectively square, half-moon, triangle, hexagon, and circle. (2.187)
Yellow, white, red, smoke-colored, and black, respectively;
and the seed-syllables, according to the rule, are La, Va, Ra, Ya, and Ha.
At the tip of the crest, twelve finger-breadths long and resembling pure crystal, resides the knowledge of Śiva known as Naṭeśa, which has the nature of the very essence of Śiva. (2.189)
Having joined [the self] to the extremely subtle Śiva-tattva, one should burn away the body.
The first knot is at the knees, and the second is situated at the navel.
The third is the throat-knot, the fourth is the *larlāka*;
the fifth is the head-knot; their severance is performed with the weapon-mantra. (2.191)
First, having recollected the seed-syllable of fire, one should join it with the seed-syllable of fire;
then, having recollected the seed-syllable of wind, one should cut through the five knots. (2-192)
And with the mantra "huṃ phaṭ," one should encircle the five knots;
having meditated upon the body as dry wood and the seed-syllable of fire. (2-193)
Having recollected the seed-syllable of fire, surrounded by garlands of flames, and having meditated upon it as a heap of ashes, one should meditate on the form of Maheśvarī. (2.194)
Having meditated upon [the deity] resembling the lunar disc, seated upon a white lotus,
and having the form of a mass of ashes, one should fashion the foot-seal (pādamudrā).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, as well as the elements beginning with earth—one should contemplate them all within the Brahman. (2.196)
The Brahma-nāḍī, slender like a lotus fiber, is situated at the place of the Śiva-tattva; having meditated upon the mandala of space there, [one proceeds]. (2-197)
Having recollected the seed-syllable of the Moon, one should then flood [the body] with nectar;
it becomes like milk, having the form of nectar, filling [it] completely up to the tips of the toes. (2.198)
Then, through the practice of yoga, one should contemplate the seed-syllable Oṃ as being without parts and facing downward;
by means of that, one should meditate upon oneself as being completely immersed and thus full. (2.199)
One should first bring the self—the auspicious body consisting of right knowledge and the abode of all beings—into [the heart], and afterwards one should contemplate the body. (2-200)
Thereafter, the assumption of the form of the Teacher shall occur for the practitioners;
having meditated upon that state, one should then fashion the gnosis-mudrā (jñānamudrā).
O Maheśvara, listen now to the description of the support and the supported:
above that is a triangle, above that a hexagon, and above that three circles.
The characteristic of the support (ādhāra) is said to be in the opposite corner and above;
the former consists of four syllables, while the latter consists of six syllables. (2.203)
The syllable, which is called the name of all phonemes, consists of the meaning of the sacred tradition (āmnāya) and is auspicious;
its form is circular like a lotus fiber, and its nature is that of light. (2-204)
Abiding upon the support that is the sixfold foundation of another's abode, its form is like a lotus fiber, circular and consisting of the nature of light. (2-205)
The primordial form, beginning with the letter *a* and ending with *kṣa*, is well-determined;
it is the self situated in the midst of the vowels (*aṃsānām*), whose essential nature is changeless. (2-206)
Empty at the beginning and end, stainless, adorned with serpent ornaments, beginningless, established as the support, circular, and having the form of a seed-syllable. (2-207)
One should place the four-syllabled mantra, beginning with *dyau* and ending with *sadya*, as the most excellent seed;
having assigned the syllables within the triangle, one should place the syllable beginning with *sadya* in the center.
One should bind [the disciple] with the primordial seed-syllable and perform the placement according to the prescribed method;
having performed the placement of the hexagon and so forth, one should place the six-syllable mantra in sequence. (2.209)
One should place the ten-syllable mantra, beginning with the seed-syllable of Ḍambha and ending with Phaṇa,
as well as the circle and the perimeter, in their proper sequence.

Having placed eleven syllables within the circle, one should place the radiant [syllable] in the middle of the circle; specifically, in the middle of the circle, one should place the seed-syllables of mind, speech, and body.
Beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *ā*,
one should arrange the sixteen letters in sequence within a circle upon another circle.

The instructor, having placed the seed-syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *kṣa* within the triangle, should place the three syllables in sequence starting from the upper corner and proceeding downwards. (2.213)
Having thus meditated on the visualization of the syllables facing southward,
one should then fashion the foot-seal (pādamudrā) and the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā).
One should meditate upon [the deity] before oneself; now listen to the procedure for the mental worship.
Having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), one should carry out all the rites.
Having first formed the Brahma-mudrā, one should purify [the hands] with the seed-syllable of fire;
one should purify the palms and backs of both hands with the Astra-mantra. || 2.216 ||
One should assign Īśāna and the other [deities] in sequence from the thumb to the little finger;
one should assign the six limbs in sequence from the little finger to the thumb.
With both hands, one should bind the mantra-mudrā and the Great Sound (Mahānāda);
this is called the Sadyāntaka placement, beginning with the little finger, which is the placement of withdrawal (saṃhāra).

The ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is said to begin with the thumb and end with the little finger; for celibate students and householders, the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) is prescribed.
For forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and ascetics (*yatī*), the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is said to be the "withdrawal" (*saṃhāra*).
One should place the limbs of Śiva in sequence, starting from the middle finger and ending with the index finger. (2-220)
This, however, is called the *pānaprastha* placement, which is the placement of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-nyāsa*).
One should place the limbs of Śiva in sequence from the middle finger to the tip of the index finger. (2.221)
Having established this Pānaprastha [mandala] extended according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should subsequently place the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) in sequence, beginning with the thumb.
Thereafter, one should place the Prāsāda [mantra] upon the fingers and their joints;
having first placed the Mūla-prakṛti, one should then place [the others] as before.
Having applied an ointment of sandalwood and adorned [the image] with fragrant flowers,
he should recite the Śiva-mantra many times and then bind on the Brahma-finger-ring.
Having recollected the root seed-syllable and having written down the letter and its form, one should touch all the limbs, beginning with the head, with both hands while holding the mantra. (2.225)
One should perform the placement (vinyāsa) of the phoneme-mantra (varṇa-mantra), the digit-mantra (kalā-mantra), and the aggregate-mantra (piṇḍa-mantra).
O Maheśvara, listen now to this specific procedure for the phoneme-mantra. (2.226)
The mantra of the syllables.

Uttering the letters beginning with *śa* and ending with *sa*, followed by those from *sa* down to the end of the earth (*pṛthvī*), and then the *ca*-group beginning with its third letter and ending with *va*. (2.227)

One should utter in sequence [the syllables] ending in the sixteenth [vowel], beginning with the moon [the letter *a*], starting from the creation [the letter *ka*], ending with the first [consonant *ka*], ending with *ha*, ending with *la*, and ending with *sa*. (2-228)
The seed-syllable of Brahmā ends with the visarga; it is the fifth seed-syllable of Brahmā.
Joined with bindu and nāda, this is the auspicious syllable-mantra (varṇa-mantra). || 2-229 ||
(32) Thus indeed [having explained] the mantra of the phonemes, listen now to the sequential placement (nyāsa) of the phonemes:
having placed the letter *a* on the crown of the head, one should place the letter *ā* on the forehead. (2.230)
The letter *i* is in the right eye, the letter *ī* in the left eye;
the letter *u* is in the right nostril, and the letter *ū* in the left nostril.
One should place the syllable *ṛ* in the right ear and the syllable *ṝ* in the left ear;
the syllable *ḷ* in the right cheek and the syllable *ḹ* in the left cheek.
Having placed the syllable *e* on the upper lip, one should place the syllable *ai* on the lower lip;
the syllable *o* on the upper teeth, and the syllable *au* on the lower teeth. (2.233)
The syllable *aṃ* is at the root of the palate, and the syllable *aḥ* is at the tip of the palate;
the *ka*-group is on the right hand, and the *ca*-group is on the left hand.
The *ṭa*-group shone on his right foot, the *ta*-group on his left foot; the *pa*-group was on his right side, and the *ba*-group on his left side. (2.235)
One should place the syllable *ma* at the region of the navel and the syllable *ya* on the skin;
the syllable *ra* at the region of the blood and the syllable *la* at the region of the flesh. (2.236)
The letter *va* is in the region of the fat; the letter *śa* is in the region of the sinews;
the letter *ṣa* is in the region of the marrow; and the letter *sa* is in the region of the semen. (2.237)
The syllable *ha* is said to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*); one should place it between the eyebrows.
The syllable *la* is at the region of the genitals, and the syllable *kṣa* should be placed in the anus. (2.238)
The ritual placement of the digits (kalānyāsa).
Now, listen to the procedure for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the digits (kalā) as taught in the sequence of the scripture:
having uttered the twelfth seed-syllable, one should then recite the root mantra. (2.239)
Recalling the five Brahmans in their proper sequence, one should contemplate the Kalā-mantras,
which possess the forms of the five Brahmans.
I shall describe the form of the five Brahmās; listen thus, O Maheśvara.
Resembling pure crystal, with four faces and four arms, radiant with ornaments of necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and earrings. (2.241)
He wears a crown of gomedaka gems and a white sacred thread;
he is endowed with a shield and a chisel, and his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Resplendent with the luster of the new moon, having the form of one just born,
arisen from Vāmadeva, red in color, four-faced, and four-armed.
An anklet resplendent with tinkling sounds, as well as a waist-belt and a girdle; a crown of coral and a golden sacred thread.
He is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding a noose and a *ṭaṅka* in his two hands;
he has three eyes, possesses triple grace, and is adorned with earrings.
This indeed is the essential nature of Vāmadeva as the embodiment of mantra;
it is the Aghora face on the right, formidable and possessing a luster like crushed collyrium.
Having eight arms, three eyes, and four faces, he wears matted locks;
he is clad in red garments and has a red upper cloth.
With limbs smeared with red sandalwood and adorned with a red garland, he holds a trident, a vetāla, a sword, and a discus in his right hands. (2.248)
With his left hands he holds a serpent, spittle, a bell, and a gesture of amazement;
likewise, he wears a blue ring and a serpent as a sacred thread.
Thus, one should contemplate the person who is the essential form of the Aghora mantra, having the appearance of saffron-colored space, with four faces and four arms. (2.250)
Holding a chisel in the right hand and a lotus, a hand-drum, and a garland in the left, he has three eyes, a gentle face, and a slightly smiling countenance. (2.251)
The sacrificial ring, the golden upper garment,
the pearl crown, and the ruby finger-ring—
this is the essential nature of the mantra-form of the Puruṣa-mantra.
Having ten arms, three eyes, five faces, and wearing matted hair.
Holding a vajra, a trident, a staff, and a sword in his right hands, and holding a noose, a goad, and a hand-drum in his left hands. (2.254)
He wears a crown of rubies and finger-rings of ruby;
he is gentle, with a complexion like crystal, and possesses the form of Īśāna.
The form of Aghora is fierce, while the remaining [forms] are declared to be gentle.
That gentle form is the nature of Brahman; it is the supreme cause of creation. (2.256)
Vāma is indeed the supreme Vaiṣṇava [aspect], the cause of preservation;
Aghora, on the other hand, is said to be the form of Rudra, the cause of dissolution.
The limb of Īśvara is the Puruṣa, which bestows sovereignty;
likewise, Sadāśiva and Īśāna are the bestowers of great liberation. || 2-258 ||

Thus [ends the section on] Brahmā as the presiding deity; now hear the procedure for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the kalās, the supreme kalās consisting of the Vedas, and the Tantric mantra of the kalās. 2-259.
One should install the power of the parts (kalāśakti) upon the Lord of the South by means of the parts;
the Brahmas of the parts have the form of males, while the powers (śaktis) have the form of maidens. (2.260)
Their lotus-like hands are adorned with the *sṛṇi*, noose, boon-granting gesture (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*);
they are complete with all ornaments and graced by crowns.
The kalās of Īśāna are five; those of the fourfold Puruṣa are four;
the kalās of Aghora are eight; and Vāmadeva has thirteen. (2.262)
There are eight *sadyakalās* and these thirty-eight *kalās*. I shall now describe the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the power of the *kalās* according to their sequence; listen. (2.263)
One should duly place these five digits (kalās) in sequence: Śaśinī, Icchāṅgadā, Iṣṭā, Marīcikā, and Jvālinī. (2.264)
First the south, then the north, and likewise the west; finally, one should well-place the five [deities] in the positions of the zenith and Īśāna. (2.265)
Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti are the four kalās;
one should assign these powers of Puruṣa to the four faces. (2.266)
In the east, the south, the north, and the west, there is the end of delusion and the destruction of ignorance; death, illusion, and fearlessness arise from this. (2.267)
One should place these digits (kalās) of Aghora in the heart and other locations:
specifically in the heart, the throat, and likewise on the two shoulders. (2.268)
In the abdomen, in the navel, and likewise in the posterior part, as well as in the chest—in these eight locations, it will be explained in due order. (2-269)
Rajārakṣā, Arati, Pālīkāma, and Samyagā;
then Kāryābuddhi, Kriyādhātrī, and Bhrāmiṇī. (2-270)
Mohinī and Abhayā are the left [hands]; these are the thirteen kalās.
[They are placed] on the penis, the anus, the two thighs, the two knees, and the two shanks. (2.271)
Thereafter, one should place Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, and likewise Medhā, in sequence upon the two buttocks, the waist, and the two sides. (2.272)
Kānti, Svadhā, and Sthiti—these are the Kalās of Sadyojāta;
one should place them on the feet, the hands, the breasts, and the armpits.
Having meditated upon the form consisting of Śiva, which comprises thirty-six principles (*tattva*), one should then place the *piṇḍa* mantras in their respective locations. (2.274)
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
having placed Aghora on the heart, one should place Vāmadeva on the private parts. (2.275)
Having placed the unborn [syllable] at the feet, one should again place the limbs;
having placed the heart at the heart, one should place the head at the head. (2.276)
Having placed the *śikhā* [mantra] upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*), one should place the *kavaca* [mantra] on the two breasts;
the *netra* [mantra] is placed on the eyes, and the binding of the ten directions is performed with the *astra* [mantra]. (2.277)
Listen now to the seed-syllables of the five Brahmās and the six limbs in their proper order;
they are within the group of space-seeds, excluding the six syllables. (2.278)
The first is declared to be Ajāta; the third is called Vāma; Aghora is declared to be the fifth; and the eleventh would be Tara. (2-279)
The thirteenth syllable is declared to be Īśāna, the seed-syllable of Brahmā;
the second is said to be the heart, and the fourth shall be the face.
The six-syllable mantra is the crest-mantra (śikhā), the twelfth is the armor-mantra (kavaca),
the tenth is declared to be the eye-mantra (netra), and likewise the sixteenth is the weapon-mantra (astra).
Accompanied by the utterances *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *auṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*, one should likewise perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) for the purpose of protection. (2.282)
O Maheśvara, listen now to the colors of the six-limbed deities:
white, pale yellow, red, black, lightning-like, and saffron-colored. (2.283)
He has four arms and three eyes, and is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
he holds a skull, a trident, the gesture of granting boons, and an axe in his hands.
The *astra* and *netra* [mantras] are fierce (*raudra*), while the remaining ones are known as gentle (*saumya*).
One should offer perfume, flowers, and incense with the *varṇa-mantra*. (2.285)
Having meditated upon the intrinsic nature [of the deity], one should worship it; immediately thereafter, one should employ the *jñānamudrā*.
Afterward, one should recite the *piṇḍamantra*; now hear the cause of the seed-syllables (*bīja*). (2.286)
The Hero, ending with the seed-syllable, with the internal resonance (nāda) as its sixteenth mora—this auspicious Piṇḍamantra is the mantra that embodies all mantras. (2.287)
Having recited [the mantra] once and meditated upon Śiva, one should bind the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā).
[Now follow] the various types of liṅgas.
I shall explain the sequence of the differentiation of the genders specifically, according to their proper order. (2.288)
The liṅga is said to be of two kinds: mobile and likewise immobile. One should always worship the Supreme Lord residing within the mobile liṅga. (2-289)
In the case of a stationary linga, one should perform worship before it preceded by the consecration of the mantra;
however, a linga devoid of the consecration of the mantra is merely a physical form.
The supreme teacher, the god Maheśvara, is the specific mobile liṅga;
the liṅga is said to be of two kinds: stationary and mobile. (2.291)
Through the disparagement of the mobile [liṅga], the immobile becomes fruitless;
the two types of mobile liṅgas are said to be the elder [disciple] and the preceptor. (2.292)
The two lords, Jyeṣṭha and Ācārya, are the causes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; among these masters, O Maheśvara, the Jaṅgama is the most excellent. (2.293)
Therefore, with every effort, one should always worship the form of the Lord;
and for the sake of both [worldly and spiritual] goals, one should worship the reality known as Sādākhya.
The true nature of the reality of existence is the supreme Sadākhya; beyond that is the pure Maheśvara, who is Sadāśiva, the form of all the gods. (2-295)
Having abandoned the previous form, one should indeed assume the form called Sādākhya;
and above that Sādākhya, one should place the form of Nṛka.

Having always meditated upon the one who has assumed human form, whose abode is the south and so forth, who is of the nature of light, who eternally dances, and who is the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; (2-297)
That supreme state, which brings about all prosperity, consists of nine syllables;
it is always four-armed, ending with the letter *n*, and is the cause of one who is anointed by the *nāda*. (2.298)
Having meditated upon the auspicious supreme Nirvāṇa, which is eternally Śiva for all gods, and upon the form of Sādākhya, one should [meditate] on Naṭeśvara in the center. (2-299)
Having established within the center of the heart-lotus the system of *nāda*, which consists of the *kalās*,
[one should meditate on it] as having one face, four arms, two feet, and a circular middle.
Having uttered the phoneme-mantra, one should contemplate the reality known as Sādākhya—the pure essence, ninefold in nature, immovable, and the size of a thumb. (2.301)
The individual self (ātman) resides in the letter *sa*; the inner self (antarātman) is the *bindu*;
the supreme self (paramātman) resides in the seed-syllable of space (*kha*); and the *nāda* consists of sixteen measures (*mātrā*). (2.302)
Having worshipped everything in due order with the heart-mantra,
one should perform the deposition of the thirty-eight parts (kalās) along with the mantra consisting of thirty-eight aspects.
Listen now to the sequence of the thirty-eight-fold ritual placement (*nyāsa*), which purifies the body and consists of the mantra for the internal sacrifice. (2.304)
One should place the *yoga* and the mantra recited by men in their respective positions in sequence;
this is declared to be the sequence for the purification of the self (*ātmaśuddhi*), while [the following] is the purification of the site (*sthānaśuddhi*).
Listen to the sequence for purifying the site:
one should dig the ground to the depth of a cubit and fill it back up gradually with that same earth;
having thoroughly examined it in many ways, one should avoid lumps of clay, stones, and the like. (2–306)
Having made the ground level, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
it should be provided with a canopy and banners, and furnished with plantain trees and *kṛmuka* trees.
One should sprinkle with water mixed with *kuśa* grass that which is joined with a garland of *darbha*, adorned with strings of pearls, and strewn with flower garlands. (2.308)
The sequence for the purification of the site has been declared; now hear the sequence for the purification of the ritual substances:
the vessel for bathing, the vessel for rinsing the mouth, and the vessel for the *argha* offering.
One should purify the vessel for the general *arghya* offering and the water jar with the *hṛdaya-mantra*; then, having inspected them, one should envelop them with the *kavaca-mantra*. (2.310)
Then, having rinsed all the vessels with water, one should fill them;
having brought them filled with water, one should perform the *kuru-mudrā* and the *saurabhī*.
Having recited the heart-mantra, one should offer perfume and flowers;
then, having bound the Saurabhī mudrā, one should sequentially place the root-syllable.
Then, having purified the upper part, one should place the temple mantra (prāsādamantra).
One should offer the bell, incense, and lamps with the Īśāna mantra.
Having sprinkled all the ritual substances with *kuśa* grass,
the auspicious one should sprinkle the area around the site and place the incense burner there.
To the east of the incense burner is Prajāpati Vanaspati; to the western part of the vessels, the place for the bell (khaṇṭā) is proclaimed.
The presiding deities of the bell are Vasu, Soma, and Yama; thus the purification of materials has been fully described. Now listen to the worship of the Earth-goddess.
One should worship the Earth Deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings by her own name—she who faces the eastern direction, is pure, and is seated upon a lotus throne. (2.317)
One should wash the three vessels, beginning with the foot-basin, using the *astra-mantra*;
having filled them with pure water, one should perform the solar placement (*saura-nyāsa*).
Uttering the seed-syllable of fire ending with the visarga, followed by "astrāya phaṭ," one should thoroughly purify the ground, the seat, and the right and left hands.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in sequence the root mantra and the six limbs:
the Praṇava joined with Vāyu (Ya), and the syllable that is the end of La (Kṣa). (2.320)
With six dots (anusvāras), a long vowel at the base, and again joined with its head;
preceded by space (the letter *ha*) and ending with the visarga—this is the Sūrya-mantra, concluding with *namaḥ*. (2–321)
One should place the Heart-mantra, joined with the *sāntabindu* (the nasal dot), upon the heart;
having placed [the mantra] for the head of Arka, one should place the *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ* upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*). (2.322)

Having placed the *hrūṃ* syllable as the armor-mantra, one should place the three-eyed mantra (*trinetra*) and the seed-syllable of fire (*agnibīja*) ending with the visarga, conjoined with the solar weapon-mantra (*saurāstra*).
One should worship the imperishable Śiva conjoined with the *kāntabindu*;
having uttered the single *abindu*, one should recite *khaṣolka* ending with *sūrya*. (2.324)
With this mantra, one should cause the offering of both perfume and flowers;
with the ten-syllable mantra, one should worship up to the incense with red sandalwood. (2-325)
Having established the venerable one, listen to the sequence of meditation on Sūrya:
he has one face, two arms, and two eyes, and he holds a lotus. (2.326)
Having established a circle of fire, [one should visualize the deity] clothed in radiant red garments,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament.
O Maheśvara, one should meditate upon my form, the Great Soul, red in color, with four faces and eight arms, like the lord of the day (the sun). || 2.328 ||
He has three eyes and four arms; he is the slayer of the demon Amogha and the maker of day.
He is mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven horses—the maker of light and the illuminator.
It is endowed with the enclosure of Uṣā, possessed of a multitude of radiance, joined with Medhā and Prajñā, and provided with the houses beginning with Soma. (2-330)
The Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—in this sequence, these are the destroyers of houses and death. (2–331)
Soma is the color of cow’s milk; Aṅgāra is red-colored;
Budha is said to be dark-colored; and Bṛhaspati is blue-colored. (2–332)
Venus is the color of a jasmine flower or a white moon; Saturn is black in color;
Rāhu resembles a dark cloud; and Ketu is said to have the appearance of smoke.
All are seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), endowed with all the [major] marks, fully adorned with all ornaments, and are proclaimed to have two arms. (2-334)
Soma is in the northern quarter, Bhārgava in the eastern direction, Aṅgāraka in the southern quarter, and Bṛhaspati in the west. (2-335)
One should place Śanaiścara in the southwest, Rāhu in the southeast,
Ketu in the southwest direction, and Budha in the northwest.
One should place a chariot and a reddish-brown horse in front;
one should then install Prabhā, Uṣā, Sandhyā, and Prajñā. (2.337)
One should worship Ravi, Sūrya, and Caṇḍeśa in the northeastern direction;
then one should worship the eight world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective locations.
One should offer all [substances] such as perfumes and flowers by means of their own names;
having performed the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and worship, one should likewise present the water for honor (arghya). || 2-339 ||
The ritual for the worship of the Sun has been declared; now hear the characteristics of its methods.
O Maheśvara, hear likewise the names of these five types.
The first is the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala), the second is the inner necklace (antarhāra), the third is the middle necklace (madhyahāra), and the fourth is the boundary (maryāda). || 2-341 ||
And the fifth is proclaimed as Mahāmaryādaka;
now hear the measurements of these ramparts in their proper order.
The measurement of the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala) should be half a daṇḍa;
the inner necklace (antarhāra) should be one daṇḍa, and the middle necklace (madhyahāra) two daṇḍas.
The boundary shall be fourteen *daṇḍas* [in length], and the fifth [side] shall be seventeen *daṇḍas*.
The location of the well shall be in the second enclosure wall, in the direction of the Lord of the Quarters (the East).
Between Indra and Agni, the place of wealth is proclaimed;
between Agni and Yama, the clothing hall is prescribed. (2.345)
The place of rest is said to be between Vāyu and Soma;
in the north of Mahāmaryādaka, the great pavilion is said to be located.

The construction of a pavilion (maṇḍapa) in a certain location according to the desire of the sacrificer, the characteristics of the enclosure wall, and the worship of the gateway have been proclaimed. (2–347)
Then one should worship Śiva, who is situated in the midst of the Śaṅkhanidhi.
On the right side is Bhava, resembling the kunda flower or the moon;
behind him is Padmanidhi, who stands firmly in the middle on the left side.
Above the door, one should worship the Lords of Obstacles (Vighneśas) who bestow all accomplishments:
Vighneśvara, Vīra, Śūra, and Kapardina. (2–350)
Kaṃbugrīva, Varada, Hastivaktra, Anantara, Kṣipraprasādana, Nāma, Avighna, Kavi, and Vināyaka. (2–351)
And the colors of the ten obstacles will be described individually:
white, black, red, coral-red, and blue. (2.352)
Smoke-colored, like the rising sun, pearl, and topaz;
Brahmā is the presiding deity there at the southern door-panel. (2-353)
Viṣṇu shall be the presiding deity of the northern door-panel; Rudra shall be the presiding deity of the central plank. (2-354)
