The pair of footprints on the two door-panels is said to have Kūrma as its presiding deity;
for the fastening of the door-panels, the two deities Śiva and Jyotsnā are the presiding deities.
For the removal of the door-panels, the two deities are Mūrti and Ketana;
for all the cloths, the presiding deity is Subrahmaṇya Maheśvara.
For the wooden planks and the deities, Vāyu is the presiding deity there;
having worshipped them with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), one should then bind them with good milk. (2.357)
The two door-rings are said to have the Sun and Moon as their presiding deities;
the eight mountain deities reside within the middle of the door-bolt.
Eight nāgas are proclaimed as the ornaments of the door panels;
one should worship the deities of the doorways (or the door-path) with their respective names. (2-359)
While reciting the Netra-mantra, he should offer the two bracelets [to Sūrya and Someśa],
as well as perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and an oblation of clarified butter.
Afterwards, the wise practitioner should insert the left hand into the southern door-panel;
with the wind-mantra, he should cause the tantras to become mobile.
One should worship the deities stationed at all the door-bolts in this manner:
the deities of the southern gate, as well as the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas. (2–362)
At the western gate are the gods and the divine sages;
at the northern gate are the gods, along with the syllables Vaṣaṭ, Oṃ, and the Vyāhṛtis.
At the fourth door of the primary nature, one should first offer salutations saying "namaḥ śarvāya";
then, on the right side, one should worship the deity Vīrabhadra.
On the northern side are Śivajyotis and Vināyaka;
at the southern gate are the gods, Marutas, Daityas, and Dānavas.
At the western gate are the gods Suyaśas and Devavidumā;
at the northern gate are the gods Adbhuta, Nala, and Rudraka. (2-366)
In the second Prakṛta-gate are the Āgnesundara deities;
on the right side of the Pārśva deities are the Nīlalohita deities.
On the northern side are the deities of the gods, with Kālabhairava as the presiding deity;
at the southern gate are the deities of the gods, for the sake of Śivānanda and Amṛta.
At the western gate was Sākṣī, the witness of the gods, for the sake of those who love truth;
and at the northern gate were the peaceful hosts of gods from of old. (2.369)
First is the door, the procedure for the worship of the door.
Listen to the procedure for the worship of the door:
one should worship Sarasvatī above the door, and likewise Vṛṣabha at its front. (2–370)
In front of that, one should worship the ten lords of obstacles (Vighneśas) and the trident;
Nandīśa on the right side and Mahākāla on the left.
In the middle is the Tīrtha called Danteśvara; Kamalavāsinī is at the southern gate of the gods, as are Daṇḍin and Muṇḍin, O beautiful one.
For the deities of the western gate, Ananta and Paśupati shall be present;
for the deities of the northern gate, Bhrukuṭī, Jaya, and Bhairava.
One should worship Śrīdevī in the upper portion and Bhūmidevī below;
one should worship Jñānaśakti and Kriyāśakti at the entrance to the womb.
Having thus performed the worship of the doors, one should thereafter worship the maṇḍala;
with the mantra beginning "vāstoṣpate," one should worship the deity Vāstu in the northeast.
Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should strike the great bell.
The deities of the jewels are the Vasus, the gods Sūrya, Soma, and Agni.
At the time of worship, one should produce the great sound of bells;
by that great sound, there is the destruction of the rākṣasas.

The *liṅga* is to be known as sevenfold, as prescribed in the scriptures: the stationary (*sthāvara*), the divine (*daivika*), the ṛṣi-related (*ārṣaka*), the elemental (*gāṇava*), and likewise the human (*mānuṣa*). (2-378)
Now hear the characteristics of these divine lingas:
the linga shall be elongated in shape and uneven, characterized by depressions and elevations. (2.379)
(45) It is joined with lines and hollows, elevated at the opening like a stream, having the form of a mountain peak, and endowed with many apertures and a pointed crest. (2.380)
With the two hands joined in the shape of a hollowed casket and devoid of the sacred thread (brahmasūtra)—endowed with these characteristics, it is called a divine liṅga. || 2.381 ||
The base of the liṅga should be thick, and likewise its top;
however, among the types of liṅgas, that which is thick in the middle has the shape of a coconut fruit.
Resembling the trunk of a plantain tree and having the shape of a bilva fruit,
the *ārṣaka* linga is said to be devoid of the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*).
Resembling the fruit of the kūśmāṇḍa, having the shape of a mātuluṅga fruit, resembling the form of an urvāruka fruit, and similar to the kapittha fruit. || 2-384 ||
Likewise, the *liṅga* is said to be shaped like a palmyra fruit;
its measurement may be according to the door, the womb [of the temple], or even the cubit. (2.385)
Or it may have the dimensions prescribed in the Śiva scriptures, with a crown-like upper portion;
it should be of a single color, auspicious, glossy, and provided with the Brahma-thread.
That which is endowed with these characteristics is called the human *liṅga*.
The first is the *vardhamāna*, while the second is the *trairāśika*. (2.387)
Now the third characteristic, the preponderance of Śiva, will be described: the *vardhamāna*, the *sthita*, and the *āsīna* [types of lingas] possess the preponderance of Śiva. (2.388)
The vehicle should be triangular, and the bed should have equal sections;
the bed is [used] while standing, sitting, and so forth, in due order.
The liṅga is divided into twenty-four parts: the portion for Brahmā is seven, the portion for Viṣṇu is eight, and the portion for Rudra is nine.
This has been declared as the *vardhamāna* [type]; now hear the characteristics of the *āsīna*.
In the twenty-three divisions, the portion for Brahmā is seven.
The eighteenth part is the portion for Viṣṇu, and likewise the eighth is the portion for Rudra;
the twenty-seventh part is the portion for Brahmā, and the ninth is the [final] portion. (2.392)
The portion for Viṣṇu is one-twelfth, and the portion for worship is one-sixth;
they call these the "bed" and the "liṅga"—now hear the names of the others from me.
There are ninety-six signs.
For the sake of establishing and stabilizing the equal fragments, [the Lord] possesses a formidable hood like a host of yogins;
his wheel is submerged in fierce, gaping breaths, radiant, and neither too thick nor too thin in its well-proportioned center.
The Mūkhaniṣkala, the Sakalaniṣkala, the Ardhanārīśvara, the Davikaṭa, the Ākuṭa, the Snigdha,
the Prakīrṇa, the Caṇḍavikrānta,
the Subhadraliṅga, the Paraśiva, and the Kṣīravipulaśāśvata.
It is purifying, as well as both low and high. || 2-395 ||

The Sargabheṣaja has been explained, as well as the Vīra, the Subhadraliṅga, the Vikṛtasita, the Śūlabandhana, the Staṃbha, the Susūryu, the Āmalīkṛt, the Aśekara, the various Kānta, the Kuśekara, the Prabhupratilābha, the Tapta, the Yava, the Sumadhyama, the Pipīlikā, the Madhama-pañcapañcapārśvāgra, the Mūlāgra, the Sumadhyamāgramūrdhvāgra-liṅga, the Caturaśra-liṅga, the Āyatāgra, the Āyatavṛtta-liṅga, the Aravinda, the Pañcakuṣṭa, the Manda, the Kaiṭa, the Sara, the Subhruliṅga-vilābita, and the Suvarṇaliṅga. Then there is the Tāmrābhavarṇa Maheshaliṅga, for Śiva, for Candra, and for Cara-śā.

The white [liṅga], the six-spoked, the seven-fold and nine-fold, the sixteen-fold nectar, the beautiful-browed Śiva-liṅga, the ruby-colored, the tip of the stone-peak, the thousand-fold stream, and the one with eight hundred streams; the *aśvattha* seed, the bean, the barley, the crystal—these indeed are the Vaiṣṇava and Śiva liṅgas.
The portion of Brahmā, the portion of Viṣṇu, the portion of Rudra, Maheśvara, and the portion of Sadāśiva—this is called the fivefold Liṅga. (2.396)
The square portion is considered the share of Brahmā, the eight-sided that of the Vasus, and the [sixteen-sided] that of Viṣṇu;
the thread for Rudra’s portion belongs to Sutāratha, while the end of the thread belongs to Maheśvara.
Above that, however, the portion called Sādākhya is proclaimed to have five parts;
the portion for worship (pūjāṃśa) has sixteen parts, and in front of that is a square.
One part [of the cord] is in the shape of a bud, while the other nine parts are the thread;
the suspension of two cords is said to consist of two parts each.
The sequence of the Brahma-sūtra has been declared; now hear the procedure for the liṅgas of the streams:
the five-stream, the seven-stream, the nine, and the twelve-stream.
The sixteen, twenty, twenty-four, or twenty-eight [spokes] extend from the eight-sided base up to the top; they may be one *yava* part wide or one *yava* high.

Having divided the portion for worship into three parts, the face should be located in the uppermost part. O Maheśvara, I shall now describe specifically the characteristics of the top of the liṅga. (2.402)

For an image that has been uprooted, one that is self-manifested, or one installed by gods and others, there is no need for the characteristics prescribed in the scriptures nor for its consecration. (2.403)
One should not perform the placement of a child, nor indeed that of one with decayed defects;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship each and every joint. (2.404)
I shall describe the manifested characteristics; listen thus, O Maheśvara:
the [mark] of Brāhmaṇas is the shape of a lotus, while that of a king is the shape of a hen's egg.
That which has the shape of a bubble for Vaiśyas and resembles a crescent moon for Śūdras—a liṅga endowed with these characteristics is said to be human. (2.406)
O Maheśvara, that which is called a self-manifested liṅga (svayaṃbhuliṅga) is a bāṇaliṅga;
it is shaped like a mountain peak and rises high like the top of an anthill. (2.407)
This, which has arisen from the characteristics [of the ritual], is proclaimed in many ways as the foremost:
namely, the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), the invocation (punarāhvāna), and the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa).
Once a human *liṅga* has been installed, one should perform all ritual acts;
having worshipped that *liṅga*, one should [unify] that *liṅga* with the heart.
Having sprinkled water for purification there as part of the worship, the preceptor should worship [the deity] in sequence with perfumes and other offerings;
then, taking hold of a flower with the little finger and the ring finger, the preceptor [should proceed]. (2.410)
One should release the flower worshipped during the morning twilight with the mantra of Īśa;
one should release it at the side of the pedestal using the thumb and forefinger. (2.411)
Thereafter, one should quickly offer that flower upon the head of the Liṅga;
for if the flower is not placed on the head of the Liṅga, the practitioner perishes in emptiness. (2.412)
Having washed the *liṅga* with the [Pāśupata] weapon-mantra,
one should offer the entire remains of the *nirmālya* from the pedestal to Caṇḍeśa.
Having purified the area of the pedestal of the *liṅga* with water from the heart-mantra,
and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should meditate upon the *liṅga* as being the true reality (*sadbhāva*).
One should touch the region of the head of the liṅga with the Īśāna mantra,
and one should touch the region of the mouth of the liṅga with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should touch the back of the *liṅga* with the Vāmadeva mantra;
the two sides up to the pedestal and the two feet with the Sadyojāta mantra using both arms. (2.416)
One should worship the limbs of the deity, beginning with the great cloth (mahāpaṭya) and ending with the sandals; one shall describe the abode of the deity—listen to its characteristics. (2.417)
Prāsāda, sadana, sadma, grha, dhāman, niketana, vimāna, bhavana, harmya, vāsa, manira, and mālaya. (2.418)
"Nilaya" is its well-known synonym;
it is characterized as a celestial mansion (vimāna).
I shall describe the characteristics of the celestial chariot (vimāna); listen thus, O Maheśvara.
The *athisthāna* is the first, the *upānat* is the second;
the third is the *jagatī*, and the *kaca* and *padma* are the fourth.
The fifth is indeed the *kumuda*, and likewise the sixth is the *paṭṭikā*;
the seventh is declared to be the *bhakti*, and the eighth is the pillar (*staṃbha*). (2-421)
The ninth is the *pālikā*, the tenth is the *kaṃpa*,
the eleventh is the *kapota*, and the twelfth is the *bhūtamālikā*.
The thirteenth is the neck, while the nose is the fourteenth;
the pinnacle is the fifteenth, and the tip of the stūpa becomes the sixteenth.
Now hear, in due order, the names of the powers (śaktis) of the sixteenth part:
the first is Ādhāraśakti, and the second is Ādiśakti.

The third is the power of action (kriyā-śakti), the fourth is the power of light (jyotiḥ-śakti), the fifth is the power of the host (gaṇa-śakti), and the sixth is the power of the locus (sthāna-śakti). (2.425)
The seventh is Raudraśakti, the eighth is Bhogaśaktikā, the ninth is Anantaśakti, and the tenth is Manonmanī. (2.426)
Ekādaśī is the Great Power (Mahāśakti), Dvādaśī is the Power of Time (Kālaśakti),
Trayodaśī is the Power of Knowledge (Jñānaśakti), and Caturdaśī is Śāmbhavī.
But the fifteenth [day] is auspicious at the summit of the stūpa, O Maheśvarī;
from the foundation up to the end of the stūpa, one should install these Śaktis in sequence. (2.428)
Thus, the definition of the abode of action (kṛti) by means of its power (śakti) will be stated; listen.
It is said to be accumulated (saṃcita), unaccumulated (asaṃcita), and also re-accumulated (upasaṃcita). (2-429)

That which is joined with stones is called *saṃcita*; that which lacks a raised platform is *asaṃcita*; and that which is provided with primary and secondary architectural members (*aṅga* and *upāṅga*) is termed *upasaṃcita*. (2.430)
(50) Listen now to the names of the vimānas, liṅgas, and śaktis in their proper order: the vimāna of this [deity] is named Nalikā, and its liṅga is Samakhaṇḍa. (2-431)
The power of forbearance (kṣānti-śakti) is the establishment of the *pralika*; it is of the nature of victory (*jayātmikā*).
The *svastika* is the established *liṅga*, which is the four-faced power of progeny (*prajā-śakti*). (2.432)
The Pratiṣṭhā-liṅga is Vārāhī, auspicious and beneficial in every way;
the Yoni-liṅga is Kriyāśakti, resembling the back of an elephant and the navel. (2.433)
Having fully ignited the power of the Sūtra, one should place the Liṅga upon the eight petals;
it is said that the power is Phalinī, and the Śrīphandana is Vikraṅgala.
The Linga, which is the fruit of the manifestation of the power of the qualities (guṇa-śakti), is beautiful with its phallic form;
it is the Linga installed by Śrīkānta, conjoined with Pārvatī as his Śakti.
The abode known as Śrīpratiṣṭhā is the root, and its gross aspect is the Liṅga;
Ātmaśakti and Cakṣuṣī are the middle, and their gross aspect is the Liṅga. (2-436)

The power of mantra (mantraśakti), the severing of the head (śiraccheda), the sacrificial post (yūpa), the non-fixed linga (aniṣalaliṅgaka), the city for one desiring protection (rakṣākāṅga-pura), and the linga known as Sakala.
It is said that *aṅgadāśakti* signifies one who is perpetually afflicted by disease;
*taruṇāśakti* is said to be the Viṣṇuchandas meter and a palace.
The power of action (kriyāśakti) is the Ṭaṅka-liṅga belonging to Saubhadra, consisting of the essence of Svadhā;
the Kailāsavikaṭa-liṅga is conjoined with the power Pārvatī.
Candra, Makuṭaliṅga, Śaśiśakti, Sadāyuta, Śūdra, Chanda, Sadana, Sthūlaliṅga, and Bhairavī. (2–440)
The Pralaṃbita, the Prakīrṇa, the Ādhāra, the Meruchandaka, the Caṇḍaliṅga, the Virāṭśakti, the Śrīkaṇṭha, and the Kāntaliṅgaka. || 2-441 ||
The Nāda-śakti, the Śakuṃbha, the Bhadraliṅga,
the Rajāyanī, the Jayāṅga, and the Pāliṅga, all endowed with the Krīḍā-śakti.
The pedestal (*vimāna*) of the *śivaliṅga* has the pure form of the power of earth (*kṣamāśakti*).
They call the tender *liṅga* that which is endowed with the primordial power (*ādiśakti*). (2.443)
Haṃsaphaṇḍantu is the abode of Vīra, which has a broad liṅga;
Padmāṅkasadana is the stable liṅga, and Manonmanī is likewise.

The purifying *liṅga* of the Padmapatra-vimāna is said to have a dwelling that is broken by the *Ṛgveda*, characterized by well-formed *liṅgas* that are uneven with depressions and elevations. (2.445)
Rudraśakti is Sadana, Kukkuṭa is Sāraliṅgaka,
and Paraśaktyagnikānta is known as Liṅgapālinī.
The abode of Rudrakānta is called the Vikṛta-liṅga;
and the Bhadraliṅga, which possesses luster, belongs to the Yogabhadra-vimāna.
The abode of Bhogacchanda is said to be the deformed Liṅga;
the Vindhya-cakra Vimāna, however, is the Śṛṅgaliṅga, which is most terrifying.
The binding liṅga for the Merukūṭa palace is the Gaṅgaśaktika;
the abode of Śrī Mahendra, however, has a pillar-liṅga on the south.
The bubble, characterized by the sign of the heap (rāśi), is said to be the power of auspiciousness (kalyāṇaśakti);
the mandala, characterized by the sign of Māra, is said to be the power of desire (kāmādhiśakti). || 2-450 ||
The power of thought (cintyaśakti), however, is the mandala called Sādākhya, marked with the liṅga;
it is said to be the Paiśāca power, auspicious and delightful to behold. (2.451)
Pālinī is said to be Śakti, whose characteristic mark is the name Maṅgalā;
Viṣṇuśakti, however, is Sadanā, possessing the luster of the Blue Mountain (Nīla-parvata).
And the Jyotiśakti [resides] in the Niṣada, the excellent Śakti-susūtkāra, the Prabhuliṅga, which is established as the Kula-Brahma-Suliṅgaka.
Vijaya is endowed with the power of *vidyā* and possesses the corresponding signs;
Lalita is heated by passion and is endowed with the power of *dhvani*. (2.454)
The non-dual Dharma is the abode of Śrīvilāsa, characterized by the middle state, devoid of gender and power, yet possessing excellent lingas as small as ants.
The Ati-pratiṣṭhā and Śakti [plans], the Somacchanda temple, the Pallava-named [plan] for the excellent liṅga, and the Viśālabhadra [plan]. (2-456)

The well-rounded *ditikraya* type, situated at the side of the elephant tusk, has its linga at the base and tip; it brings peace when the *indraka* is in the middle and the *āśraka* is present. (2.457)
The armor, the power, the Śrīvarta, the upward-facing limb, the power of movement, the lotus-house, the residence, the quadrangle, and the excellent linga. || 2-458 ||
Having consecrated the coral *śrīliṅga* joined with the power of *vidruma*,
one should likewise offer the *darāśakti* to the *kriyāvarta* *dhātrīliṅga*.
That heart-liṅga, which is the locus for the absorption of the Great Power (mahāśakti),
is the Vāsavīśālabhadra of the well-formed liṅga that is suspended.
Regarding the mark of the bamboo flute, they say that the auspicious mark of Kāma is the golden mark, which is endowed with the power of Kṛṣṇa. (2.461)
The Gaṇava shrine is the abode of Śāla, possessing a liṅga with the luster of copper;
it is the fierce Maheśa-liṅga of Kāmaśaktakaṇṭha.
The Śiva-liṅga is said to belong to the Bhadraliṅga-vimāna;
in the Rudraśakti hall, there is the Candraliṅga with Aṅgaśakti as its consort.
The abode ending with Padmā has mobile liṅgas and so forth as its power;
the eternal liṅga of Dhairya has Bhūtaśakti and Viṣṇuka.
The *phaṭkāra-liṅga*, *kālī-kali*, *vikramālaya*, and *gopura* belong to the excellent sevenfold *liṅga*; the power (*śakti*) of the Sun, however, accomplishes all rites. (2.465)
It possesses a charming abode for the nine-fold stream-liṅga, and a copper-colored palace for the splendor of the sixteen-fold stream-liṅga. (2.466)
The [mandala] of the Thousand White Liṅgas has a broad *kāmaśakti*;
that of the Excellent Liṅga at the Peak has *siddhis*, or else it is the *śakraka*.
They call it the Maṇikaliṅga, which consists of the syllables Kṣānti, Hā, Rāja, and Vahni;
it is the abode of the power Kṛṣṇā, auspicious, and adorned with a garland of moons.
The gopura at the front of the river-hall possesses the splendor of a stone liṅga;
however, the flame from the crest of the liṅga is like a bow for the earth and other elements.
The power of speech (vākśakti) is the abode of victory for the liṅga of eighteen streams; Nivṛtti is the eternal abode for the liṅga of one hundred and eight streams.
The *adhyardha-liṅga* is established above the *daṅga-kāla*, measuring one *māṣaka*;
the *moha-śakti* is the abode of beauty, characterized by the *lava-liṅga*.
The seat of the power of resolve (dhṛtiśakti) is a crystal linga with a shadow;
the seat of the field-power (kṣetraśakti), however, is a white (nāgara) linga as its throne.
The Nāga-shakti has a Drāviḍa-style vardhamānaka as its seat, while the Kṣānti-shakti has a Vesara-style seat; this is recorded as the prescribed bed.

The abode of the powers of the *liṅga* is established as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*); its essential nature is the bliss of the individual soul, and its central form is that of the cosmic dance.

Therefore, one should worship the Guru, who is the dancer situated in the midst of the sevenfold self, whose form is light, who abides in the nature of both qualities and the absence of qualities, and who is like the all-pervading Lord capable of everything. (2.475)
Being honored by conchs, black drums, cymbals, the sounds of bells, and the cities along with great-sounding dancers, he should remember the Southern Śama.
One should worship Naṭeśvara, who stands in the center of the six liṅgas;
therefore, having meditated upon his central form with every effort.
Having uttered the *liṅga-mantra*, hear now its extraction:
[it consists of] the fourth [vowel] of the third [group], endowed with the bindu and the nāda. (2.478)
This has been declared as the mantra of the *liṅga*; now hear of the abode of the powers (*śaktis*).
The foundational seat known as Ādhāra is the very nature of the primordial power (*ādiśakti*). (2.479)
The power that has become the Jagatī is Kumuda, whose power consists of the qualities (guṇa);
the power Paṭṭikāpālinī is the throat, whose power is auspiciousness (kalyāṇa).
Now, the lower band is Kāmeśī, the great upper band is Manonmanī;
the uppermost band is Mahāśakti, whose nature consists of the bliss of the supreme foundation.
May the power of Sound (nāda-śakti) and the power of Padmabhairava stabilize it;
may the power of the root, stem, and limbs of the creeper, as well as the power of Padmavāsava, likewise stabilize it.
The power Mālinī resides in the pericarp; Śoṣaṇī is the secondary power.
Kumāraśakti is the limb, while Pālikā is another power.
Vīrakāṇḍa, Virāṭśakti, Potikā, and Agrāṇīyakā;
Staṃbha would be Daśaśakti, and Uttara is Rudraśaktikā.
Vājana possesses the power of the Vāminī; Raktamālya has the power of Aṅga; Kapota indeed has two powers; and Ambukāmā is presided over by Ādhi. (2.485)
Facing forward is the power of Rudra (rudraśakti), the propelling [power] is the power of the King (rājaśaktika);
the seventh is the class of the pigeon (kapotavarga), and the altar (vedikā) is the power of the Hero (vīraśaktika). || 2-486 ||
The *jyotiśakti* should be at the throat, with the height of the *rudraśakti*;
and the *upakalyāṇaśakti* should be adorned with a garland of *dṛta* flowers and *abhisindvaka*.
The pinnacle (śikhara) is the supreme power (śakti), and the dome (sthūpya) is the regulator of the command (ājñā).
The corner (karṇa) is the power of time (kāla-śakti), and the great nose (mahānāsī) is of the nature of victory (jaya).
It has a great height and elevation, with nine peaks and nine powers.
In its center, below the *stūpī*, O Pārvatī, is a lotus possessing the power of Pārvatī. (2.489)
The throat is the power of compassion (karuṇā-śakti), the pitcher is the vessel of milk;
the upper pitcher is the power of the crest (śikhā-śakti), and the Śrīvatsa is the power of sound (dhvani-śakti). || 2.490 ||
The power of the conch-sound, the impurity which possesses the power of mantra,
the bud which is the abode of the blue water-lily, and the power of the final cosmic dance.
Thus has been described the abode consisting of Śakti, which possesses a manifest form; the manifest is the *sakala-liṅga*, while the unmanifest is the *niṣkala-liṅga* in the form of light.
The light, situated in the midst of radiance, is the wondrous dancer of the south;
it is beyond the qualities (nirguṇa), stainless, eternal, the central one, and the supreme state.
The supreme dance of the Supreme Power, Vedic, belonging to the Lord of the South, immutable, eternally bestowing boons, and devoid of cause or illustration. (2.494)
On the right is Prasāda, Śāna, Pavitra, and the Lord Ādīka;
situated in the center is the one abiding in the Mūla-form, the Sky-abiding, the Void, and the Resonance.

[I bow to] the Guru Sādāśiva, who consists of eternal bliss, who is accompanied by Ambā, who is the witness, who transcends all mental constructs, who is everything, who is the abode of existence, and who is ever-arisen. (2.496)
Equal, consisting of the state of equal flavor (samarasībhāva), facing in all directions and upward,
the Lord of the South, the great secret, eternally performing the wondrous dance (tāṇḍava).
O Maheśvara, I shall describe his temple named Śānti;
it may be of three types: Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara. (2-498)
That which is square at the base of the stūpa is declared to be the Nāgara style; the Drāviḍa temple should have an eight-sided neck and base. (2-499)
O Maheśvara, that which begins from the neck and extends to the end of the tail is praised; I shall now state the names of the sixty-nine triplets of the Trivarga.

The *nalika*, the *pralika*, the *svastika*, the four-faced (*caturmukha*), the *sarvatobhadraka*, and the brilliantly shining *hastipṛṣṭha*; the *śrīcandavṛttabhadra*, the *śrīkānta*, and the *śrīpratiṣṭhita*. (2–501) 2. (56)
And Śrībhadra, Śiracchanda, Gopura, and Sarvadākṛti. || 2-502 ||
Viṣṇucchandas, Saubhadra, Kailāsa, Candramas, Ārdra-chandas, and Lalita— these are considered the Devikā meters.
Sumeruchandaka, Śrīkūṭa, and Kumbha;
Jayāṅga, Vimalāṅga, and Vimalākṛti. || 2-504 ||
The haṃsa-rhythm, the vṛṣa-rhythm, and the garuḍa-rhythm;
the lotus-marked, the lotus-auspicious, and the bed, cock, and end. (2.505)
Rudrakānta, Yogabhadra, Homacchanda, Sudarśana, Skandakānta, Viṣṇucakra, Merukūṭa, and Maheṃdra. (2–506)
Budbudaka, Śrīmaṇḍa, Saumughya, Jayamaṅgala, Nīlaparvataka, Niṣadha, and Sindhuka. || 2.507 ||
Vijaya, Lalita, Kānta, Mandara, Śrīvilāsaka, Jātī, and others—these thirty-two [types of] abodes and so forth belong to the gods. (2.508)
The Somacchanda, the Nāgacchanda, this auspicious Kāmyāvarta,
the Śrīvartaka, the Padmagṛha, and likewise the Prakṣyagṛhamukha.

These twelve [sins] of the twice-born—namely, performing the funeral rites for those whose lineage has ceased, living in the house of a widow, being malicious toward the selfless, and being excessively addicted to sensual pleasures—are [the causes of their downfall]. (2.510)
Tantritāṅga, Vijayāṅga, Viśālapatraka, Parama, Gāṇapa, Śālavaṃkarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, and Śālaka. (2.511)
Its foundation is lotus-based, its fortitude is firm, its abode has coral gate-towers;
it possesses all graceful attendants, is lovely, and is indeed vast. (2.512)
The auspicious palāśa leaf, the great royal parasol, the *mālikara*, Nandin, Viśālaka, and likewise the two *pṛthivījaya*s. (2-513)
Beautiful in all its limbs, a chamber of radiance, and an increaser of pleasure—thus, there are ninety-six varieties of celestial vehicles (vimānas) according to their classes. (2.514)
O Maheśvara, from the first brick up to the pinnacle (stūpī), this form is of the nature of Śakti;
therefore, my supreme and auspicious form consists of Śakti.
The Guru is the form of the Bindu, the great secret, the embodiment of all sacred seats (pīṭhas);
he is the circular one, abiding as the self of all, whose form is the Veda and who is a perfect mandala.
The supreme reality has the form of a seat (pīṭha) and is the very nature of the creation of the world;
because it is like a potter’s wheel, from that [wheel] arises the very nature of creation. || 2-517 ||
The narrative consisting of the creation of the world has the form of the solar orb;
it is the seat whose nature is the threefold space-element, dwelling everywhere.
Therefore, the entire great seat (mahāpīṭha) is the middle of the southern gate;
it is the support of all the deities, a lotus endowed with a pericarp.
Having always meditated upon my form, which is established on the feet, has the nature of the Śuddhajñānamudrā, and resides within the center of my entire self— 2-520.
My entire form and appearance consists of the central bindu;
my supreme and most excellent abode is the temple at the southern gate.
Resorting to the southern gate, it has the nature of the six supports;
it is the abode of all the gods, the form of emanation, and perfectly centered.
The sound situated in the center of the form of the *pīṭha* has the nature of a dance;
it is the beautiful form of sound situated in the center of the village of the heart. || 2-523 ||
I bow to the supreme Guru, who is the form of the drop arising from the Tāṇḍava dance of the Vedas, who is the beautiful maṇḍala,
the abode of the assembly, eternal light, and eternally dancing.
Having the form of a dancer, to be known by its own sounds, having the nature of the five supports, pure, and having issued from the celestial chariot (vimāna), it is the abode of the southern gate.
One should worship the Supreme Lord situated within the *sumantraka* at the center of the *sumadhyastha*. (p.
58) It is taught that the *liṅga* consists of *nāda*, while the *pīṭha* has the nature of *bindu*. (2.526)
In the absence of a liṅga, one should likewise contemplate that form within the pedestal.
The sequence for the purification of the liṅga has been declared; now hear the purification of the mantra.
All mantras beginning with the neck [of the ritual diagram] and ending with the salutation (namaskāra) are prescribed;
they should be employed at the time of the rite, and one should perform their purification. (2.528)
The sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is indeed the Praṇava; by this designation, the entire mantra is definitively determined as the Praṇava, beginning with the name "Ādi. (2.529)
Truth, truth: one should always chant my meditation, the Praṇava;
for everything is my form—the pure and imperishable Oṃkāra.
The syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ), consisting of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, together with the *bindu* and *nāda*, should be known through yoga as the supreme essence of the five deities. (2.531)
The letter *a* resides in the heart; the letter *u* is designated as being in the throat;
the letter *m* is situated in the middle of the palate; and the *bindu* is established in the center of the brows. (2.532)
The supreme five-syllabled yoga consists of Nāda, Lālāṭaka, and the letter A;
the letter U should be joined with Svi, and the letter O is the left face.
The letter *ma* is the terrible face; the *bindu* is that face of Puruṣa;
*nāda* is the face of Īśāna; and that which transcends *nāda* is Aṇṭeśvara.
The subtle five-syllabled mantra has been declared; now hear the gross five-syllabled mantra:
the syllable *na* is the face of Sadyojāta, and the syllable *ma* is the face of Ghora.
The letter Śi is the face of Īśa, the letter Va is the left face, and the letter Ya is the face of Puruṣa; thus there arises the glorious five-syllabled mantra. (2.536)
The syllable *sa* is Uvaṃdeva, established as the essence of the three principles (*tritatva*).
On the path of the seed-syllable of space (*ākāśabīja*), the mantra shall consist of twelve syllables. (2.537)
The six limbs of Brahman are short; the eye is long with a bindu;
everything is possessed of the *vidyut* [vowel *i*]; the weapon (*astra*) ends in the visarga and possesses a bindu. (2.538)
One should join the auspicious fifth [vowel] to the end of the sixth and the thirteenth;
it is conjoined with elisions at the beginning, elisions in the middle, and elisions at the end.
This mantra is proclaimed as the description of the case endings, vowels, and consonants:
the letter *ha* is the form of Śiva, while the letter *sa* is the form of Śakti.

One should join the mantra of Śiva, consisting of the letter *ha*—known as the bindu and nāda—and the letter *sa* joined with its group (*varga*), along with Śiva and the bestowal of the *haṃsa*. (2.541)
The fourteenth seat is indeed the *nāda*, conjoined with the fire of dissolution;
in the sixteen-syllable phoneme, it is endowed with both the *bindu* and the *nāda*. (2.542)
This mantra of Ambā has been declared; now hear the procedure for the nine-syllable [mantra]:
it is joined with the letters ending in *sa* and *ha*, followed by the third letter of the sky (*kha*).
The fifth syllable of the sixth [mantra], ending with the letter *ya*, consists of the two letters of Varuṇa and Anala;
it is joined with the sixth vowel, and endowed with the bindu and nāda. (2.544)
The procedure for the nine-syllable mantra has been declared; now hear the procedure for the eight-syllable mantra:
the fourth syllable of the eighth [group] and that very same preceding syllable. (2.545)
The serpent-like, peak-syllable, lovely one, which is the fifth of the sixth group, joined with the sixth and the fourteenth—this eight-syllable mantra is auspicious. (2.546)
Then, O Maheśvara, we hear the Śārabha mantra, which is fierce, the fifth, the eater of the five, and the third of the seventh group. (2.547)
The sixth group among the middle and final sets consists of six, four, fourteen, and thirteen elements;
it includes the peak-syllables and long vowels, beginning with the seventh peak-syllable and ending with *vaṣaṭ*. (2.548)
Having performed the previously mentioned worship and offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter, one should perform ten thousand oblations with the twelve-syllable mantra. (2.549)
One should perform rites for prosperity in the eastern quarter, incantations for causing enmity in the southeast,
for attracting in the southern region, and likewise for enchantment in the southwest.
Rites of pacification (śāntika) are to be performed in the western direction; likewise, eradication (uccāṭana) in the northwest;
subjugation (vaśya) should be applied in the north; and similarly, killing (māraṇa) in the northeast.
Know that spring is the forenoon, summer is likewise midday, the rainy season is the afternoon, and the cool season is the evening. (2.552)
At midnight, it is the autumn season; at dawn, it shall be winter. Perform attraction during spring, but perform inciting enmity during summer. (2.553)
The rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) is performed in the rainy season; likewise, the rite of killing (*māraṇa*) in the winter.
The rite of pacification (*śāntika*) is for the autumn season, and the rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*) in the late winter (*hemanta*). (2.554)
Having attained the fruit of the sequence of the Dharma, one should contemplate the dance of the others;
in the south, the abode of Keśinī, one should perform the rite of fire-offerings (homa).
In the four directions, with the four Vedas reciting hymns and auspicious words,
one should offer oblations daily for six months or half a month, performing fifty thousand [recitations].

Having recited the three syllables once, listen to the sequence of the name-mantra: the sound *nāda*, the letter *na*, the first of the sounds (*nāda*), and the fifth of the sixth group of consonants.
The first syllable of the fourth [varga], endowed with the eleventh vowel, and the seed-syllable of the beginning of the eighth [varga], joined with its own root-long vowel. (2.558)
The seed-syllable of the seventh [letter], preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, is this secret name-mantra established in the supreme light. (2.559)
This mantra and so forth, which belongs to the Lord, is extremely secret and not to be given away;
however, the mantra consisting of the Upper Śaiva [tradition] is to be bestowed upon my devotees. (2.560)
The sequence of the name-mantras has been declared; now hear the procedure for the hero-mantras:
the second [syllable] followed by the third, conjoined with the bindu and the nāda. (2.561)
This has been declared as the Heroic Mantra; now hear the sequence of the Protective Mantra:
the first seed-syllable of the fifth [vowel] and the sixth [vowel] with the fifth seed-syllable.
The third of the eighth [letter], the fourth of the seventh, joined with my second syllable, and the seed-syllable at the beginning of the seventh. (2.563)
The sequence of the protective mantra has been declared; now hear the sequence of the Brahma-mantra:
the third letter of the sixth group, conjoined with the fire of dissolution (the letter *ra*). (2.564)
Listen to the ritual procedure for the Viṣṇu-mantra, which is joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Viṣṇu arises from Speech and is adorned with the *bindu* and the line (*rekhā*). (2.565)
One should employ [the mantra] beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, in the dative case.
The sequence for Viṣṇu mantras has been declared; now hear this wealth-mantra.
The end of the fourth [syllable] of the fifth [group], endowed with the bindu and nāda, is declared to be this mantra of wealth; now hear the sequence of the Lakṣmī-mantra.
The primary seed-syllable of the eighth [vowel] is conjoined with the fire of dissolution (the letter *ra*), joined with the fourth vowel (*ī*), and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*. (2.568)
This mantra of Lakṣmī has been declared; now hear the sequence of the mantra of Skanda: the seventh letter of the *ya*-group conjoined with the fifth vowel. (2.569)
The third [syllable] of the seventh [group], however, is joined with the Bindu and Nāda; this entire mantra, consisting of the nature of Śiva, begins with one's own name and ends with "Namaḥ. (2.570)
The sequence for the purification of mantras has been declared; now hear the characteristics of the seat. (p.
62) The first mantra of the seed-syllable of space (*kha*) is that which effects the emanation of the root energy (*mūlaśakti*). (2.571)
All that arises from the Divine possesses the power of command and action;
it has Ādhāraśakti as its name and place of origin, and it is the source of Dharma and the other [Puruṣārthas].
Listen now to [the description of] the seat and other requisites for the purpose of the visualization-offering (*dhyānapūjā*):
the goddess who arises from the world, like a beautiful root of a pearl necklace. (2.573)
She has four arms and eight hands, possessing the luster of molten gold;
she has twelve eyes and four nostrils, with her hair bound upon her head.

One should visualize the Śakti seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), holding a noose, a goad, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a thunderbolt, a chisel, a mace, and the gesture of wisdom (jñānamudrā).
The wise teacher should meditate upon Śakti, who is adorned with all ornaments, who is the sole refuge for the entire world, and whose form is the foundational support. (2.576)
The seed-syllable of Śakti and its sprout, containing within them the stalk and the qualities (dharmas) and so forth;
the Śakti is saffron-colored, and the seed-syllable resembles coral. (2.577)
The sprout has the luster of silver, and the stalk resembles lapis lazuli; it is joined with the feet beginning with Dharma and is established upon Adharma and Artha.
First is the seat of Ananta and Ākāśa, held in the hand of the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti) and containing the five seats; after that is the Lion Throne (Siṃhāsana).
The third is the yoga seat (yogāsana), while the lotus seat (padmāsana) is considered superior;
the fifth is declared to be the stainless (vimala), which one should arrange by proceeding upwards.
The seat called Ananta is circular and situated above;
joined with eight serpents, it is called the Ananta-seat. || 2-581 ||
The narrative called Ananta has been proclaimed; now hear the sequence of the lion-thrones (siṃhāsana).
Dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya—this is the tetrad. (2.582)
Dharma is the true nature of reality, while knowledge is indeed in the form of an elephant;
dispassion takes the form of a lion, and sovereignty takes the form of a horse. (2.583)
Each one was surrounded by tens of millions upon tens of millions of lions;
and all of them were in the very form of rājāvarta (emerald) lions.
The Unmanifest (avyakta), Necessity (niyati), Time (kāla), and Portion (kalā)—these four should be placed in order on the four sides of the square in the cardinal directions. (2.585)
With the heels placed together, this is the Keśava posture; thus the Siṃhāsana is formed.
The sequence for the Siṃhāsana has been declared; now hear the procedure for the Yogāsana.
That seat is pure, shaped like a tortoise, and the color of fire;
having first placed the *praṇava* (oṃ), one likewise places the syllable 'a' in the fire.
The letter Ā is in the southern quarter, and likewise La in the southwest;
the letter Ī is in the western quarter, and the letter U in the region of the northwest. (2.588)
One should place the letter *ū* in the northern direction, the letter *ṛ* in the northeastern region, and the letter *ṝ* in the central part; thus there shall be the yogic seat (*yogāsana*).
Thus the yogic posture has been described; now hear the procedure for the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and likewise Kālī and Vikaraṇī—|| 2-590 ||
Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī—these are the eight Śaktis. (2.591)
One should place [the letters] in due order upon the tips of the filaments and in the pericarp;
thus the lotus posture (padmāsana) has been described—now hear of the stainless posture (vimalāsana).
p. 64) One should worship Gaṇāmbikā in the north and Mahādevī in the east;
Tannobhūr in the south and Pracodayāt in the west. (2-593)
One should conceive of the pure seat as pervaded by these powers:
in the center of fire is the station of the sun, and in the center of the sun is the moon.
In the midst of darkness (tamas) is passion (rajas), and in its midst is goodness (sattva);
[one perceives] the self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), and the supreme self (paramātman).
The threefold principle of the Self (ātmatattva) has been declared; one should arrange them in successive layers above one another.
The sequence of the principle of the Self has been explained; now hear the sequence of the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva).
One should sequentially deposit the Brahmavidyā, the Śivavidyā, and the Guruvijñāna; then, having deposited the Brahma-tattva, one should place the Vidyā-tattva above it.
Beyond that is the principle of Rudra, and above that is Maheśvara;
at the summit of that is the Sādākhya principle, and beyond that is the Bindu principle.
Above that, one should worship the principle of Nāda; beyond that, the principle of Śakti; and beyond that, the supreme principle of Śiva, which is the embodiment of knowledge. (2.599)
In the center of that is the abode of the eye, and in the center of that is the seat of flowers;
all this is the preeminent seat, possessing the luster of crystal.
The circular form is the nature of Sadāśiva, the form of space, higher than the highest;
listen now to the sequence of Śiva’s creation through the essential nature of the Bindu mantra. (2.601)

The *nāda* is situated within the *bindu*; the resonance (*dhvani*) is situated within the *nāda*; the Self (*ātman*) is situated within the resonance; and likewise, the supreme state is beyond peace (*śānti*). (2.602)
Śiva is the Brahman higher than the highest, immeasurable and beyond reproach;
incomparable, subtle, eternal, omnipresent, and the Lord. (2.603)
Because it is pure, it is called Śiva; because it is beyond the supreme and higher than the highest, it is the ultimate.
Because it is Brahman and because it is the state of being Brahman, it is designated as Brahma. (2.604)
Because it is distinct from the means of valid cognition, the object of cognition is not the Lord;
it should be known as blameworthy due to its impurity, and blameless due to its purity. (2.605)
It is incomparable, peerless, and faces the south;
it transcends the sky, is supreme, subtle, eternal, and devoid of any cause. (2.606)
Because of its pervasiveness, it is called all-pervading; because of its sovereignty, it is called the Lord.
For the sake of creation and for the protection of the world, it is the cause of the world's origin. (2.607)
For the benefit of practitioners, he would voluntarily assume a body;
for the sake of protection, he [assumed] the wondrous Dakṣiṇeśvara along with Bhāvāsandī.
The eternal dance, the great light, the Lord who is the support of all pillars,
whose form is bliss, situated in the center, Śiva, the supreme cause.
Then that [reality] is said to be threefold: again, as the partless (niṣkala), the both-part-and-partless (sakalaniṣkala), and the with-parts (sakala), in due order.
The partless (niṣkala) is of four kinds, and likewise the manifest (sakala) is so;
the manifest and the partless are each proclaimed as ninefold in sequence.
From a thousandth part of the Śiva-tattva arises that which is named Śānti;
they declare that Śānti is the bringer of peace, and these are its synonymous designations.
And from that very thousandth part arises the one named Śakti;
and from Śakti indeed arises Vidyā, which is declared to be its synonym. (2.613)
And from that very thousandth part, the manifestation of the form of Nāda arises;
Nāda and its Pratiṣṭhā are proclaimed to be synonyms. (2.614)
And from that very thousandth part, the principle of the Bindu (bindutatva) arises;
both Bindu and Nivṛtti are its designations used as synonyms. (2.615)
Always taking recourse to the supreme state along with the hosts of Tāḍavīra heroes, [they possess] natures such as the unmanifest and so forth, and likewise they are inactive. (2-616)
Thus, the fourth is indeed called the partless (niṣkala) Śiva-principle; for Maheśvara, the partless is established beyond meditation and worship. (2.617)
Thus, the partless (niṣkala) has been declared; it is remembered as the supreme state (para-bhāva). From that, by a tenfold and single portion, the emergence of the Sādākhya [tattva] occurs. (2.618)
According to the manner of the *liṅga* and the *pīṭha*, the characteristic of the principle called Sādākhya is as follows:
Liṅgaśiva has arisen, and Sadāśiva is of the nature of *nāda*. (2.619)
On the pedestal (pīṭha), Śakti has arisen, known by the name Manonmanī;
and in the liṅga as well as on the base (pīṭhikā), there are Śiva and the one arisen from Śakti.
In this way, the *liṅga* is indeed masculinity (*pustva*) and the *pīṭha* is indeed femininity (*strītatva*).
The *liṅga* and *pīṭha* are partless (*niṣkala*), while Śakti and Śambhu are with parts (*sakala*). (2.621)
The *niṣkalā* is devoid of parts (*kalā*), while the *sakalā* is endowed with parts;
[these are for] ascetics, mantra-practitioners, men of knowledge, and yogis.

For the purpose of the signs of meditative worship, one should always worship the Lord of Gods, who is both with parts and without parts, according to the manner of the *liṅga* and the *pīṭha*. (2.623)
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), the path of principles (tattvādhvan), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan),
the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), and the path of kalās (kalādhvan) constitute the essential nature of Sādākhya.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in detail the sequence of the stations on the paths:
the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) has the skin as its support, and the path of words (padādhvan) likewise has the head.

The path of reality (tattvādhvan) is the heart; the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is the pores of the skin; the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) is the seat of the blood; and the path of kalās consists of semen, marrow, and bone. (2.626)
And by means of the path of the *kalās*, the entire body thus becomes the form of the *sādākhya*;
endowed with the thirty-eight *kalās*, it exists as the *sakala* (the manifest). (2.627)
One should then conceive Sadāśiva, beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta;
one should fashion his five heads by means of the Īśāna mantra. (2.628)
One should, however, fashion four faces for the Puruṣa;
with the Aghora mantra, one should fashion the eight [limbs] beginning with the heart.
With the Vāmadeva mantra, one should assign the thirteen [parts] beginning with the secret place;
with the Sadyojāta mantra, one should arrange the eight [parts] beginning with the feet. (2.630)
Eight, thirteen, eight, four, and five are known as the kalās of Aja, Amogha, Vāma, Ghorākhya, and Puruṣeśa. (2.631)
Thus, the auspicious Niṣkala Tāṇḍava has been described in its entirety;
they know the conceptualization of hands, feet, belly, and so forth as Sakala.
He who is called Sādākhya, the Lord of all gods, manifest and facing in every direction,
dwelling in the center of the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus.
He was a youth with five heads, ten arms, four faces, twelve eyes, four noses, and endowed with four throats. (2.634)
Having two feet, with the appearance of crystal, and wearing a white sacred thread;
resembling ten million suns, he bears the digit of the moon of gnosis.

In the right hands, he holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a trident, an axe, and a vajra, as well as a shield, a noose of rays (or a noose of *kuśa* grass), and a staff; in the other [left] hands, he holds the gesture of granting boons (*varada*). (2.636)
Wearing white garments, he was adorned with all ornaments, including a turban and an upper robe; he was gentle and bore a coolness like the rays of the moon. (2.637)
Endowed with all limbs, anointed with all perfumes, he is the inner self of all beings; one should always contemplate that reality. (2.638)
Śambhu, the beloved of Pārvatī, the supreme one, who has the five elements as his presiding deities, whose nature is the five Brahmans, and who is designated by the five-syllabled mantra. (2.639)
The essential nature of Sādākhya is endowed with these characteristics;
on its left side is the primordial power Manonmanī.
Just as heat is inseparable from fire, so too is power inseparable from the All-pervading Lord.
There is no Śiva devoid of power, nor is there power devoid of Śiva. (2.641)
Therefore, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is composed of Śiva;
[one should meditate on the Goddess] with one face, four hands, and adorned with all ornaments.
Broad at the slopes of her hips, slender in the waist, and elevated with full breasts,
she is endowed with the power of Vāmā and others, and is known by the name Manonmanī.

The Brahmā-mantras, the limbs (aṅgas), the Vidyās, the Vidyeśas, the Gaṇeśas, as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the weapons, are produced from that [source] in their respective order. (2.644)
All of them were surrounded by their respective retinues and endowed with their respective severed [limbs];
they were complete in all their limbs and possessed a radiance like that of infinite suns. (2.645)
Thus is the form of Sādāśiva, complete with its *liṅga* and *pīṭha*;
however, the power of that which is called Sādākhya cannot indeed be described.
The Sakala and Niṣkala have been declared; now hear about the Sakala.
The forms beginning with Īśvara are proclaimed as the Sakalas. (2-647)
Just as Sadāśiva has been described, so too is Īśvara said [to be];
one should likewise arrange the enclosure beginning with Brahmā as before. (2.648)
One should know that Sambhu, who abides in the principle of Vidyā and is endowed with all auspicious marks, is the Liṅga; Maheśvara, together with the Golaka, is the Sakala.
At the conclusion of the Linga worship, one should worship Īśvara in due order.
It is said that the arising of Rudra occurs from a thousandth part of Īśvara. (2.650)
The four-armed, three-eyed god has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel; endowed with the brilliance of lightning, he holds an axe and a deer as weapons.
With all his limbs complete and adorned with every ornament, he stands;
and on his left side is the goddess Umā, endowed with all auspicious marks.
From a ten-millionth part of Īśvara, however, arises the Viṣṇu-tattva;
Hari is dark-complexioned, with beautiful red arms, and bears the conch and the discus. (2.653)
With palms joined in reverence, one should likewise fashion the feet of the pedestal;
for from the tip of that Viṣṇu’s [pedestal] arises the origin of Brahmā.
He has four arms and four faces, wears a crown of matted hair, holds a water-pot and a rosary, is yellowish-red in color, and possesses beautiful eyes. (2.655)
Sāvitrī and Bhāratī are at his sides; he is remembered as the embodiment of creation (sṛṣṭimūrti).
Rudra is the embodiment of withdrawal (saṃhāramūrti), and Viṣṇu is the embodiment of maintenance (sthitimūrtika). (2-656)
The one renowned as Sṛṣṭimūrti and Brahmā are considered to be threefold;
these three forms are said to be established within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

The Niṣkala (partless) is the place of dissolution, while the Makāra is both Sakala-niṣkala (with-part and partless). The Sakala is the place of enjoyment; it possesses the authority over both dissolution and enjoyment. (2-658)

O Lord of the South, it is said that the other [form] is partless (niṣkala) and wonderful; indeed, the "with-parts" (sakala) and the "partless" (niṣkala) are recited as being distinct from one another.
But another dance is always to be meditated upon by him who is capable and the destroyer of bonds;
thereafter come the three deities from whom the thirty-three arise.
First, the eleven Rudras, joined by the twelve Ādityas;
the eight Vasus and the two Aśvins—these are the thirty-three deities. (2.661)
And thirty thousand million gods indeed create a body for themselves within those three forms by means of the essence of the elements.
Through the connection with the stainless sovereignty, the heart shall destroy [ignorance];
having meditated upon the Lord as the cause of all, one should contemplate the dancing Īśvara.
Then, with flowers in hand and seated upon a seat, one should invoke the God—
the all-pervading Sadāśiva— while recollecting the root mantra and meditating upon the Supreme Lord.
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva as the Supreme, one should perform the invocation with the Sadyojāta mantra;
the installation with the Vāmadeva mantra, and the confinement with the Aghora mantra.
The human being should maintain proximity [to the deity], while the worship is performed by Īśāna;
just as the fire situated within the sacrificial pit is made to blaze forth by means of the wind.
In that very same way, the Lord Śiva is generated by means of the name-mantra;
having invoked him with the mudrā called Āvāhinī and established him with the Sthāpinī mudrā.
Then [he should display] the five-faced cow-mudrā, the power-mudrā (śaktimudrā), thereafter the harsh one,
the linga-mudrā, and the mudrās of the lotus-eye and the weapon.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as before with the five Brahmans and the six limbs, and one should offer perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp. (2.669)
O Maheśvara, listen now to this specific form of the *liṅga*:
the base of the *liṅga* is said to be the feet, and the tip of the *liṅga* is called the mouth. (2.670)
The two sides of the thread are the four arms, and the end of the thread is called the back.
From Īśvara, Brahmā arises toward the south for the sake of creation. (2-671)
To the left of Īśvara is Viṣṇu, the cause of maintenance;
from the nose, Vāyu arose, and from the two ears, the ten directions. (2.672)
He who arose from the lotus-hand is celebrated as Gaṇeśa;
the six-faced one was born from the heart, and Bhāskara was produced from the navel.
Indra was born from the back, Agni emerged from the eye;
the god known as Soma emerged from the left eye. (2.674)
The Yakṣas and gods [arose] from his two breasts; Rudra from his right eye;
weapons issued from the tips of his hands; and the Sandhyās were born from his nails.
From his thighs were born the serpents, from his knees the sages,
from his feet all the gods, and from him arose the knowledge of Śiva.

At the time of reabsorption, one should worship the Sādākhya [deity] in the center of the form of the Liṅga, which is the primordial cosmic dance (tāṇḍava) wherein everything attains the state of being a liṅga.
O Maheśvara, I shall describe the sequence of the bestowal of grace by Mahāsadāśiva:
he who has five faces, five heads, and three eyes in each face. (2.678)
He is serene, possessing sixteen arms, a single body, and four necks;
he has ten ears, two feet, and a face slightly smiling.
In the right [hands], there is, in sequence, a trident, an arrow, a vajra, a sword, an axe, a wheel, and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), as well as the gesture of fearlessness (abhayamudrā).
He holds in his left hands a bell, a serpent, a noose, a bow, a goad, a shield, a foot, and an expression of wonder. (2.681)

Endowed with the Primordial Power (Ādiśakti) and having a black serpent as his sacred thread, one should offer [the oblation] to the faces and heads with the Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and other mantras. (2.682)
Having recited the *sadyojāta* mantra, one should offer water for the feet at the [deity's] feet;
with the *vakra* mantra, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth in the mouths.
With the Īśāna mantra, one should offer the mirror upon the heads;
with the Vāma mantra, the fragrance upon the faces; and with the Īśāna mantra, the flowers upon the heads. (2.684)
Then, O Maheśvara, one should offer incense with the *sadyojāta* mantra, a lamp with the *ghora* mantra, and an offering of food (*naivedya*) with the *vaktra* mantra, in due order. (2.685)
One should prepare milk mixed with cardamom, camphor, jasmine, and sandalwood,
using the five Brahmans and the six limbs [of the mantra], while forming the *dhenumudrā*.
While reciting the seed-mantra of the root-prakṛti,
one should utter the seed-syllable of Varuṇa and fill the water vessel.
Thereafter, with the mantras of Īśa and the others, one should gradually perform the consecration;
in the four directions and the four corners, one should cause the water for rinsing and the arghya offering to be presented.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water infused with kuśa grass;
the urine should be three times the amount of the dung, and the ghee should be four times the amount of the urine.
Curd is said to have five qualities, and milk should have eight qualities.
Cow urine has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and cow dung has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
Milk has Rudra as its presiding deity; curd is said to belong to Maheśa;
clarified butter has Sadasat as its deity; one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
In the *Pañcasāra*, one should present the food offering (*naivedya*) and display the *jñānamudrā*.
[One should recite] *devasya tvā*, *agnimīle*, *ā vo rājā*, and *tryambakam*. (2-692)
The procedure for the five products of the cow has been declared; now hear the ritual for the water of fruits:
the wood-apple, the plantain, and two oranges.
One should worship the mango, the *kelī* fruit, and the water from the *tintriṇī* fruit by reciting their respective name-mantras and offering perfumes, flowers, and other such articles.
The ritual for fruit and water has been declared; now hear the ritual for seed and water:
barley, wild rice, mung beans, and rice grains for the sake of success. (2.695)
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings this auspicious *saugandhika* golden rice and seed-water while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlabīja*), [one should proceed]. (2.696)
The procedure for seed-water has been declared; now hear the procedure for jewel-water:
ruby, agate, topaz, and emerald. (2.697)
One should worship coral, crystal, blue [gems], and the auspicious water containing pearl-jewels with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, using the Varṇa-mantra. || 2.698 ||
Thus has the water of jewels been described; now hear the procedure for the scented water:
sandalwood, costus, black pepper, and saffron. (2.699)
Kaccola, picchilā, musk (kastūrī), as well as agallochum (agaru), uśīra, clove (lavaṅga), and likewise the campaka bud.
One should offer the oblation of perfumes and so forth with the name-mantra.
Thus has the procedure for the water of perfumes been explained; now hear the rule for the water of flowers. (2.701)
The *caṃpaka* blossom, the *mallikā*, the *pāṭalī*, the *ketakī*, the mountain flower (*giripuṣpa*), the *punnāga*, and the *kunda* as well. (2-702)
The *nandyāvarta*, *śriyāvarta*, *mandāra*, *karavīraka*, jasmine, blue lotus, and *hrīvera* and other such [plants] are mixed together. (2.703)
One should offer incense, flowers, and incense smoke with the Śiva-mantra.
Thus has the offering of water with flowers been described; now hear the procedure for the worship with food.
Likewise, the consecration with foods increases longevity and health;
food is the supreme essence of life, established for all living beings. (2-705)
Therefore, the consecration with food is auspicious and pleasing to me;
it is specifically known as being of two kinds: the form of food and the form of the Immortal (Amṛta). || 2-706 ||
The ritual of food-offering (annapūjā) is supreme; it has never been equaled in the past, nor will it ever be so in the future.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the consecration using food alone. (2.707)
Having offered [the image] its gender-mark and form, one should present perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, milk-rice, and also betel-leaf. (2.708)
The ritual for the offering of food (annapūjā) is eternally auspicious, accomplishing all aims; it conquers untimely death, is purifying, and bestows prosperity upon kings and kingdoms. (2.709)
Perform the offering of food, the supreme means of subjugation, the fulfillment of the sacrificial fee, the pure rite that brings about all peace, and victory through the worship of food. (2.710)
The seed-syllable of the Mother is supreme; therefore, food is proclaimed [as her form].
He who performs the worship of food attains the highest goal. (2.711)
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship with food alone;
having performed the rinsing of the food, one should install the root-syllables in their proper sequence.
One should cause the offering of perfume, flowers, incense, and likewise lamps.
The procedure for the worship with food has been declared; now hear the procedure for the worship with water.
As before, this consecrated water should be filled in a vessel made of gold,
or else one of silver, copper, or a sacrificial tree.
One should place Dakṣiṇeśvara in the middle of that water;
one should offer dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, unbroken rice, and flowers to Dakṣiṇeśvara.
One should cause the offering of perfume, flowers, incense, and likewise lamps; as well as water-worship, secret recitation (japa), and that which is beautiful and provides stability. (2.716)
It brings about all accomplishments, is pure, and destroys all diseases;
it consists of consecrations, times for recitation, and mantras.
The *Tryambaka*, the *Umārudra*, the *Āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the *Śaṃ ca me*, the *Īleśataḥ*, the *Kadrudra*, the *Namaḥ te*, and the *Sadasaspatim*. (2-718)
Jātavedas, Īśāna, Haṃsa, and Ātman; likewise Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Vāma, and Sadyojāta and the others thereafter. (2.719)
"Sahasraśīrṣā," "Annapat," "Pūṣan," "Imā āpaḥ," "Agnim īḷe," "Ye devāsaḥ," "Agne mama agne," and "Gauri devi" [are the verses] in the invocation of the gods. (2-720)
"O Agni, you [are] the King of the Waters; that is the Truth of Savitṛ.
"Om"—this is the Brahmasāman; all these begin with the Praṇava. (2.721)
Having recited the thirty-six mantras individually and once each in sequence for the purpose of consecration, one should perform the consecration slowly and steadily. (2.722)
The ritual procedure for water-worship has been declared; now the characteristics of the vessel are described:
it may be made of gold, silver, or likewise produced from copper.
A conch shell, or mother-of-pearl, or even a horn of cattle, or else a vessel made of clay—any of these is recommended as a bathing vessel. (2.724)
Having consecrated [the vessel] with the five Brahmans— one filled to the brim with the best [grains] and the middle one filled with *śiva*— one should tie the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*).
While slowly and gradually reciting the mantra of the name, one should perform the consecration;
having fashioned an image of food as the form [of the deity], one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara in front of it.
Having meditated, one should cause the fragrance and flower to be offered while reciting the name;
then, ending with incense and lamps, one should offer the food oblation while reciting the name. (2.727)
One should recite the mantra "Aṇṇapūrṇe" everywhere; even that which is half-filled with an āḍhaka becomes a full āḍhaka. (2.728)
One should fill conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and horn-horns with their own respective measures;
one should wrap them all around with thread, leaving an interval resembling a lattice window.

Having prepared the sacrificial ground according to the rules with rice, unbroken grains, and sesame seeds, one should arrange eight *āḍhakas* or half of that amount of water in separate jars for each. (2.730)
One should take half a measure of śāli rice, half of that amount of sesame seeds likewise, along with ritual brooms,
cloth, and gems, all placed upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The preceptor should worship the jars, which are especially adorned;
Rudra is the deity at the mouth of the jar, and Mādhava is the deity in its center.
The *pṛṣṭha* chant should belong to Prajāpati, and the deities presiding over the water-jar (kalaśa) [should be worshipped];
one should offer perfume, flowers, and incense with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. || 2.733 ||
One should worship Naṭeśvara— though formless, yet manifesting in form— in the center of the great mirror or at the tip of the liṅga,
as the Lord of the southern door.
One should perform the consecration or the excellent anointing either upon a mirror or upon a fine liṅga;
these two places of worship are secret and wonderful, being the southern abode.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe the sequence of consecration in detail:
having uttered the name-mantra while recollecting the three-syllable mantra. (2.736)
Having bathed [the image] with pure water measured by the tip of a cow's horn from the tips of one's hands, one should likewise apply a coating of turmeric.
One should cause fragrant *āmalaka* fruit and incense to be offered;
then, with pure scented water, one should perform the consecration very slowly. (2.738)
Having recited the name-mantra once, one should place a flower upon the head;
at that time, one should cause the water for the feet, the water for sipping, and the respectful offering (arghya) to be presented.
Taking a clean cloth, one should fashion the garment-seal (vastramudrā);
one should then cause that cloth to enter the linga, the pedestal, and the site. || 2-740 ||
Having taken the cloth for entry, one should cause it to be offered to Caṇḍeśa;
with the mantra beginning "vāstoṣpate," one should worship Vāstunātha. (2.741)
Indra should perform the sprinkling over these [substances] on the left with the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭhā";
then, taking a fine cloth, he should bind it with the heart-mantra (hṛdayāṇu).
Having wrapped the *liṅga* with a cloth in four parts,
one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* in sequence, starting from Īśāna and ending at Sadyojāta, using one part [of the cloth].
And for Manonmanī up to the end of the sacred seats (pīṭha), there is the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) of the limbs and so forth;
likewise, sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and the lordly [substances].
One should cause flowers, garlands, and the sacred thread to be offered with the Īśa-mantra;
having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times, one should worship that fragrance.
One should cause the necklaces, shoulder-ornaments, and bracelets to be given with the heart-mantra;
one should cause the ring and the crown to be given with the root-mantra. || 2-746 ||
One should worship the pure waters of the Gaṅgā at the tips of one's matted locks with the first part of one's own name;
having recited the Astra-mantra a hundred times, one should [protect] the Khaṭvāṅga with the Kavaca-mantra.
One should offer incense and perform a dance before the five faces of the Lord;
incense and lamps should be presented accompanied by the ringing of a bell. (2-748)
One should again offer water for sipping while reciting the Śiva-mantra once;
at that time, having removed the cloth, one should ring the bell.
At the time of worshipping the deity, one should worship the supreme concealed cloth,
as well as the fire of time (kālāgni), the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), and the fire of Śiva (śivāgni).
There, upon seeing Śiva, one should place a tripod atop [the pedestal] in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even bell-metal.
Having prepared an excellent [mandala] made of rice flour or else of cow dung, provided with nine squares and endowed with the pericarp of a lotus. (2.752)
One should sprinkle the heart with the fruit of the *astaśastra* [mantra];
then, one should fill the hollow of both hands with two *bhāra* measures of the powder ground from *gomuṣṭi*.
With five wicks made from pure cotton fibers,
joined together and soaked in the ghee of a tawny cow, [one should place them] upon the pericarp in the four directions.
Having uttered the syllable-mantra conjoined with fire by means of the mantras beginning with *sadya* and ending with *īśāna*, the wise preceptor [should proceed]. (2.755)
Having bound the *surabhi-mudrā*, immediately thereafter the *dīpa-mudrā*, one should hold the divine vessel with both hands while reciting the mantra. (2.756)
Having performed three circumambulations, especially around the top of the *liṅga*,
and having sprinkled it with the *arghya* water, one should likewise take up the sacred ashes (*bhasman*).
Having recited the Śiva-mantra once, one should place the root-mantra in sequence;
at the end of that, while uttering the Śakti-mantra, one should present the mirror.
Having uttered the Aghora mantra, one should cause the fan to be offered;
then, with the Hṛdaya mantra, one should cause the parasol and the fly-whisk to be offered. || 2-759 ||
Having recited the Vāyu mantra, one should cause the two sandals to be offered;
thereafter, one should present a handful of flowers with the mudrā known as namaskāra.
Then, having performed an embrace, one should cause the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) to be bestowed;
one should offer vessels of flames with the head and with both hands.
The supreme Rudra-gaṇikā and the celibate student (brahmacārī) should maintain [the practice];
one should place a lamp in the eastern direction upon water contained within a golden pitcher.
One should cause all the musical instruments to be played upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, the characteristics of the recitation (japa) are described.
Japa is said to be fourfold for all those who desire to perform recitation: mental, that which involves the throat and lips, whispered, and clearly articulated. (2.764)
Dust [japa] is ten times more effective than the manifest; that from the throat and lips is a hundredfold;
that from the mind is a thousandfold; now hear about japa performed with the fingers.
Counting with the fingers yields a single fruit;
that which is performed with the fire-vessel (agnikoṣṭha) is said to be ten thousandfold, bestowing sons and illumination. (2-766)
A rosary made of kuśa-grass knots has a value of one hundred; one made of coral has a thousand;
one made of crystal has ten thousand; but for those made of rudrākṣa beads, there is no limit.

One should perform rites for liberation with the thumb, rites of sorcery with the index finger, rites for desire with the middle finger, and one should effect pacification with the ring finger. (2.768)
Now listen to the sequence of deities for the drawing in of the best of poets:
the thumb has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and the ring finger has Rudra as its presiding deity. (2.769)

The middle finger has Dakṣārhā as its presiding deity, the ring finger has Dharmā as its presiding deity, and the little finger has Sūrya as its presiding deity; now hear the fruit of the place for recitation.
One should obtain the fruit of one [recitation] when in a house, a thousand when in a cow-pen,
two thousand on a riverbank, and ten thousand is considered the result when on a mountain.
In the ocean there are ten crores of divine abodes, and they are innumerable;
but within those divine abodes, the southern gate is especially the primary abode.
Recalling the auspicious dance that grants all perfections in those various places, a man who recites it a thousand times, or half of that, or a hundred times, [attains success]. (2.773)
Through constant union with this [mantra], there is the destruction of all sins;
merely by its recitation, one goes to the imperishable world of Śiva. (2.774)
And listen, O Maheśvara, to the characteristics of the food offering (naivedya):
white rice, great rice, red rice, or barley. (2.775)

Black rice, wild grain (nīvāra), bamboo-seed rice, or even mung beans—let these be taken for the purpose of the rice-offering, as they are the primary substances for the food offering (naivedya). (2-776)
Having been produced from the four castes and crushed again and again by those [women],
he should be heated in the rays of the sun and likewise thrown onto a grindstone.
Facing either the east or the north, having struck with the pestle,
one should avoid [the wood] that has three joints at the top and that which resembles a conch shell.
With reference to the ninefold path, one should prepare the food offering (naivedya) there;
having worshipped at dawn and evening, one should likewise present it at midday.
At that time, having cooked two *prasthas* [of food], one should offer it;
there should be one lamp at the two daily times, and two lamps at night. (2.780)
Having worshipped at dawn and at midday with two *prastha* measures of rice as an oblation,
one should offer double the amount of a lamp in the evening.
One should offer two *prasthas* at each of the two times;
four lamps are prescribed, but one should give double that amount in the evening.
For the middling [vessel] at the lowest [grade], it is prescribed that one should give an āḍhaka of rice at midday;
at two times of day, the quantity is two prasthas, and there should be twenty lamps.
In the three middle [mandalas], however, the wise and learned practitioner should offer oblations three times a day, joined with the mantra of the first path, using the *baliliṅga* [mantra].
One should know that from the middle [period] comes the middling [offering]; at the three times of day, the sacrificial oblation (havis) is one āḍhaka.
However, the worship performed at midnight is said here to last for one and a half watches (yāma).
Three times a day, accompanied by offerings of food, flowers, and dice,
and joined with the sound of musical instruments, it was endowed with dance and song.
At midday, there should be the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) accompanied by incense and lamps.
I shall now describe the superior [practice] from the middling one: three *āḍhakas* at each of the three times of day.
And having offered [the oblation] three times a day, accompanied by fifty lamps;
or twice a day, accompanied by musical instruments and twenty courtesans.

From the highest [vessel] there, one should take one *droṇa* every three periods; for half a watch (*yāma*), however, one should take half a *droṇa*. There should be one hundred and eight lamps. (2.789)
The food-offering should take place at the three times of day, joined with oblations at those same three times;
it should be accompanied by all musical instruments and provided with dance and song.
Or one thousand and eight, or a hundred, of Rudrakanyās,
endowed with beauty and youth, and adorned with all ornaments.
In that [rite], at the three times of day, one should cook four sacrificial offerings— such as milk-rice and others— using a *droṇa* measure of rice from the middle [portion].
Having had pure food cooked separately by the measure of a *droṇa*, there should be a *droṇa* [of oil] even for half a watch, as well as two hundred lamps. (2.793)

At the three periods of the day, one should prescribe the bali-offering, the homa, and incense for the Śītāris, accompanied by all musical instruments and the proclamation of all auspicious verses. (2.794)
Accompanied by eight hundred courtesans and filled with the sound of hymns and musical instruments, one should perform the dance at the two junctions of time (the twilights), as it is taught. (2.795)
With reference to the most excellent of the excellent, the sequence of sacrificial oblations (haviṣya) is now declared:
having cooked milk-rice (pāyasa) with six droṇas of rice grains.
At midnight, five hundred auspicious lamps [should be offered];
at the three times of day, two *bhāras* of pure rice and clean cooked food [should be given].
There should be offerings and fire-oblations at the three times of day, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments;
one should especially perform a dance consisting of two hundred and sixteen [beats].

Thus, the ninefold procedure for the offering, beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa) and so forth in sequence, has been declared. The fourfold [offering] consists of milk-rice, kṛsara, bhakṣya, and pure food (śuddhānna). (2.799)
(82) Twice the amount of rice, combined with milk and plantain fruit, with one-fourth part of mung beans split open, and mixed with jaggery according to one's capacity. (2.800)
This is declared to be milk-rice (*pāyasa*); now hear about *kṛsara*-rice:
having added a fourth part of sesame powder to the rice, [one should prepare it]. (2.801)
Having cooked that clarified butter in a fourth part [of the liquid] according to the prescribed rule, this is called *kṛsāra* rice; now hear about *gulānna*.
Having prepared half a *bhāra* of rice, or half a *bhāra* of *taṇḍula*, one should add half a *guḷa* of split mung beans and one *prastha* of milk. (2.803)
Listen to the characteristics for cooking half or a quarter *droṇa* of ghee:
having first performed the ritual bath and being devoted to the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), [one should proceed]. (2.804)
Wearing a white sacred thread and clad in white garments, being pure,
he should wash his feet and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rules.
One should apply the auspicious triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the previously mentioned procedure,
with the sacred thread in hand, observing silence, and constantly reciting the Śiva-mantra.
Having first washed the rice grains with six portions of water,
the wise one should purify them with the principal seed-mantra.
One should fill it with pure water and an excess of rice;
then, having kindled the fire with the *śikhā* mantra, one should offer these [substances] with the *astra* mantra.
With the *puruṣa* mantra, one should [offer] the *maulī* in the west;
with the *nirīkṣya-netra* mantra, the cooked *caru* should be offered by one who is elevated.
Thereafter, one should douse it with clarified butter while recollecting the Vāma-mantra;
then, one should examine whether it is well-cooked by means of the Tatpuruṣa-mantra.
