One should purify the auspicious vessel (*subhāṇḍa*) and the side [of the body] with the Aghora mantra alone.
One should apply a triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) one finger-width wide upon the vessels using ashes. (2.812)
One should worship the embankment with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
likewise, one should worship all the vessels in this manner. (2.813)
With the mantra consisting of the syllable *huṃ* alone, the practitioner of mantras should raise everything up in sequence and install it in due order on the western side of the pavilion.
One should cause the oblation to be prepared with side-dishes and other items;
the vessels for the offering may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even a plantain leaf. (2.815)
One should bring [the offering] in a vessel of pure bell-metal or even one made of palāśa wood;
it may be a small bowl or a vessel standing upon three legs in the middle. (2.816)
Taking a golden vessel endowed with all auspicious marks, which is six units in height, most excellent, and covered with pure cotton— (2.817)
One should first pour clarified butter over it, then fill the cooking vessel with cooked food;
the offering to Śiva should consist of sacrificial food (haviṣya) and the like, served in a covered vessel.
Having a form resembling the full moon, with fingers separated like mung beans,
it should be accompanied by fruits, all kinds of side dishes, and cow's clarified butter.
Having performed the inspection and other rites, and having concealed [the offering] with the heart-mantra,
one should bind the Surabhi-mudrā while reciting the heart-mantra.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra once, one should offer it with the Hrīṃ-mantra;
the bali for the retinue should consist of one part out of four parts.
The wise practitioner should perform the fire offering (homa) with one part out of four parts;
that which remains in the vessel is here called the "one part of the four parts. (2.822)
One should offer half [of the remainder] to Śakti and half of that remaining portion in the vessel. Then, having again offered water for sipping (ācamana), one should offer fragrant water.
Thereafter, one should cause betel-leaf to be given, accompanied by all ornaments;
one should cause the leaf to be given with three times as much fruit and combined with oil.
One should cause the offering of fruits and flowers to be presented with the heart-mantra;
and one should also give every kind of special substance to Caṇḍeśvara.
The procedure for the disposal of the *nirmālya*:
The *nirmālya* of Sadāśiva is not to be eaten by any living beings;
it may be consumed by animals, elephants, or cast into the waters. (2.826)
The attendants should receive all the offerings;
just as the remains of one's own guru are to be eaten, so too [should be the remains] of the son and the disciple. (2.827)
And for all [these acts], the offering of food and so forth must indeed be presented to the Guru alone;
if another person were to take that food, it would cause a defect. (2.828)
The characteristics of the food offering (naivedya) have been declared; now hear, O best of men, about the enclosures:
the womb, the sciences, Gaṇeśas, the world-protectors, and the five weapons. (2.829)
Having established [the deity] at the base of the lotus, one should worship the inner enclosure;
likewise, one should worship the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) on half of the lotus, and the Ganeśas on half of that.
One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) at the tips of the lotus petals, and then the weapons upon the lotus.
The eastern face is Puruṣa, whose body is reddish-brown like saffron.
One should worship Aghora in the south, possessing a luster like split collyrium;
and Sadyojāta in the west, with a luster resembling cow’s milk.
To the north is Vāmadeva, resembling the *japā* flower;
all the Brahmā-deities likewise have three eyes and four arms. (2.833)

One should worship the heart, which is white in color and located in the northeastern direction (Īśāna), with its beautiful lotus-like hands holding a trident, an axe, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
One should worship the red-colored head in the western direction, and the yellow-colored crest (śikhā) in the south-eastern direction. || 2.835 ||
One should worship the armor, which has the luster of the rising sun, in the position of Vāyu;
the eye in the northeast corner; and the weapon to the south and north.
And all the deities of the six limbs have three eyes and four arms, bearing a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, a skull-bowl, and the gesture of granting boons.
The Raudra weapon and the Netra weapon are fierce, while the remaining ones are known as gentle;
likewise are Kaṃbī, Gaṇāmbikā, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, and Umā.
Vāmī, Nīlī, Cakrī, Śaṅkhī, Khaṭvāṅgī, and Tvasī—these indeed are declared to be the ten powers of conceiving an embryo (garbhavaraṇa). || 2.839 ||
Now listen to the sequence of the divine powers (devaśakti) in the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśāvaraṇa):
one should install them starting from Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin, beginning from the eastern petal and proceeding in order. (2.840)
Ananta, Sūkṣmasaṃjña, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin. (2.841)
These eight lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras) have three eyes and four arms; they carry a battle-axe, a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and likewise the gesture of granting boons.
O Lord of Knowledge, the colors are, in sequence: red, white, blue, yellow, black, and saffron-like collyrium.
Bhūti, Medhā, Kānti, Prabhā, Tuṣṭi,
as well as Śruti and Medhā— these are the eight powers (śaktis) of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
The enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge has been described; now hear about the enclosure of Gaṇeśas.
One should worship Gaurī in the north, and one should worship Vṛṣabha in the east. (2.845)
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa in the south, one should worship Nandīśa in the west;
Mahākāla in the southwest, and Hṛṅgīśa in the northwest.
One should worship Caṇḍeśa in the northeastern direction and Ṣaṇmukha in the southeastern direction;
they have two eyes and two arms, are dark-complexioned, and [the goddess] Gaurī holds a lotus in her hand.
The bull is white in color, with sharp horns and great strength;
he has the face of an elephant, three eyes, the luster of saffron, and four arms.
Holding a noose in his right hand and a *kuśalaḍḍuka* (a type of sweetmeat) in his left, he has four arms and three eyes, and is the color of a hibiscus flower. (2.849)
At all the gates and other locations are the deities; the illustrious Śrī Nandī is the leader of the gods, holding a vajra and a tomara with his palms joined in reverence.
Four-armed and three-eyed, with a luster like a dark rain cloud,
he bears a sword, a vajra, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.
One should meditate upon Bhṛṅgin, who has two arms and two eyes, is endowed with the banner and the gesture of fearlessness, is smoke-colored, and destroys bad dreams. (2.852)
Four-armed and three-eyed, Caṇḍośa is the fierce leader;
blue in color, he holds the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, as well as a trident and a battle-axe.
Mahāsena is red in color, six-faced, and has the peacock as his vehicle;
he is endowed with twelve eyes and possesses twelve arms.
A trident, a vajra, a sword, an arrow, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*),
an axe, a bell, a peacock, a shield, a boon-granting gesture (*vara*), and likewise a goad.
Having worshipped the commander of the divine army, one should offer rice mixed with jujube fruits (gulānna).
Bhadrā, Devayānī, Kānti, Kālī, and Mantriṇī—[these are the goddesses]. (2.856)
Mālinī, Virūpī, Mandī, and Caṇḍā are the eight Śaktis;
this is declared to be the Gaṇeśa enclosure. Now hear about the Lokeśa enclosure. (2.857)

One should worship Indra, armed with the thunderbolt, in the eastern fire; Agni, bearing the spear, in the southeast; Yama, the bearer of the staff, in the south; and Nirṛti, with a sword in hand, in the southwest. (2.858)
One should worship Varuṇa, the lord of waters, holding a noose in his hand, in the western quarter; and Vāyu, holding a goad in his hand, in the northwestern direction. || 2-859 ||
One should worship Gadāhasta in a place peaceful with sleep;
one should worship Śūlahasta in the northeastern direction.
White, red, black, blue, yellow,
smoke-colored, yellowish-white, and pure white are, in sequence, the splendors of the World-Lords.
The elephant, goat, buffalo, lion, crocodile, deer, horse, and bull are, in order, the eight vehicles of the guardians of the directions. (2.862)
Śacī, Svāhā, Sudevī, and likewise the one named Vilobhinī;
Kālakaṇṭhī, Nīlī, and the goddess Jitakāri. (2.863)

These eight Śaktis are proclaimed in succession as belonging to the World-Guardians (Lokeśas). The enclosure of the World-Guardians has been described; now the enclosure of the Sun (Saura) is being stated.
Sūryadeva, Mahāśāstra, Brahmā, Vighneśvara, Sarasvatī, Jyeṣṭhā, Viṣṇu, and Kṣetrapālaka. || 2-865 ||
The ruby is coral-colored, the gold is intensely red,
the crystal is smoke-colored, and the emerald is dark with a black luster, in that order.
Uṣā and Pratyuṣā, Siṃhikī and Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī and Kalyāṇī, Jñānī and Ānandadāyinī. (2.867)
Praguṇī, Śīlābhūmī, and the goddess Supālinī are declared to be the Sauramāvaraṇa; now hear about the Astrāvaraṇa.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, as well as the goad, the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus—these indeed are the weapons. (2.869)
Śakti and Gadā are female in form, while Pāśa and Padma are neuter;
the remaining [weapons] are masculine in action, each having one face and two arms.
Yellow is the form of Vidyujjapā; coral has the luster of gold;
and there are the ruby, the pravāla, the black, the white, and the red.
Kālinī, Virūpī, Vāruṇī, and likewise Vimukhī; Nīlinī, Sammukhī, Mardinī, and Bhṛṅgamālinī.
One should worship these powers of the weapons with their respective names;
this is called the "weapon-envelopment" (astrāvaraṇa), and one should worship it beneath the petals.
Between Gaṇeśa and Lokeśa, one should worship the Seven Mothers:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
One should worship Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and the Seven Mothers, as well as Vīrabhadra and Vighneśa, in the eastern direction. (2.875)
One should worship the Lord of Yakṣas according to the rules in the northern direction,
and one should cast an offering upon the sacrificial pedestal for all spirits and piśācas.
If the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) is installed outside the outer gate, or if it is installed in another location, the king and his kingdom will perish. (2.877)
O Maheśvara, I shall describe the sequence for the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) in detail:
at the end of the staff (daṇḍa) within the inner mandala, the auspicious pedestal (bhadrapīṭha) is established.
Within the middle of the internal necklace (antarhārā), the pedestal for the vehicle is said to be located;
at the end of the middle necklace, one should fashion the flower-pedestal.
The courtyard pedestal (aṅgaṇapīṭha) is established at the foundation of the boundary-markers (maryādā) and so forth;
however, one should fashion the offering pedestal (balipīṭha) outside the great boundary-markers. (2.880)
[One should offer] that which is joined with perfumes, flowers, and water, and provided with incense and lamps,
to Vṛṣa, Yakṣeśāna, and the Mahākāla-gaṇa.
Having performed the worship of the great seat (mahāpīṭha), which is accompanied by all the hosts of gods—
the gods, the ancestors, the sages, the Daityas, and the Dānavas— [one attains success].
Yakṣas and rākṣasas, as well as nāgas, bhūtas, and viśācakas;
kinnaras and apsarases, and likewise the maruts and mātrkas.
The Anāvṛṣṭi hosts, the Rohiṇī hosts,
the Kumāra hosts, the Kūśmāṇḍa hosts, and likewise the eighteen hosts.
One should worship the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas in the center of the pedestal, Prajāpati [in the center], and all beings and piśācas outside the pedestal. (2.885)
One should place Vṛṣabha in the eastern quarter, Īśa in the south,
Mahākāla in the west, and the host of gods in the north.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should cause the *bali* offering to be presented everywhere;
specifically, three *balis* should be offered in the middle, the southern, and the northern regions of the pericarp.
One should cause the offerings to be presented in due order to Prajāpati, the gods, and the sages, extending from the Nāgas up to Īśāna, and to the ancestors and others.
Having performed the cleansing and sprinkling, one should again perform the auspicious worship,
offering fragrance, flowers, incense, and the sprinkling separately for each.
One should cause an offering (bali) the size of a fist or half of that to be given everywhere;
one should cause perfume and flowers to be offered with a mantra beginning with one's own name. || 2-890 ||
The procedure for the sacrificial pedestal has been declared; now hear the procedure for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
I shall explain the fire-ritual which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
The rite of fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
(p. 90) Three lines facing east represent Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara as their presiding deities. (2-892)
Having prepared the sacrificial ground as before, perform the generation of the Śiva-fire;
that produced from a sun-crystal is the best, while that from *maraṇi* wood would be middling.
One should especially bring forth the Jātavedas fire of the Vedas into a vessel made of gold,
silver, copper, the seven metals, or even clay.
Having cast that fire there while reciting the Śivatantra, one should purify it with the Astra-mantra and enclose it with the Kavaca-mantra. || 2-895 ||
One should visualize [the seat] as being rendered immortal by means of the primary seed-mantra;
then, one should place the grass mat together with flowers upon either the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus provided with a pericarp,
one should invoke Vāgīśī, the performer of sacrifice, into its center.
One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings as having bathed after her season;
thereafter, one should meditate upon the god Maheśvara, who has three eyes and four arms.
One should also meditate upon him there as endowed with all the primary marks, adorned with every auspicious sign, and united with the goddess Vāgīśvarī. (2.899)
Having circumambulated that sacrificial pit three times while reciting the heart-mantra once,
one should face the fire and, reciting "devasya tvā," place [the oblation] into the womb [of the fire].
Having recited the heart-mantra, one should cast [the substances] and collect them together in one place;
afterwards, one should perform seven oblations while correctly reciting the heart-mantra. (2.901)
In the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), one should perform seven oblations to the Puruṣa;
in the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana), however, one should perform the fire-offering seven times with the head [of the mantra].
In the rite of birth (jātakarman), one should offer seven oblations with the left [hand];
and in the procedure for the naming rite (nāmakarman), one should offer seven oblations with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya). (2.903)
In the rite of eating food, one should indeed offer oblations with the head-mantra;
however, in the rite of tonsure and the rule for the sacred thread, one should perform it seven times with the heart-mantra.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *śiromantra*, the preceptor should perform the *samāvartana* rite;
and for the sake of marriage, he should offer oblations seven times with the *hṛnmantra*.
The offering of incense and lamps should be performed individually with the heart-mantra;
likewise, through the fire-oblation (homa) in this sequence, the auspicious birth from the Śiva-fire occurs.
Holding the *sṛk* and *sruva* ladles in the left hand, one should touch the tips with the tips of the *kuśa* grass held in the right hand, and touch the middles with the middles. (2-907)
One should touch the base with the bases; in this way, the purification of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is accomplished.
[Likewise] the clarified butter vessel, the sacrificial porridge vessel, the *praṇītā* vessel, and the *pātra* vessel [are purified]. (2.908)
One should wash [the vessel] with pure water while reciting the weapon-mantra (śastramantra).
One should fill the *praṇītā* vessel with water and cast a bundle of grass (*kūrca*) into it.
One should sprinkle the entire collection of oblation materials with those waters;
then, having filled the vessel for the clarified butter with *ājya* along with a *kūrca* grass-bundle.
Having thus circumambulated the fire three times clockwise,
one should then perform the placement of the clarified butter (ājya) in the western and northern directions.
Perform the sprinkling with the *hṛdaya* mantra, the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) with the *sadyojāta* mantra,
the inspection with the *netra* mantra, and the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

The placement of the enclosing sticks (paridhi) is auspicious when their tips point eastward and northward; one should worship the positions of the enclosing sticks starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna.
O Maheśvara, listen now to this meditation on the form of the auspicious fire:
it is of a single form, with two faces, four limbs, and two nostrils. (2.914)
Having three girdles, two feet, three eyes, and a triangular form;
wearing a sacred thread, with matted locks upon his head, and surrounded by seven tongues of flame.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Aruṇā, the one called Kṛṣṇā, the one named Suprabhā, Atiraktā, and Bahurūpā—these are proclaimed as the seven tongues. (2.916)
The golden one is situated in the western portion, the yellow one in the middle;
likewise, the red one is in the northern portion, and the black one is situated in the southern direction.
Suprabhā is in the eastern direction, extremely red in the location of Agni; Bahurūpā is in the northeast; these are proclaimed as the locations of the tongues. (2.918)
One should thus meditate upon the auspicious fire of Śiva, which brings about all peace;
in the center of the god of fire is Sādākhya, well-established.
Above that, one should worship Sādākhya facing the south,
offering water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, perfume, flowers, and incense.
One should cause a lamp, an offering of food, and betel to be given to Naṭeśvara;
with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and never with the *aghora-mantra*, one should offer the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into the fire.
One should offer clarified butter with the Puruṣa-mantra, parched grain (lāja) with the Ghorāstra-mantra,
groats (saktu) with the Vāma-mantra, and milk indeed with the Sadyojāta-mantra.
One should offer barley with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, cooked rice with the *sadyojāta-mantra*, sesame with the *īśāna-mantra*, and likewise green gram and black gram with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
At the end of each substance, one should perform a single oblation while reciting the Tryambaka mantra;
having muttered the Varṇa-mantra a hundred times, one should offer oblations with boiled rice.
One should constantly perform one thousand oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) for the conquest of untimely death,
and one separate homa for each of the deities of the five enclosures (pañcāvaraṇa).

Having offered an oblation with one’s own name, and having adorned [the deity] with a bell, incense, and so forth, one should afterwards offer betel-leaf, and then cause perfume and flowers to be presented. (2.926)
Having recited the three-syllabled mantra even once, one should perform the fire oblation while standing in the center;
one should constantly effect the embracing of the fire, which is of the nature of Śiva.
One should bind the *jñānamudrā* and take possession of that ash;
one should apply a triple-line mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with a single finger on the forehead, the two arms, and the heart. (2.928)
In the remaining twelve sectors, one should place the deity Agni in the middle of the primary triangle, with a measurement that is half and then half again of those [preceding].
One should establish the fire with the heart-mantras as being enveloped by garlands of flames;
one should meditate upon the Naṭa, whose nature is sound (nāda), resembling ten million suns.
Having meditated on Śiva, who abides in the form of light, one should mutter the mantra once.
The sequence for the fire-ritual has been declared; now hear the procedure for the daily festival.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the perpetual festival at the three times of day;
it bestows all accomplishments, is pure, and purifies all sins. (2.932)
The most auspicious of all auspicious things, the destroyer of all enemies, [it overcomes] the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, and likewise the nāgas. (2.933)
Having heard that sound of Bali, they will undoubtedly proceed;
in the southern part of the pavilion, there is a square mandala.
A vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal is said to be endowed with all auspicious characteristics and adorned with every mark of good fortune. (2.935)
The width of the bowl is said to be either one cubit or two cubits;
there, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with a height of two finger-breadths.
The pericarp therein should be one-third [of the diameter], with a height of two finger-breadths.
Having prepared it in this specific manner, one should place that vessel upon the mandala. (2.937)
One should perform the lowest of the low worship with an annaliṅga at midday;
the puṣpaliṅga in the forenoon, and that consisting of rice grains in the evening.
It is of three kinds: superior, middling, and finally, inferior.
The superior is said to be one āḍhaka, while the middling is half of that. (2.939)
Then, one should cook auspicious rice in five parts water;
it should be neither undercooked nor overcooked, and neither too hot nor too cold. (2.940)
One should fashion the food-offering with ghee, curd, and milk;
its height should be twelve finger-breadths, and its base should be double that.
The height is said to be two finger-breadths, and the circumference is stated to be two finger-breadths;
the middle part should be twelve finger-breadths, and the top should be three finger-breadths.
The lower part is said to be two finger-breadths, and the upper part should be one finger-breadth.
Having worshipped the enclosure of the Vidyā, listen to the sequence for the visualization of the deity.
Fierce, with three eyes and four arms, blazing with millions of points on his crest,
he holds a rosary and a trident, and displays the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting.
Having meditated upon the Lord Pāśupati, one should worship him in the *baliliṅga*;
one should perform the lotus-mudrā, the salutation, and fashion the peace-mudrā.
Having meditated upon the image within that liṅga, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
the most skilled in ritual procedures should then arrange the ten weapons around it.
Having taken up the lotus-seat (padmapīṭha), one should wear the sandals and maintain the topknot;
one should go to the east with the trident, and the staff of Śiva immediately thereafter.
Wearing a red turban and upper garment, adorned with a red garland, with a sacred thread in his hand, observing silence, and holding a staff one cubit in length. (2.948)
One should bear upon one's head a *liṅga* or an image that has been worshipped;
in the forenoon it brings pleasure to Brahmā, while at midday it is dear to Śiva. (2.949)
Now listen in due order to the meditation on Viṣṇu for the evening twilight and his propitiation;
the previously mentioned color of Brahmā has been stated, and now the color of Rudra is described.
Wearing a white turban and upper garment, and adorned with a white garland,
one should maintain my auspicious image at midday.
Wearing a yellow turban and a yellow upper garment, and adorned with a yellow garland,
one should wear the auspicious Liṅga in the evening, which brings pleasure to Viṣṇu.
One should sprinkle the disciple facing south with water while reciting the heart-mantra;
having established the deity upon his head, one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (2.953)
Whether mounted upon a palanquin, a vehicle, or a mechanical chariot, or else traveling on foot, one should perform the circumambulation. (2.954)
With kettledrums and maddalas, as well as jhallaris and victory-bells,
with kāhalas, tālas, and jaṅghas, and likewise with the sounds of lutes and flutes.
Equipped with a tail-fan and a chowrie, joined with a parasol and banners, provided with incense and lamps, and adorned above by a canopy. || 2-956 ||
It was accompanied by the dancing of courtesans and endowed with divine song; it was joined with the sound of those offering praise, consisting of songs and auspicious recitations. (2.957)
O Maheśvara, having performed three circumambulations of the temple, which was accompanied by the sound of the Vedas and endowed with divine dances, [he departed].
Having first performed a circumambulation accompanied by rhythmic clapping (tāla),
Bhṛṅgiṇī then proceeded silently through the city gate, joined by the sound of conch shells.
Accompanied by rhythmic singing and attended by the sound of the Vedas,
the second circumambulation was performed together with dance and instrumental music.
The *bhṛṅgīṇītāla* is employed for all [these], while the *ḍakkarī* is for the performer and the instrumentalist;
the *vakula* is for the *kuñcitā*, and likewise the *kūṭaka* for the *viṣama*.
Having circumambulated the outer seat (bāhyapīṭha) three times in a clockwise direction, [one performs] the offering of the *balitāla* and the *tālakam*. (2-962)
One shall prepare a vessel of bell-metal with a handle nine *tālas* long and a tip nine *koṭis* long,
and offer the sacrificial oblation (*balidāna*) in due order to the deities beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna.
At the time of dawn, one should perform the Gāndhāra; at midday, the Takkarāgaka; thereafter, one should perform the Kauśika; and likewise, at the evening hour, the Indala.
"O Maheśvara, at the fifth watch, at midnight, is the time for singing.
Thus, by these [means], the temple has been consecrated with three circumambulations.
Having performed the washing of the feet, one should begin the worship of the sandals (pādukā).
Regarding the worship of the sandals:
having uttered the heart-mantra, one should worship [the sandals] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (2–966)
One should cause water for the feet, a seat, the arghya offering, incense, and a lamp to be presented;
one should worship the image or the liṅga in the same manner as before, following the prescribed sequence. (2.967)
As before, one should install [the deity] in the eastern position with the weapon-mantra;
having worshipped the *baliliṅga*, one should install it on the outer pedestal.
Having worshipped the God of gods, one should offer salutation with the *caṃ* mudrā;
then, having performed circumambulation three times by way of both the right and the left,
one should perform the circumambulation which removes suffering, without crossing over the *somasūtra*.
Holy fords, giving, merit, asceticism, and likewise sacrifice—there is no circumambulation equal to these, which bestows the accomplishment of manifest results. (2-971)
O Maheśvara, listen as I describe the characteristics of the twice-born: those who observe the vow of silence, who do not think of anything else, and who contemplate Śiva. (2.972)

Having arrived, one should perform circumambulation of the celestial palace (vimāna). At the time of the offering (bali), however, there is a special rule regarding the preceptor (ācārya) who is served by his disciples. (2-973)
At other times, one should not cross a river that lacks defects; one should not step over a shadow-line, nor the shadow of a cow, a Brahmin, or a king, nor the shadow of an elder. (2.974)
The circumambulation of Śambhu is auspicious and is the cause for the protection of the world;
one must not overstep the Soma-sūtra, which has the width of the staff of the celestial chariot.
There shall be longevity, strength, health, and victory over untimely death;
endowed with worldly enjoyments, he goes to the world of Rudra.
Regarding the circumambulation of celestial palaces, the rightward path is said to be the most excellent;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the circumambulation three times.
For the sake of knowledge, for victory, for subjugation, and for wealth; for purification, for the pacification of disease, for protection, and for the accomplishment of one's aims. (2.978)
The circumambulation performed here for the sake of *aṇimā* (minuteness) and *mahimā* (magnificence) is thus described;
therefore, one should perform the circumambulation starting from the southern gate of the temple. (2.979)
One should call to mind Naṭeśvara, the deity of the southern gate;
one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground and perform the eight-limbed salutation (aṣṭāṅga).
The head, the two hands, the two ears, the chin, and the pair of arms constitute the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-namaskāra); now hear about the five-limbed prostration (pañcāṅga).
Having placed the head, hands, two arms, and knees together on the ground— this five-limbed salutation is thus remembered as being of two kinds.
At its conclusion, one should perform the auspicious *tāṇḍava* dance which brings me joy;
at that time, one should chant songs, hymns, the Vedas, and likewise the *jayantī*.
One should perform an embrace with the *liṅga*, followed immediately by the *jñānamudrā*;
then, one should cause flowers to be offered as a sacrificial gift (*upahāra*) to the Lord of the South.
A handful of water.
Pure water taken in a handful is intended as *culukodaka*.
Having taken the water for the *arghya* offering with the right hand, it should be filled completely. (2-985)
The wise one should indeed offer all of this—the excellent handful of water and oneself from the soles of the feet—with his mind directed toward me. (2-986)
One should perform the worship of the book preceded by the meditation on the Āgamas;
[this is] the procedure for the dismissal.
I shall describe the procedure for dismissal; listen thus, O Maheśvara.
Taking a flower with both hands while reciting the Īśāna mantra,
one should place it upon the middle of the head [of the disciple], who is turned away and possesses the form of Śiva.
Then, having uttered the *śakti*-mantra, one should place [the deity] in the center of the heart;
one should then contemplate the deity surrounded by all the gods as before. (2.989)
Having meditated within the center of the heart-lotus upon that which has the nature of the *bindu* and *nāda*,
one should always contemplate the auspicious dance of the imperishable one facing south.
One should cause water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), fragrance, and flowers to be presented,
while reciting the syllable-mantra (*varṇamantra*) and remembering the three-syllabled mantra (*tryakṣaramanu*).
One should meditate on the dance that is eternally manifest, which has the nature of the sound of a bell;
one should perform the foot-steps (pādamudrā) at the face, the heart, and the secret place.
I shall describe the worship of the Kṣetrapālas; listen thus, O Maheśvara.
The worship of the Kṣetrapālas, especially at midnight, is auspicious.

The seed-syllable of the peak (kūṭabīja) situated at the end and middle of the letter *a* is well-guarded; joined with the sound of the seed-syllable, it is the internal state of abiding and protection. (2-994)
The single syllable is supreme, fierce, protective, and the destroyer of enemies;
it is the king of fields, the remover of decay, the pacifier of death, and auspicious.

(99) While reciting the seed-syllable of the peak (*kūṭabīja*), one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), fragrance, flowers, incense, and lamps—offering all of these. (2.996)
One should likewise worship him mounted upon a dog with his own name and so forth;
O Maheśvara, listen as I describe the meditation on Kṣetrapāla. (2-997)
With hair standing erect and three eyes, adorned with serpent earrings,
his face was formidable with fangs, and he possessed a luster like that of crushed collyrium.
Holding a trident and a ḍamaru drum with his two right hands,
and a skull-cup and a staff with his two left hands, he possessed a cruel form.
Wearing a terrifying garb, consuming fire, and wearing the serpent-sacrifice as his sacred thread—
he is declared supreme when possessing eight arms, four arms, or two arms.
Having thus meditated upon the deity of the field (kṣetradeva), who destroys death,
one should then invoke the god above the lion throne.

Having performed the lotus posture (padmāsana) during the bath and having always worshipped with garments, perfumes, beautiful flowers, incense, and lamps, one should prepare the yoga posture (yogāsana).
And one should present [the offering] at the proper time when [the deity] is seated upon the infinite throne;
especially so when the Lord is seated upon the lion-throne, having performed a dance.
The lotus posture (padmāsana) for all beings, according to the proper sequence, possesses a merit equal to the worship of Śiva; such has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again. (2-1004)
Thus ends the second chapter, on the procedure for worship, in the Kriyāpāda of the Trisahasrasaṃhitā within the Makuta-tantra. || 2 ||

In the *Makuṭa*, the chapter on the ritual procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*). Now, I shall explain the ritual procedure for initiation, which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments (*siddhi*), following the description of the fruits of initiation.
It pacifies untimely death and increases longevity and health. || 3-1 ||
That which bestows the state of Śiva while destroying the cage of sins is indeed called *dīkṣā*,
by virtue of its nature as both giving (*dāna*) and destroying (*kṣapaṇa*). || 3-2 ||
The place for initiation is on Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Vindhya, Pāriyātra, or Himālaya;
or by the banks of the Gaṅgā, the banks of any river, at the ocean, or even in a hermitage.
In a flower garden or a pure place near Jalpeśvara,
on a mountain peak, in a forest, in a cow-pen, in Śrīpura, or beneath a milk-tree (3–4).
In the Brahma-pit, at the Kadamba tree, in the beautiful abode of the Guru,
especially in a temple or in a house with a southern door.
One should designate the site for initiation at the root of a *kuṇḍa* tree.
The sequence for the site of initiation has been declared; now hear the rule for the time of initiation. (3–6)
And during the time of the northern solstice, in the bright fortnight on an auspicious day, as well as at the solstices, the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun. || 3-7 ||
In all months, on a day endowed with the teacher’s approval,
at an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction, one should perform the rite of initiation.
Having first examined the virtues and vices of his disciples for a full year,
he should accept those endowed with virtue and reject those devoid of virtue.

p. 101) In order to favor the disciples, the wise teacher should first cause them to offer a tooth-stick; having performed the bath according to the previously described procedure, he should do so endowed with the ritual rules. (3-10)
The pavilion (maṇṭapa), which embodies all the gods, is pure and fulfills all desires;
having performed the purification of the ground as before, one should perform the decoration of the pavilion.
Now hear, in due order, the colors, scents, and tastes of the four castes:
the color of the Brāhmaṇas is white, while that of the Bhūbhr̥ts (Kṣatriyas) is red. (3.12)
The color of Vaiśyas is yellow, while that of Śūdras is black.
The scent of clarified butter belongs to Brāhmaṇas, and the scent of blood belongs to kings (Kṣatriyas).
The scent of Vaiśyas is like that of a lotus, and that of Śūdras is like the smell of alkaline ash;
their tastes are sweet, astringent, bitter, and pungent, respectively. (3.14)
These sacrificial grounds range from the twice-born (dvija) down to the Śūdra;
thus, the sacrificial ground is endowed with these very colors, fragrances, and tastes. (3.15)
It is provided with four doors, adorned with four archways, equipped with canopies and banners, and decorated with garlands of *darbha* grass. || 3-16 ||
It was adorned with garlands of banners, embellished with wreaths of flowers,
and surrounded by betel-nut trees, plantains, and strings of pearls.
It was adorned in the ten directions with many small offering bowls (pālikās),
and encircled by three lines drawn either with lime or with ashes.
Having prepared [the area] together with offerings of flowers, parched grains (lāja), dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice (akṣata),
and having fixed a peg (śaṅku) on all sides at equal intervals and with well-strung lines.
The stakes at the rear are made of *khadira* wood, as are the *apāmārga* and *campaka* trees;
their height should be twelve finger-breadths, joined with a circumference of half that measure. (3.20)
The arrangement of the mandala consists of three times nine bays and is joined with thirty-two lines.
One should gradually stretch the threads, starting from the east and ending in the north.
Having stretched a thread from the southwest to the northeast and from the southeast to the northwest, one should draw a circle within the auspicious mandala.
Furthermore, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with white powder;
the pericarp with yellow-colored powder and the filaments with reddish-orange powder.
Its root is made of unbleached cloth; because of its white color, the petals are [white]. The size of the hand-lotus is such that the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is four finger-breadths wide.
One should draw the door according to the measurement of the lotus and its width according to the prescribed rule;
there should be three lines outside the lotus for each door.
The measurement for the three outer parts of the lotus is [one unit], while the measurement for each half of the lotus is half of that;
now hear the sequence of colors for the middle, on every rim at the edge of the lotus.
In the east it is red in color, in the south it is black;
in the west it should be white, and in the north it has the luster of gold.
In the southeast there is the fire-colored [one], and the blue-colored one in the southwest;
in the northwest there should be the smoke-colored one, and the white-colored one in the northeast.
One should draw a nine-colored ninefold tree outside the lotus;
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in sequence the colors for the four gates and so forth.
The doors should be drawn with red pigment, while the outer area is marked with yellow; one should then apply the three colors in sequence.
One should depict both the primary ornaments and the secondary embellishments using white pigment, well-mixed with flour made from rice and wheat and finely ground pearl powder. (3.31)
In the center, there is a full ruby and a blue pigment;
in the southeast, with yellow powders, and likewise blue powder in the south.
And specifically having prepared powdered gomedaka in the southwest, powdered pearl in the west, and powdered vaidūrya in the northwest; 3-33.
In the north, there should be coral-colored [powder];
in the northeast, powdered ruby; as well as minerals, flowers, and the *brahmapuṣpa* along with blue lotuses.
With *dhūrtūra*, *bṛhatī* flowers, and leaves of *nandyāvarta*;
with turmeric and the color of *śāli* rice, using these pigments from the center to the northeast (Īśāna) direction.
And with these same colors, one should draw nine trees on the exterior:
the *kalpa*, the *bilva*, the *śamī*, the *vaṭa* tree, and the *campaka*.
One should arrange nine [images] of the Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Punnāga, and Candana;
and likewise sixteen, thirty-two, or one hundred and sixty-four.
Having laid out these petals in sequence, as well as the great mandala itself,
[one should offer] either a thousand, or one hundred and eight, or sixteen, twelve, or eight [offerings].
Having laid down the lines in this manner, the Śiva-maṇḍala is described;
it may consist of twenty-five, thirty-two thousand, or eight hundred [squares].
Having arranged the *itthandala* in its proper sequence, it is called the *jñānamaṇḍala*.
(p. 104) The triad of maṇḍalas has been declared; now hear the procedure for the hand (*hastavidhi*). || 3-40 ||
Eight *reṇu*s are said to be one *keśa*; eight *keśa*s are likewise one *līkṣā*. Eight *yūkā*s are one *yava*, and eight *aṅguli*s are one *tāla*. (3–41)
Two tālas shall constitute one hasta; O Maheśvara, I shall now describe the measurements:
it may be one hasta, two hastas, or even four hastas.
It may be five, eight, or ten cubits, or likewise sixteen cubits; it may also be twenty cubits or twenty-five cubits.
Thus, it should be thirty-two cubits; one should not make it larger than that.
Once the mandala is prepared, it is to be worshipped, and within its center is the worship of Śiva.
One should cause to be offered fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp to the imperishable one who stands facing south in the midst of all the gods. (3–45)
Having recited the *tryambaka* mantra and meditated upon Naṭeśvara in the center, one should offer cakes,
the five fruits, and milk with the *astra* mantra.
One should first cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with one āḍhaka measure of rice; one should properly offer the entire caru, or else offer half of it.
One should give half of that to the attendants and half of that to the disciple,
without touching it with the teeth, according to the rule while recollecting the five Brahma-mantras.
Having performed the ritual rinsing (ācāma) according to the rules while reciting the meditation on Vīreśa, and having then uttered the mantra into the right ear of the disciple; 3–49.
Having recited that mantra five hundred times, one should again bind the amulet;
with the mantra "viśve tvā ete," one should bind it on the right hand.
For women as well as for Śūdras, one should cause the sacred ash to be given on the left hand without the use of mantras;
specifically, with the mantra "bṛhatsāma," one should cause the ash itself to be bestowed.
He was reclining on a bed of ashes at the right side of Śiva. [He said:
"Obeisance to Śambhu, the three-eyed, tawny-hued, great-souled one. (3.52) p. 105)
Having recited this mantra one hundred times— "Salutation to Vāma, who possesses all forms, the lord of dreams"— one should dwell for the night before Śiva.
At that time, having meditated upon the form of the Guru as the presiding lord on the right,
one should prepare five water-pots for the purpose of pacifying obstacles.
Together with its thread, its cloth, and its jewels, prepared as before, one should consecrate it with the Īśāna mantra upon the central pitcher of the palace. (3.55)
One should install the [faces] Puruṣa, Aghora, and Vāma upon the wheel as before;
having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, one should then install the form of Brahman.
Having recited the heart-mantra, one should offer the food offering and other items;
having thus made the formal resolve according to the rules, one should perform the morning bath. (3-57)

One should report whatever is seen in a dream, whether auspicious or inauspicious; one should collect [the results] in the case of auspicious dreams, and perform a fire-oblation (homa) in the case of inauspicious ones.
Having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules,
[he should wear] a garment of fine silk, a cloth of woven silk, or a variegated silken robe.
Alternatively, with a new cloth made of cotton,
while reciting the Netra-mantra ten times, [he should cover] the eyes of the disciple.
Facing north, being well-composed, one should bind [the flower]; having uttered the Puruṣa-mantra, one should indeed accept the flower. (3.62)
One should offer a handful of flowers with the Īśāna mantra;
having performed three circumambulations, one should cause [the disciple] to give [the offering] with the Vāma mantra.
Upon whichever face the flower falls, that [deity] shall be its name; likewise, its lineage, its thread, its sphere of activity, and its jewel-tree. (3.64)
Listen now to Śiva-tattva, Kāla, and Mūrti in their proper order;
[they consist of] Īśāna, Vaktra, Vidyeśa, Aghora, Brahma, and Śakti. (3.65)
Rudra is called the ninth [letter] for the Vamas; Mahat is called the tenth.
For Brahmins it ends with Śiva, and for Śūdras it ends with Gaṇa. (3.66)
One should pronounce the name of an anuloma son born of a Vaiśya woman and so forth, ending with Śakti;
namely, Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, and Jaimini. (3.67)
Agastya, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara, and Romaśa [are the authors];
[the texts are] the Śivasūtra, the Nādasūtra, and the excellent Sūtra of Śakti-Brahman.
The Soma-thread, the Great-thread, and the Nine-threads are indeed at the head;
Śiva, Śikhānanda, Jyotsnā, and Sāvitrī, who possesses the six qualities. (3.69)
The Śaivas who pervade the sky are remembered as being of nine types:
the Kalpa, Bilva, Śamī, the Vaṭa tree, and the Campaka. || 3.70 ||
The aśvattha, plakṣa, punnāga, and sandalwood trees—these nine kinds of trees—as well as ruby, pearl, topaz, and sapphire; || 3.71 ||
Vaiḍūrya, gomeda, gāruḍa, and pravālaka;
the first is Ūrdhvaśaiva, and the second is Ādiśaiva.
The first is Anādiśaiva; the second is Anuśaiva; the third is Avāntaraśaiva; the fourth is Miśraśaiva; and the sixth is [the fifth], which is Miśraśaiva. (3.73)
The seventh is Bhedaśaiva, the eighth is Guṇaśaivaka, and the ninth is Ājñāśaiva; thus the Śaiva systems are ninefold in sequence.
The principle of Śiva, the principle of Fire, and that which consists of the knowledge of Power; the qualityless principle of differentiation, and the Self-knowledge whose essence is Śiva. (3.75)
The nine principles have been declared; now hear the nine times:
Vidhātṛ [is the lord] at the time of creation, while Keśava is [the lord] at the time of maintenance. (3.76)
At the time of withdrawal he is Rudra; at the time of enjoyment he is Maheśvara;
at the time of yoga he is Sādākhya; and at the time of knowledge he is Binduka. (3.77)
At the time of Dhvani, however, it consists of Nāda; at the time of Ājñā, it consists of Śaktis;
and at the time of Śiva, there is the distinction of Īśāna as well, following that sequence. (3.78)
He is the embodiment of Śiva, the embodiment of Śakti, the essence of Nāda, and the form of Bindu;
he is the source of Sadāśiva, Maheśāna, Rudra, Keśava, and Brahmā.
The forms are said to be ninefold; now hear of their nature as Śakti:
Ādiśakti, Kriyāśakti, Jñānaśakti, and Gaṇātmikā. (3.80)
The power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the power of victory (jaya-śakti), the power called the bliss of yoga (yogānanda-śakti),
and the power whose nature is the support of differentiation (bhedādhārātma-śakti)— these are remembered as the ninefold powers.
The various distinctions of names have been fully declared; now hear the sequence of the colors of the gates.
The southern gate is the most excellent, following the order of the four castes.
O Maheśvara, the eastern gate is praised for Brāhmaṇas;
the southern gate is for Kṣatriyas, and the northern is auspicious for Vaiśyas.
O Maheśvara, the western gate is for Śūdras;
however, for all the [other] castes, the southern gate is the most excellent.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as before with the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
then, one should effect the withdrawal of that [deity] residing within the five sheaths by means of the heart-mantra.
Having recited the root mantra once, one should gaze upon the head of the disciple;
and having gazed, one should place the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta) upon that spot. || 3.86 ||
Having correctly proclaimed the pledges (samaya) in the presence of the God of gods, [one should study] the faultless Śiva-scripture, which is firmly established upon the feet of Śiva. (3.87)
One should not even step over the shadow of the preceptor or those possessing seniority; one should also completely avoid the company of any woman who has not received initiation.
One should not consume the remains of offerings (nirmālya), nor should one revile food mixed with ashes.
One should initiate a disciple along with his kinsmen and his wife.
Having thus caused [the disciples] to hear the pledges, one should thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (homa),
having closed all doors and restrained the senses.
The place for the restraint of sound is known as the organ of action;
by means of the seed-syllable *Anala*, however, one effects the restraint of the organ of sight. (3.91)
The ear with its sense-faculty devoid of moisture, the eye, the nose, the excellent tongue, the sense-faculty of touch, the anus, and the restraint of the faculty of speech. (3.92)
By the measure of the Samaya-indriya, there is the Ahaṃkāra-analendriya;
it has nine gates, the seed-syllable of sound (Śa), and the fire-seed-syllable (Ra). || 3-93 ||
Having placed the five seed-syllables, one should place the [five] senses in sequence;
one should recite "sattva," "rajas," and "tamas" with the beginning of their respective names.
Having thus restrained [the breath] according to the rule, one should draw it out by means of the powers of Śiva;
one should restrain everything until Paśupati himself was present.
The body, which consists of all the gods and is the collection of all knowledge, was flooded by Śiva, who was white as nectar. || 3.96 ||
Resembling the orb of the sun, with the seed-syllable established in its center;
it is the sprout of the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) and the beautiful sounding principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
The imperishable King of Mantras, renowned as the Śiva-tattva, is the pure Praṇava "Om"; it is the downward-facing lotus of yoga. (3.98)
Having first thus thoroughly prepared [the disciple], he should afterwards engage him;
[he should contemplate the Self] situated in the center of the heart-lotus, endowed with the three qualities (guṇas).
Resembling an indranīla gem, it is the form known as the twenty-fifth;
it is the Haṃsa-mantra, abiding in its own nature, blissful, and of the essence of nectar.
This mantra of the Upper Śaiva [tradition] is an auspicious seed-mantra (bījamantra) and the Guru;
it is the nature of the supreme reality and consists of the form of supreme bliss. || 3-101 ||
For the purpose of revealing the supreme reality, one should worship Śiva, the beloved of Pārvatī, who is established as the beginningless primordial head of the individual soul (pudgala). 3-101.
Facing the southern direction, [one should meditate upon] Sadāśiva, whose nature is Śiva, who is embodied as the Jñānamudrā, and who is well-characterized by the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
Having raised [the deity] again according to the rule, one should deposit the six paths:
the path of mantra, the path of words, the path of principles (tattva), and the path of worlds (bhuvana). || 3.103 ||
One should first join the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) and the path of kalās (kalādhvan) with the principles (tattvas):
earth, water, fire, air, and space. (3.104)
The wind, consisting of the five elements, is situated within the fire of the cosmic dissolution;
that which pertains to earth is described as being associated with Nivṛtti and Brahmā.
One should know that the waters exist as long as the nature of Viṣṇu exists through their support;
and one should know that fire exists as long as the nature of Rudra exists as fire.
The Aghora mantra is for the sake of knowledge (vidyā), and the Puruṣa mantra is for peace (śānti);
the Great Lord himself abides as the form of Vāyu, Śānti, and so forth. || 3.107 ||
Beyond Śānti is that which consists of the letter Kha, the imperishable reality called Sādākhya.
Nivṛtti is situated below the knees, and Pratiṣṭhā stands below the navel. (3.108)
The seat of knowledge (vidyā) extends to the end of the throat; peace (śānti) has the mouth as its range;
that which transcends peace (śāntyatītā) extends to the cranial aperture (brahmarandhra), consisting of the nature of both the supreme and non-supreme Śiva.
For *nivṛtti* the mantra should be Sadyojāta; for *pratiṣṭhā*, however, it is Vāmadeva; for *vidyā*, the Aghora mantra; and for *śānti*, the Puruṣa mantra. (3-110)
Then, one should perform oblations with the Īśāna mantra using the mantras of the preceding [deities];
having offered a hundred oblations for each, or half of that, or half of that again.
Having offered one hundred and twenty-five oblations, the fivefold oblation is praised;
having offered one hundred oblations for the preceptor, these oblations are especially distinguished.
For the destruction of enemies, one should offer a hundred oblations into the heart;
one should perform thirty-eight oblations with the mantra consisting of thirty-eight syllables.
Having recited the *varṇamantra*, a single oblation (*ekahoma*) is recommended;
having meditated three times on the form of the disciple, one should bind the body of the disciple.
One should draw forth all of that which destroys the bondage of the noose;
having recited the Aghora mantra, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the Aghora-weapon mantra.
That which is gathered and dispersed is surely called the binding of the noose;
having taken hold of the disciple's body, one should cause the hand of the mantra to be bestowed.
At that time, one should cause [the substance] to be given while recollecting the Śiva-mantra,
specifically upon the crown of the head, while recollecting the body of the mantra.
For each of the Vidyeśvaras, eight oblations are prescribed;
one should then unite the body of the Gaṇeśvaras with the body of the disciple.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the mantras of all the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Thus, after the mantras, the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the other principles (tattvas) is described.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space;
and the pentad of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. (3.120)
Speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals constitute one pentad; and hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell constitute another pentad. (3.121)
The intellect (manas), the awakening (buddhi), the ego (ahaṃkāra), primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise the person (puruṣa);
passion (rāga), necessity (niyati), knowledge (vidyā), as well as limited agency (kalā), time (kāla), and the deluding power (mohinī).
Śuddhavidyā, Śuddhakalā, and likewise thereafter Sadāśiva, Śakti, and the Śivatattva—these constitute the nature of Śuddhamāyā. (3.123)
Having thus established the thirty-six principles (tattva), one should assign them each to their own respective place;
one should then deposit the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Śiva.
One should first apply Kālāgnirudra to the big toe;
one should then apply Andhakāra to the region of the shank.
There are twenty-eight crores of most dreadful hells, and thirty-two kings of these hells are proclaimed. (3.126)
Raurava, Kumbhipāka, and the most terrible Raurava; Kūṭa, Balipūjā, and the dreadful Mahāpūti. || 3-127 ||
And [the hells] Jantupūta, Tapta, Asitālava, as well as Kṣārakā, Kṣurikādhārā, Dhanurdhārā, and Śara. (3.128)
The Svāna, Sūkara, Vyāghra, Siṃha, and Gajendraka; likewise the Mahāvairaraṇī and the Asibhaṅga. || 3-129 ||
Krakāma, Kāma, Kakuda, Gardabha, Kāyakā, Kīrṇavajrā, Sarvapāṃśu, and Lohaka. || 3-130 ||
Nīlayan, Yantā, Cakrayantā, and Śubhīrukā;
Ardhajaṅgha, Ūrdhvajaṅgha, and Jānukarṇa—these follow in sequence.
Tala, Vitala, Nitala, and likewise Sutala. (3.131) p. 112)
Rasātala, Mahātala, Talātala, and Pātāla.
Thereafter, one should place the seven netherworlds (pātālas) in the middle of the thighs,
followed by Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Suvarloka, and likewise Maharloka.
One should likewise conceive of the Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka in their proper order above the penis; thus indeed are the seven worlds to be visualized. (3-134)
One should place the worlds of Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra,
respectively, above the penis and below the throat.
One should visualize Goloka and Śivaloka above the throat;
one should then perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' in their respective locations.
One should place the seed-syllable of the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) in the middle of the mouth;
one should also place the seed-syllable of the power of Mahāmāyā and the mantra of Śiva.
One should place [the mantras] at the tip of the nose, in the heart, in the secret place, and in the middle of the body.
Having thus performed the placement above the phonemes (varṇa), one should thereafter perform the placement above the kalās.
One should contemplate *nivṛtti* in the region of the heart, *pratiṣṭhā* in the range of the throat, *vidyā* at the palate, *niśānti* in the mouth, and *atītā* at the crown of the head. (3.139)
In this manner, having established the path from his [the disciple's] constituent part (kalā) up to the principle of Śiva (śivatattva),
that teacher may then initiate even those who are hostile.
Just as copper, when processed with mercury, reaches the state of being no more than gold, so too one who has attained mastery through the Command shall not even remember saṃsāra. (3.141)

Having thus correctly performed [the rite], those practitioners who are freed from beginningless [bondage] by initiation are not liberated from the fetters of birth merely by the *hūta* [invocation]. (3.142)

Then, one should perform the oblation of fuel-wood with the *hṛdaya* mantra, the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *aghora* mantra, clarified butter with the *puruṣa* mantra, and parched grain (*lājaka*) with the *aghorāstra* mantra.
One should offer the *gulma* with the Heart-mantra, the fruits with the Śiva-mantra,
the parched grain (*saktu*) with the Vāma-mantra, and the milk with the Sadyojāta-mantra.
Likewise, one should offer white mustard seeds with the Heart-mantra, rice with the Sadyojāta mantra, sesame with the Īśāna mantra, and then mung beans and black gram with the Heart-mantra.
In the absence of all [other] materials, however, an oblation of clarified butter (ājya) is recommended;
by means of an oblation of clarified butter, one enjoys the fruit of all substances.
Now, the consecration at the conclusion of the fire offering (homa) will be described; listen to it in due order.
It may be performed with a thousand jars, or even with half that number of jars.
Or else, with one hundred and eight jars containing all the ritual substances,
he should perform the consecration with as many jars as the poor can afford.
Having made twenty-five, or else nine or five;
or two jars, or one, or even just the hand of the Guru. (3.149)
As before, one should place the ritual jar (kalaśa) and worship Śiva as previously described;
having placed a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp to the south.
One should place the disciple facing north in the center of that lotus,
after having had the Brahmins who are experts in the Vedas pronounce the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha).
One should place the Ṛgveda in the eastern quarter, the Yajurveda in the south,
the Sāmaveda in the west, and the fourth Veda in the north.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one should thereafter cause it to be proclaimed with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums,
as well as with the resonance of musical instruments and those uttering cries of victory and auspiciousness.
And with the sounds of lutes and flutes accompanied by dance and song, and especially with the auspicious recitations of the Brahmins; (3.154)
By the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, and those who observe the great vows;
by the Buddhists, the Ārhatakas, and all the various groups of heretics.
Having bathed and being firmly resolved, the disciple, seated upon a lotus-seat, is served with garments, food, staffs, and other appropriate provisions. (3.156)
Having worshipped as before and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon it in the proper sequence,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, accompanied by incense and lamps.
Just as the Ācārya is without parts (niṣkala), so too should he become possessed of all parts (sakala);
thereafter, the Ācārya, the best of teachers, should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Having performed the ritual rinsing (ācāma) according to the rules, adorned with perfumes and flowers,
and having discarded his previous garment, he is dressed in silk or similar fine cloth.
Resplendent with ornaments such as necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and earrings,
he wore a golden sacred thread and a ring set with nine gems.
With all his limbs smeared with sandalwood paste, adorned with flower garlands and other ornaments, wearing a white sacred thread, a turban, and an upper garment. (3.161)
Holding water and flowers with both hands while wearing the purifying ring (pavitra), one should offer one’s body, wealth, and life-breath to the true gurus. (3.162)
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground with his head, filled with devotion,
he then favored the disciple by taking him under his protection for the sake of his well-being.
Accompanied by the tumultuous sound of the Saṃgha and accompanied by a rain of flowers,
one should place his foot upon the head of that destroyer of bonds.

Afterward, having uttered the *prāsāda* mantra and taken the staff that bestows boons (*varadaṇḍa*) as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he should place the disciple’s hand upon it and fashion the foot-imprint (*pādamudrā*). (3.165)
He should recite the Śiva-mantra into the right ear of the disciple;
that disciple, having also recited that mantra, should remain standing with palms joined in reverence. (3.166)
This knowledge of the Pūjā-tantra is the palace in the supreme state;
having attained it, how could all people experience this division of suffering? (3.167)
"And how did my conduct become characterized by action and devoted to Śiva, O Lord?
Īśvara said: "Excellent, excellent, O Himavat's disciple! All of that shall be told; listen. (3.168)
One should not even step over the shadow of the preceptor or those who bear the marks of seniority; one should also strictly avoid the company of any woman who has not received initiation.
Having touched the work of one who is uninitiated, one should recollect the mantra of Śiva;
he who eats the food of one who is uninitiated is undoubtedly a Caṇḍāla.
Having always meditated upon my form, one should recollect the mantra of Śiva;
furthermore, women and Śūdras should avoid the sacred thread and the upper garment.
Likewise, one should cause the worship of Śiva and meditation on Śiva to be performed;
however, for those initiated into Nirvāṇa, one may cause them to be performed among all castes.
Those belonging to the three higher castes should especially wear it at all times; it is proclaimed that for a Brahmin alone, it begins with the *praṇava* and ends with *svāhā*.
For Kṣatriyas, mantras are proclaimed to begin with *namaskāra* and end with *svāhā*;
for Vaiśyas, the mantra is proclaimed to be joined with *namaskāra*. (3.174)
For a Śūdra, one should omit "namaḥ" and "vaṣaṭ" and begin with "praṇava";
however, for one who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa, one should join [the mantra] with the "praṇava. || 3-175 ||
Nirvāṇa, the supreme state, does not depend on distinctions of birth or caste;
yet, among all castes, for the sake of initiation, a Brāhmaṇa is specifically the Guru. (3-176)
Out of affection for you, I shall explain the initiation into Nirvāṇa; listen to it in due order.
Having established a single water-pot, adorned as before, [verse 3-177].
Having placed an eight-petaled lotus, one should deposit [the vessel] in the center;
having fashioned it in the shape of a golden lotus, it should be provided with a tuft of wool and clothed in a garment.

First, having performed the rite of depositing the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), which is endowed with all auspicious characteristics, one should place a seat upon that *tumbha*, invoke Śiva, and worship him. (3.179)
One should worship in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and incense as before;
one should then place that seed-syllable of the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti) within the middle of the pitcher.
Alternatively, one should perform the consecration with both hands right on the riverbank,
having seen the syllable *akṣara* risen up and established at both ends.
Having performed a circumambulation, one should worship the teaching itself;
first is the state of yoga, and second is the seal of knowledge.

Having formed the third [mudrā], the *draṃhaṇa*, and the fourth, the *varada* and *abhaya*, the fifth should be the five-faced [mudrā]; having meditated upon these, one should contemplate [the deity] in the center.
Facing the southern direction, the true path is indeed described;
O Maheśvara, I shall explain to you the specific distinction regarding the south.
They say that one who was previously accepted as a son becomes endowed with Śiva;
or else, by drinking water colored with turmeric, the birth of a son occurs.
The path of the servant is especially [the same as] my own form;
having always meditated upon my form, that which is performed becomes my own action. (3-186)

The path of the True One, the path of the Companion, the path of the Son, and the path of the Accomplisher—there has never been, nor will there ever be, a path equal to the path of the Servant. (3-187)
Therefore, having made the teacher’s seat the Vedas, the true path, and the supreme state of nirvāṇa, one should realize the teacher as the Self. (3.188)
Therefore, the form of the teacher is indeed the very form of Mahādeva;
the teacher is the god Mahādeva, the teacher is the god Sadāśiva.
Therefore, one should meditate upon this divine secret, the supreme goal, the bestower of the single syllable; one should honor no one other than the Guru. (3.190)
Having undergone a hundred births as a dog, one is even born among the Caṇḍālas;
[one assumes] the form of a wandering mendicant and the form of a senior preceptor.
The Guru should worship the form of the Ācārya-liṅga as his own self. O Maheśvara, listen as I describe the procedure for the initiation of the eyes (nayanadīkṣā). 3-192.
Some [attain] the end of eternity,
while others indeed attain the state of the classes through the falling of my glance.
The initiation of the eye has been fully explained; now hear about the initiation of touch.
Having touched [the disciple] with great affection, one should cause him to serve [the deity] with a focused mind. (3.194)
And one shall attain the world of Śiva, which is the form of nectar together with time;
therefore, a wise man should initiate [others] with every possible effort. || 3.195 ||
The ritual procedure for initiation by touch has been declared; now hear that which is vocal.
Having uttered my mantra into the right ear in that manner, || 3-196 ||
Listen to the sequence of initiation and meditation regarding the nature of whose syllable;
this is declared to be the oral initiation (vācika-dīkṣā), and after that, listen to the mental one (mānasī).
One should mentally perform all auspicious rites, such as the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya) and so forth.
Thus has the mental initiation been described; now listen to the procedure for initiation according to the scriptures. (3.198)
All this which has been given to me is my desired refuge;
by the mere power of single-minded meditation, one goes to the world of Śiva.
The sequence of the path of initiation has been declared; now listen as the festival is described.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation," in the Kriyāpāda of the Trisahasrasaṃhitā within the Makuta-tantra. || 3 ||
Now begins the chapter on the procedure for the festival of Śiva (Śivotsava).
Regarding the time for the sowing of sprouts:
the sowing of sprouts is most excellent prior to the festival of Śiva.
In binding, in auspicious rites, at the commencement of battle, and for purification. || 4-1 ||

In initiation (dīkṣā), in the installation (sthāpana), as well as in the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), in the plowing (karṣaṇa), in the purification of the image (pratimāśuddhi), and also in the collection of stones (śilāsaṃgrahaṇa). || 4-2 ||
On the ninth day before the auspicious day of the meal, on the day of the rising of the Kṛttikās,
and likewise on the ninth or seventh day prior to the day of consecration.
On the fifth day, on the third day, and indeed on that very day, the sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) is performed;
[this is] the characteristic of the *pālikā* vessels.
The *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva*—these three types [of vessels] shall be used. || 4-4 ||
The vessel may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay;
it should be eighteen finger-breadths high according to the measurement of one's own fingers.
The *pālikā* vessels with two openings are recommended; they are said to be sixteen finger-breadths in height.
Half of that is the width of the base, and one-sixth of that is the thickness of the rim.
Having divided the height of the *pālikā* into three parts, one should sequentially fashion the base, the shaft, and the mouth; one-third of the width is said to be the rounded cavity (*bila*).
Thus the sequence of the feet has been declared; now the staff (daṇḍa) is described here.
One-third of the width is said to be the width of the staff.
The characteristics of the *pālikā* have been declared; now hear, O Maheśvara, the characteristics of the *ghaṭikā*.
The width of the water-clock vessel (ghaṭikāghaṭa) should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgula) wide.
Then, one should have a water-clock (ghaṭikā) made, measuring half of that [in height] and one-fourth in width, according to the method described for the *pālikā*, and provided with five faces.
The characteristics of the arrow-reed (śarāva) according to the Sūtra, page 120.
The width of the opening of the bowl is declared to be twelve finger-breadths;
its base is half that in width, and its height, including the cavity, is likewise half.
O Maheśvara, one should have it made according to the method described by Pālika;
[avoiding] what is cracked, hollow, black, fissured, angular, or joined together. (4.12)
The best of practitioners should avoid Apūrṇa and Khaṇḍarī.
Śūlī, Mukunda, Dhātṛ, and Pālī are the presiding deities of the first [group]. (4.13)
In this manner, the small pitchers (pālikā) should be taken and placed in the ten directions— namely,
in the east of the temple, and likewise in the south and the north.
Regarding the procedure for establishing the seed-sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa):
on a pure pavilion smeared with cow dung and marked with eight threads,
one should take the central space as the "sky-square" (vyomapada) and erase the eight squares surrounding it.
Having abandoned three [units] within, the wise one should first place two *pālikās* in the four directions in sequence, on both sides of the two gates.
One should place two *ghaṭikās* in the corners and at the two feet; in the remaining spaces, one should establish rows of arrows with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
With the tips of *kuśa* grass and *darbha* blades, the wise man should make the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) free from gaps and holes, having prepared it with eight *droṇas* of rice.
In its center, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
and in the middle of the pericarp, one should place a moon-ornamented water-pot.
The sequence of worship:
having prepared [the image] as before, complete with its thread, cloth, and jewels, one should worship it according to the rule and worship by way of meditative concentration. || 4-20 ||
Having worshipped Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī on both sides of the water-pot,
one should thereafter offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and present betel leaf.
(121) One should fill the offering vessels and so forth with sand, cow dung, and earth;
thereafter, one should especially offer food offerings (naivedya) and betel leaf (tāmbūla). 4-22.
The seed, well-collected in a golden vessel, should be filled with milk;
likewise, sesame, mustard, mung beans, black gram, and peas are nourishing.
The preceptor, facing either east or north, should sow the seeds—kulattha being among the seven types of seeds—as the presiding deities of the seven grains. (4.24)
One should sprinkle the *pālikā* vessels and other items with water contained in a water-pot (*somakuṃbha*).
There, one should honor the preceptor (*ācārya*) with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
The supreme and other [methods] for the ritual procedure of the festival procession.
The festival is said to be of three kinds: nine days, seven days, and five days.
The nine-day festival is the best, while the seven-day is likewise the middling one.
The first [type] should be known as lasting five days; the festival is traditionally said to be of three kinds.
One should designate it as lasting three days or even one day, according to the teacher's wish.
One should perform the *avabhṛtha* rite at dawn and complete it in the evening;
prior to the commencement of the festival, the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) are now described.
One should dig there a pit one cubit deep, provided with girdles;
the girdles should be of the same form as the sacrificial pits.
Having adorned it with girdles, let it be provided with a single girdle;
its height should be nine finger-breadths according to the measurement of its width.
Above that, it should be four finger-breadths high and provided with a single girdle;
O Maheśvara, I shall now specifically describe the three-girdled [pedestal] in terms of finger-breadths.
The upper part should be four finger-breadths wide, while the middle part should be three finger-breadths;
the lower part, moreover, should be two finger-breadths in both width and height. (4.32)
One should place the yoni upon the girdle like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree;
its height should be one finger-breadth and its width four finger-breadths.
p. 122) That [measure] should be seven finger-breadths in length; now hear concerning the days. In the months beginning with Kṛttikā, starting from Kārttika, it ends with Kṛttikā. (4-34)
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, however, it ends with Ārdrā; in the month of Pauṣa, with Puṣya;
in the month of Māgha, with Maghā; and in Phālguna, it ends with Uttarā.
In the month of Caitra, it should end with Citrā; likewise in Vaiśākha, it should end with Viśākhā;
and in the month of Jyeṣṭha, it should end with Mūla—the day ending the festival is auspicious.
In Āṣāḍha it lasts until Uttarāṣāḍhā; in Śrāvaṇa until Śravaṇā;
and in the great month of Bhādrapada, it is said to last until Pūrvabhādrapadā. (4.37)
Likewise, on the full moon day of Āśvayuja and on the day of the festival in the constellation Aśvinī, the day is auspicious.
This Śiva festival should be performed in all months, ending with the month of Ārdrā.
On the day of the patron (yajamāna) and likewise on the king’s birthday—the characteristics of these days have been declared—as well as the trees suitable for the staff (daṇḍa). || 4.39 ||
It is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. || 4-40 ||
The temple with its surrounding wall and the temple ending at the top of the spire,
as well as the assembly halls with their surrounding walls— these are the three types of the most excellent sequence.

Listen now to the threefold classification of the middle [measurement], starting from the end of the *ukṣasthala* and likewise up to the hip and the gateway; as well as the lowest [classification], in their proper order. (4.42)
Or else, [the central axis] should extend from the throat to the navel; likewise, it should end at the edge of the *bhūtamālā*.
Now listen to the description of the five-cubit *vimāna* with its equal staffs.
For a chariot (*vimāna*) measuring three cubits, the staff (*daṇḍa*) is said to be double that length;
one should employ a staff of four cubits, two and a half cubits, and also half a staff [for other types].
It should be five cubits long, with a staff (*daṇḍaka*) starting from the middle finger upwards;
it must be free of blemishes, straight, and devoid of worms or hollows. (4-45)
Sandalwood, as well as *dāru*, *bilva*, and *campaka*;
*kramuka*, *veṇuka*, and the *panasa* and *kula* trees. || 4.46 ||
The *kundapuṇṇāga*, *khadira*, *marjuna*, and likewise the *ketaka*—these are prescribed as the best [materials] when the circumference is twenty-six *aṅgulas*. (4-47)
A circumference of twenty-four finger-breadths is prescribed for the medium [size],
while one of twelve finger-breadths should be made there for the inferior [size].
The width at the tip of this [vessel] is proclaimed to be twenty-four finger-breadths;
the base should be ten finger-breadths wide, extending to eighteen finger-breadths at its end.
The best, the middling, and the lowest are said to be the "measuring-cubit" (annāha).
It should be made using the *mānāṅgula* (measurement-finger); one should have it constructed according to that measure. || 4-50 ||
The best [type] is one cubit in measure and provided with five planks;
it is prescribed as being twenty-seven finger-breadths in length.
Having performed the intermediate procedure for a [pitcher] measuring eighteen finger-breadths, which is very well-remembered as ten finger-breadths, one should then fashion the lowest one.
Having made the length one cubit (hasta) and the width four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula), the handle should be divided into three parts, with one part being curved. || 4-52 ||
Having divided [the area] into seven parts, one should arrange the eighth part;
with the invocation and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), it becomes the most excellent nine-cubit hand-measure.
The middle [size] is seven cubits, and the lowest is five cubits;
having thus prepared the three types of cloth according to the prescribed rule, [one should proceed].
The characteristics of the banner-cloth.
According to the path described in the *Pañcatāla*, the middle [measure] is the fourth;
the lowest is the three-beat measure (*tritāla*), joined with a plantain leaf.
Having made it triangular and elongated, provided with two tails, one should cover the tip of the middle finger and join it with the width of the tail. (4-56)
The tail may be for the sake of expansion, or there may be two tails, or three tails;
endowed with these characteristics, such is the form of the banner as it is proclaimed. (4–57)
On the auspicious northern side of the bull, smeared with cow dung.
With eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, one should likewise prepare the sacrificial ground for the cloth;
[therein is] a bull seated in the lotus posture, adorned with all ornaments.
He is white, in the form of a bull, with two red horns;
likewise, all his hooves are raised, possessing a luster like that of the rising sun.
One should draw the auspicious bull, either seated or standing, as well as the vehicles of the eight world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions. (4.61)
One should fashion a peak in the form of Indra’s elephant, equipped with nine banners;
likewise, a lotus in the region of Agni and a buffalo in the southern region.
A lion is prescribed for the south-eastern quarter, likewise a crocodile for the western quarter,
