a deer for the north-western quarter, and a horse is proclaimed for the northern quarter.
Having drawn a bull in the northeast and likewise that [bull] on its right side,
one should worship the vehicle there under its own name.
Especially with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the worship of the Root Deity is auspicious;
especially one should worship the wondrous Lord Dakṣiṇeśvara.
According to his means and capacity, the supreme preceptor should perform the worship;
he should prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) made of eight *droṇas* of rice.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with white rice-grain lines, measuring two cubits in width and four finger-breadths in height.
Afterwards, one should draw a square and other figures with an *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds;
having established a seat of *kūrca* grass upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should worship the auspicious [deity]. (4.68)
One should place the pitcher upon the *kūrca* mat; it may be made of gold, silver, or copper, or even of clay, provided it is very sturdy and of auspicious form.
Having wound it with a thread made of gold, silver, or cotton,
one should place it according to the rules upon the mandala.
It should be completely filled with scented water and endowed with the five jewels:
ruby, pearl, lapis lazuli, sapphire, and coral.
One should place these five jewels into the bull-pitcher;
having deposited the Śiva-mantra into the jar, one should recollect the mantra of the [five] letters.
One should place a *kūrca* there upon a seat adorned with mango sprouts, which is beautifully decorated like a wheel with flowers. (4.73)
Having wrapped it with a cloth, one who knows the mantras should offer incense and flowers;
having worshipped the bull upon the jar with the root mantra.
Having placed a banner on the south and likewise a banner-pole on the north,
one should cause the previously mentioned offerings for the world-protectors of the eight directions to be presented.
Having performed a circumambulation slowly, one should take refuge in [the deity] and protect it;
having placed [the image] in the pavilion previously mentioned, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers. || 4.76 ||
I shall describe the sequence for the location of the banner; listen thus, O Maheśvara:
the place for the banner is in the middle of the door and the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Whether it be two cubits, three cubits, or even just one cubit in size,
one should install the image there with a staff, and place the staff-pole in that location.
One should make the altar (vedikā) smooth; the altar is prescribed to be three cubits [in width]. Its height should be three tālas, and it should be placed above the girdle (mekhalā).
Having conceived [the design] higher and higher, the palm-tree [pinnacle] should be made at least one *tāla* in height;
its width, however, should specifically be half of that height, or even less.
All the girdles (mekhalās) are said to be square on all sides;
in this manner, one should construct the most excellent of altars (vedikā) with these auspicious characteristics.
Above that, one should fashion a structure joined with a lotus, one tāla in height,
either circular, square, or in the shape of a lotus.
It is purified by being smeared with cow dung, adorned with flour-dust,
marked with three lines of ash, and decorated with white flowers.
There, one should cause the Brahmins to recite "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) and then have them proclaim it;
[the chariot] should be joined with the top of a flagpole and adorned with bells and garlands.
One should cause eight flowers to be offered to the world-protectors of the eight directions,
and perform the binding with cords in sequence using the ten-syllable mantra.
Having uttered the five-syllable mantra during the rite of erecting the banner,
one should worship the vehicle there with the seed-syllable beginning with the first letter of its own name.
Having lifted up the tree-pitcher, one should likewise [establish] the temple, as well as the village, city, and town, with the mantra of Dakṣeśvara.
Alternatively, one should slowly perform a circumambulation of the royal capital,
taking refuge at the site of the banner together with the installation of the sacrificial post.
One should bind the noose upon that very syllable Oṃ with the mantra;
one should then perform the fastening of the banners facing toward the temple.
Furthermore, regarding the banners there, that which was previously described as "Sundara" is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament. (4.90)
Clad in white garments, anointed with white sandalwood paste, adorned with white ornaments and garlands, and wearing a white sacred thread; || 4.91 ||
Having bound a new cloth around his head and being provided with a waist-thread,
he should sprinkle [the disciple] with the Astra-mantra and worship him according to the sequence.
O Maheśvara, one should offer food made from split chickpeas and milk-rice; that food is for the sake of victory, sons, and enjoyment. (4.93)
Likewise, one should place a bull and a water-pot at the base of the banner and in its middle;
one should wrap the staff with cloth and with beautiful, fresh darbha grass tips.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should cause incense, lamps, and other offerings to be presented;
thereafter, one should worship at the three junctions of the day and offer milk-rice (pāyasa) until the end of the rite.
I shall now describe the deities of the banners: Bhṛṅgīśa, Nandikeśvara, Mahākāla, and Caṇḍeśa; one should worship them in the directions beginning with the altar.
The staff has Śarva as its presiding deity; the stick is the goddess Sarasvatī;
the board has five deities; and the hollow part consists of Pārvatī.
The rope has Takṣaka as its presiding deity, the foot has the Wind-god (Māruta) as its deity,
the bull has Lord Śiva (Īśa) as its deity, and the trident has the Moon (Jyotsnātha) as its presiding deity.
The axe has Śiva as its presiding deity; the lamp has Śiva as its deity;
the two chowries have the Moon and Sun as their deities; and the bell has the Bull as its deity.
The wise practitioner should worship all [deities] beginning with Bhṛṅgīśa by their respective names;
having established banners in the eight directions, he should worship them thoroughly.
At the time of hoisting the flag, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara and honor all the gods in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
In the evening, at an auspicious moment, one should begin the beating of the drum;
one should prepare a square mandala in front of the pavilion.
Having prepared the sacrificial ground as before with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice,
one should place the nine powers upon the eight petals in their proper order.
One should worship with water for the feet, water for sipping, and the respectful offering (arghya), each by its respective name,
while reciting the root mantra conjoined with the syllable Om.
Then, having placed a drum in the middle of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should worship it;
for the drum has Skanda as its presiding deity, and its touch has Vāyu as its presiding deity. (4.105)
The sound there was joined with Pārvatī, and Śambhu was the presiding deity;
Vāsuki was the leather girdle, Īśa was the bracelets, and the Moon and Sun were [the earrings].
The wise one, having worshipped the seven Mātṛs, the Kīlas, and Skanda as the presiding deity for one hour with fragrant scents and other offerings, [should perform the rite] with the Heart-mantra.
Having uttered the *nandimātra*, the Guru should strike the drum;
he should not strike the musical instrument with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra.
Accompanied by the *śivatāla*, *jātitāla*, *kaṭatāla*, and *vitālaka* rhythms, joined with conch shells and *kāhala* drums, and attended by singers, instrumentalists, and dancers. (4.109)
At the village boundary, one should offer a bali-oblation to Brahmā and Īśāna, as well as a ritual stake,
yellow turmeric powder, parched grain, and flour mixed with curd.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the deities with these materials, calling each by its own name;
having performed the circumambulation slowly, one should thereafter enter the temple.
One should worship there during the three junctions [of the day], beginning with the invocation and ending with the ritual bathing at the sacred ford;
one should worship the deity of the banner (dhvajadevatā) adorned with all ornaments.
With reference to the Utsavanti-tīrtha, there is the Vaṅga, the Pratyaṅga, and the Sāṅga;
the Saptāṅga, the Catussāṅga, and that which is celebrated as the Saptapratyaṅga. (4.113)
The tree, the flagstaff, and so forth, along with all the offerings for the bali, are established;
the installation of the flagstaff is proclaimed as a constituent part of the festival.
The swing-chariot (ḍolāratha), the chariot-racecourse (yantraraṅga), the temple of the machine-god (yantradevālaya), and likewise the pavilions for the machines (yantramaṇṭapikā). || 4-115 ||
There were mechanical trees, mechanical actors, and mechanical gate-towers;
likewise, there were mechanical horses, mechanical lions, and mechanical elephants.
The bull-machine, the spirit-machine, and likewise the deity-machine;
variously adorned with peacock feathers and various types of fans. (4-117)
One should have various kinds of umbrellas and chowries made;
one should decorate the temple both above and below.
The worship of the sacrificial hall.
Having constructed a beautiful pavilion on the six directions of the Ālaya, one should decorate it as splendidly as possible with canopies, strings of pearls, and other ornaments. || 4.119 ||
One should construct the sacrificial hall (yāgaśālā) either in the northeast or in the southeast;
there, one should cause a pavilion (maṇḍapa) to be built, supported by sixteen pillars.
It should be ten cubits, nine cubits, or even seven cubits in size;
it must be provided with four doors and adorned with four archways.
Adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass and beautified by a canopy and banners,
one should construct an altar in the center, occupying one part out of nine parts.
Then, in the middle of the altar, one should fashion a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with auspicious white powders, which is one cubit high, pleasing, and resembles the surface of a mirror.
Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce an auspicious day according to the rule with six, five, or four *droṇas*, one should then have it proclaimed. (4.124)
On the first night of the festival, however, one should worship Śamatha in the south;
one should present the great sacrificial offering and perform the worship of the image.
At the commencement of the festival, the wise one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) as before;
having established [the image] in the center of the altar, accompanied by the five gems (pañcaratna).
A water-pot endowed with the proper characteristics, provided with a tuft of grass and wrapped in cloth, filled with sandalwood water and placed upon a lotus in its center. || 4.127 ||
Four-armed and three-eyed, holding a trident in his hand and wearing matted locks, the god bears the crescent moon and is adorned with serpent ornaments. (4.128)
Having donned a golden sacrificial thread and a ring set with the nine gems,
one who has been initiated for the festival should worship Śambhu, the Lord of the sacrifice, as the Master of the Sacrifice (Yāgeśvara).

[One should worship] the Vardhanī vessel, provided with a tuft of grass (kūrca), established on the left side [of the deity], who has four arms, three eyes, and is adorned with all ornaments. || 4.130 ||

One should place there, surrounding [the central deity], the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), who hold the gesture of fearlessness (abhayamudrā) and the knowledge-gesture (jñānamudrā), as well as a lotus and a goad.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering; thereafter, water with gems, water with flowers, water with sesame seeds, water with barley, and scented water. (4.132)
One should arrange eight pitchers from Indra to Īśāna;
one should worship Indra and the others within them, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
One should fashion the ten weapons out of either iron or wood;
all of them should have the forms of deities and heads equipped with their respective weapons.
One should worship all of those [seals] outside the pitchers in sequence;
in the directions starting from the east, one should worship the weapons, beginning with the vajra, proceeding clockwise.
One should worship the deity of the wheel in the north and the deity of the lotus in the south;
furthermore, one should worship the forms of the eight auspicious symbols on the exterior of the altar.
One should worship the auspicious trident with three joints in the direction of the wind (the northwest);
this is the fire-rite (agnikārya).
One should first generate the Śiva-fire and worship that auspicious one as before. || 4-137 ||

One should offer oblations into the seven tongues [of fire] to the three-eyed, four-armed deity, who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, whose form is sacrifice, and who has consumed the sacrificial offerings. 4-138.

One should offer a collection of fuel sticks with the Heart-mantra, clarified butter with the Puruṣa-mantra, sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora-mantra, and parched grain (lāja) with the Ghoratara-mantra. (4.139)
One should offer roasted barley flour with the Vāma mantra, milk with the Sadyojāta mantra, barley with the Hṛdaya mantra, and white mustard seeds with the Sadyojāta mantra. (4.140)
O Maheśvara, having offered rice-grains with the Śivagāyatrī mantra, sesame seeds with the Īśāna mantra, and black gram with the Udbhaṇa mantra; || 4.141 ||
Having offered the *vyāhṛtis* at the end of the substances, the names of the Rudras will be stated:
Dhūmayāna, Bhūta, Vasudhā, Taruṇa, and Kalā. (4.142)
The Rakṣonetra, the Aviccheda, the Sāra, and likewise the Ādika; the Jñānapuṣpa and others, the Gīti and others, and the fourteen Śarvarudras.
Each of these is eightfold, making one hundred and twelve;
one should offer oblations to the fourteen Rudras and the eight Rudras, using the beginning of their respective names.
At the end of the Rudra-mantra, having offered the Vyāhṛtis while reciting the Varṇa-mantra,
one should perform the fire-ritual as prescribed, using all the substances mixed together.
O Maheśvara, one should offer the bali-oblation in the evening and in the morning at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice;
[one should meditate on the deity] as three-eyed, four-armed, peaceful, red in color, and with a smiling face.
He holds a skull-cup, the *dhurtūra* flower, and the *arka* flower;
he possesses the crescent moon and wears matted locks that are beautifully disheveled.
Joined with the serpent-play (sarpakrīḍā), standing upon the apaskanda posture,
the right foot is contracted and the left foot is likewise raised.

In the right hands, let there first be the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and another, the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*); in the left hands, however, let there first be the end of the swing (*ḍolānta*) and the other, the fire-vessel (*agnipātraka*).
On the left ear there is an earring, and on the right a *kṛkuṇḍala*;
on the left shoulder is the hand in the *abhaya* gesture accompanied by a serpent. || 4.150 ||
Having thus meditated upon the form of Naṭeśa, one should worship him with the mantra;
thereafter, at the conclusion of the Śaiva Ekāha rite, pure food [should be offered].
Pure rice mixed with yogurt, combined with sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka) and cakes, along with fruit mixed with jaggery, is remembered as that which brings satisfaction to the Gaṇas. || 4.152 ||
Fruit, powdered turmeric, rice mixed with turmeric, and roasted barley flour (saktu) combined with curd and abundant flowers, bring delight to the Bhūtas. || 4.153 ||
Mixed with bilva leaves, tips of kuśa grass, and śāli rice, and joined with plantain fruit, this is a cause of gratification for the ṛṣis. (4.154)
On the fourth day, indravallī, haridrā, rice, and priyaṅgu mixed with ghee should be offered; this is called the bali-offering for Śakra.
On the fifth day, one should offer lotus flowers along with *rajanī* and parched grain, together with milk-rice (*pāyasa*); this is auspicious and brings delight to Brahmā.
On the sixth day, pure rice mixed with ghee and combined with the fruit of the *bṛhatī* plant should be offered; this is called the Vaiṣṇava bali.
Indeed, let them eat kṛsarā rice mixed with coconut fruits and combined with coconut water;
this auspicious offering brings delight to Rudra. || 4-158 ||
On the eighth day, milk-rice combined with curd and plantain fruit should be offered; it is auspicious and brings pleasure to Śiva. (4.159)
On the ninth day, one should offer auspicious food consisting of milk-rice and cakes, saturated with clarified butter; this brings delight to the one called Sāda. (4.160)
On the tenth day, rice with sugar, milk-rice, and pure rice mixed with ghee should be offered; this is auspicious and pleasing to the Lord.
Pure food mixed with rice and filled with milk should be offered on the eleventh day; it is auspicious and brings pleasure to Gaurī.
On the twelfth day, one should offer auspicious rice mixed with curd and pieces of sugar-cane; this brings pleasure to Śiva and is auspicious.
Alternatively, pure boiled rice mixed with sugar, curd, and clarified butter is auspicious and brings great delight to all the gods. (4.164)
Having performed worship especially with the respective mantra, one should cause [the gift] to be given—
either a *droṇa*, or half of that, or half of that again, or half of that once more.
One should offer the bali-oblations individually, each the size of a hen’s egg;
one should especially decorate either the village or the city itself. (4.166)
The Street Ornament.
The path, from which grass and other debris have been cleared, free from depressions and elevations, swept clean, pure, and sprinkled with drops of water. (4.167)
Having recited the syllable-mantra (varṇamantra), one should sprinkle [the site] with pure water,
as well as with many banners and even sky-banners (ākāśadhvaja).
With betel-nut trees, plantains, and rows of lamps, with many full jars adorned with variegated cloths and other ornaments. || 4.169 ||
One should adorn all the planets with garments, fragrant scents, and garlands;
then, for the sake of the festival, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) as prescribed in ancient tradition.
With cymbals, trumpets, drums, and the like, abounding in lamps and incense, accompanied by banners and peacock-feather fans, and with those reciting hymns and auspicious verses; || 4.171 ||
In the center of the golden ground, one should place a trident and a liṅga,
and install the ten weapons all around within the golden abode.
In the absence of such a machine, all would likewise fall upon the surface of the earth;
[the king], adorned with every ornament, wearing a turban and an upper garment, [would likewise fall].
The preceptor, joined by his disciples and surrounded by Brahmins,
should offer oblations separately to each deity from Brahmā to Īśāna in the proper sequence.
The tip of the trident is of the nature of *kalā*, while its base is of the nature of Rudra;
it is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*). One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship in this sequence.
Having worshipped [the deity] with fragrant flowers, together with the sacrificial offerings (bali) beginning with the vajra and ending with the lotus, one should assume the form of Rudra.
Having placed [the image], adorned with flowers, firmly in the center of the head, they should carry it in front during the festival, equipped with various ornaments. (4-177)
Equipped with various weapons and devoted to the True One, they went before him;
behind them were those mounted on elephants, and behind them were those whose vehicles were horses.
Mounted on mechanical devices, they were thereafter attended by celestial women;
at the end of that were horse-machines, and at the end of those, elephant-machines.
In the midst of the temples of the *yantras*, they are accompanied by dance and song;
the first [deity] is seated comfortably, while the second has a bull as his vehicle.
The third is Tripuraghna, the fourth is Candraśekhara,
the fifth is Ardhanārīśa, and the sixth is likewise Harihara.
The seventh is Bhaikṣamūrti, the eighth is Kālanāśana;
the ninth is Kāmadahana, and another is Kalyāṇasundara.
The eleventh, however, resides in the *liṅga*; the twelfth is Sadāśiva;
and the thirteenth is Nṛtteśa, endowed with all ornaments. (4.183)
Whether on a chariot, in a palanquin, or even upon an elephant, the Pāśupatas should be at his front; and in front of them, the Mahāvratas.
In front of them are the Mahāśaivas; in front of them, the Brāhmaṇas in due order;
in front of them are all the Bhairavas; and in front of them are the servants of the Siddhas. || 4.185 ||
In front of him let all the singers go, and in front of them the dancing women;
and at the end of that procession, the Lord, accompanied by Śakti, should proceed slowly.
Surrounded by throngs of women adorned with every ornament,
[he was accompanied] by various banners with peacock feathers, parasols, and various yak-tail whisks.
Accompanied by various kinds of people, bearing diverse noisy instruments,
and especially with trident-lamps and mechanical lamps.
Adorned with hand-lamps and staff-lamps shining everywhere, Caṇḍanātha, fully decorated, should proceed behind him on all sides. (4.189)
At the end of that, one should cause it to be proclaimed there, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments: with *paṭaha*, *maddala*, *tāla*, *bherī*, *dundubhi*, and *jhallaka* drums.
One should especially cause it to be proclaimed with hand-drums (paṇava) and cymbals (jhallara);
at its conclusion, the Vaiśyas and Śūdras should go forth accompanied by cries of victory.
At the end of that [age] there will be all castes, and at the end of that, those in the form of elephants;
then there will be the elderly, children, youths, eunuchs, and those who enjoy worldly pleasures.
At the end of that, the servant devotees should gradually and slowly depart,
following the Lord with their inner selves absorbed in Him.
At every step, men obtain the fruit of the horse-sacrifice;
being liberated from all sins, they shall thereafter attain the state of Śiva.
In this manner, one should perform circumambulation of either a village or a city,
specifically designating the sacred seats (pīṭhas) starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna.
In the granary, one should offer the bali-oblation to Sarasvatī;
in the pavilion, to Prajāpati; and at the gateway, to the deity Nandin.
Vāsuki shall be mentioned as the presiding deity at the rampart;
Śrīdevī at the royal gate, and Naṭeśvarī in the assembly hall.
These two are the presiding deities of the east for Āditya and Mahendra;
Masādevī is in the garden, and Gomukhī is in the cow-pen.
At the site of Durgā, however, there is a specific [form] (the deity Anādyaskāṇya);
at the site of Rudra, she has the form of Rudra, while at the site of Viṣṇu, she is indeed Vaiṣṇavī.
Vāgdevī is in the station of Brahmā, Manonmanī is in the station of the Guru;
Candradeva is on the forehead, and Śiva is likewise in the well (kūpa).
At the anthill is the King of Nagas, and on the mountain is Parameśvarī;
at the site of the yantra are the Gandharvas, and at the rivers is Karuṇālayā.
In the place of the elephant is Vighneśa; in the place of the horse is the Aśvins; in the place of the cow is Pārvatī; and in the cremation ground is Piśācikā. (4.202)
One should offer bali to these deities by their respective names;
for all of them, one should present the offerings together with the materials, each by its own name.
[The materials are] mango, coconut, and plantain fruit. (4.204)
One should cause parched grain, cakes, rice mixed with ghee, and betel leaf to be offered;
this pacifies the suffering of poverty and bestows the fulfillment of all desires. (4.205)
By the mere offering of a bali-oblation, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having slowly gone to the temple, one should cast the bali upon the sacrificial pedestal.
Having washed one's feet, one should enter the temple while the deity remains in the pavilion together with the entire host of gods.
The great sounds of the mṛdaṅga drums and other instruments are situated in the eastern direction;
the dancer and the drummer, however, are stationed in the south.
The singer and the flute-player are stationed in the north;
the preceptor is in the eastern quarter, and the king is in the west.
On both sides of the god, courtesans stood;
before the god, a dance and song accompanied by rhythmic cymbals were performed with great splendor.
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and cause it to be carried out by celestial women;
[one should offer] ashes, flowers, a lamp, an umbrella for Acyuta, and two chowries.
One should place a mirror and a golden pitcher upon a three-legged stand;
then one should offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya), and place a flower upon [the deity's] head.
Having placed unbroken grains (akṣata) upon their heads, one should especially offer fragrant scents;
having first given them water for sipping (ācamana), one should cause incense and lamps to be presented.
One should place a circle of lamps around the head, moving clockwise;
at its conclusion, one should cause ashes to be applied and then show the mirror.
At the end of that, one should offer fans; at the end of that, umbrellas and chowries, held by courtesans, together with lamps provided with fuel. (4.215)
Or, having placed it at the front of the pedestal, one should throw it outside the enclosures;
and in all ritual actions, one should proceed in this very manner day after day.
Prior to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), however, one should undertake a hunting expedition;
by the power of initiating battle, one should circumambulate the village clockwise.
On that night, especially, the wise man should tie the protective amulet (kautuka),
whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, or even of cotton thread.
Having recited the heart-mantra, one should cause the declaration of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be made there;
at the beginning of the festival, on the first night, one should bestow the auspicious marks upon all.
On the first night of the festival, one should worship the Supreme Lord;
thereafter, one should offer oblations of five colors into the five faces.
In the east, however, there is milk-rice; in the south, rice with ghee;
in the west, rice with jaggery; and likewise, turmeric rice in the north.
One should perform worship at the three junctions of the day, accompanied by the retinue, offering pure food with the face turned upward and a five-colored oblation.

The wise man should worship the image, the limbs, the *aṅkolaka*, the trident, and the deity of the sacrifice at the three junctions of the day; this bestows prosperity upon the king and the kingdom. (4.223)

At the conclusion of the worship and the fire-oblation, as well as the offering of the *bali* and the circumambulation, I shall describe the procedure for the full festival; listen to this, O Maheśvara. (4.224)
On the western side of the palace, one should prepare a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of rice grains;
there, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
Then one should wash both the mortar and the pestle with the Astra-mantra.
Then, in the center of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should place the mortar upon a seat of the Praṇava. (4-226)
Having placed it there and wrapped it with a cloth, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
having worshipped it in due order, one should cause it to be adorned with sprouts.
Having placed haridrā, uśīra, kuṣṭha, karpūra,
and sapichala into the middle of the mortar, one should fill it completely.
Having recited the *sadyo* mantra, one should worship Maheśvara;
first the preceptor should perform the rite of the powder (*cūrṇa-karma*), and then the king.
At its end were the disciplined Brahmins; at its end were the devoted people, and the attendants of Rudra and courtesans adorned with new garments and ornaments.
Having adorned it with sprouts and worshipped it in due order,
accompanied by dance, song, and instrumental music, he should repeatedly perform the application of fragrant powders.
Having applied an ointment of oil to the lingas, mirrors, tridents, images, and the retinue, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara.
The preceptor should cause powder to be given to the king and to the attendants;
thereafter, he should cause the powder to be given with oil to all the castes.

Accompanied by the sounds of conchs and kettledrums joined with the resonance of drums and other instruments, and having caused the Brahmins to proclaim [the rite] with recitations of auspicious benedictions; || 4.234 ||
Having quickly gone around the village or even the city clockwise,
one should afterwards enter the pain at a river, a stream, or a pond.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound there, adorned with an eight-petaled lotus,
and having installed a trident upon it, one should place water-jars in front of it.
O Maheśvara, having established the sacrificial deity to the north of the trident,
he should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and present betel.
One should prepare a sand mandala facing the image, having set out nine vessels that are very sturdy and auspicious. (4.238)

Furthermore, in the northern part of the sacrificial ground, one should cause the Brahmins to recite the "Puṇyāha" (auspicious day) formula for the purification of the vessels; thereafter, one should sprinkle them with water.
One should place the five jewels therein: a diamond, an emerald, a ruby, a sapphire, and a pearl. || 4-240 ||
Having offered water for the feet in the eastern quarter and water for sipping,
one should then place the *arghya* offering in the west and the unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in the north.
In the southeast is the vessel for the sacred water (tīrtha),
in the southwest the fragrant water, in the northwest the substances for smearing, and in the northeast the flower-water.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Narmadā, and the Sarasvatī;
the Sindhu, the Godāvarī, and the Kāverī—this is the sevenfold group of sacred fords (tīrtha).
Having drawn [the essence] from the center of the *bindu*, one should place it within the fragrant waters;
one should then worship the deities beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin in the pitchers in their proper sequence.
One should place the *kūrca* (bundle of grass) here, as well as the limbs and minor members;
having wrapped it with a cloth, one should place *tulasī* there.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth in due order, one should perform the rites up to the ceremonial bath; then, one should offer the water for the feet (pādya) with the Sadyojāta mantra.
One should offer the rinsing water (ācāma) and the arghya water with the *Īśāna* mantra using the [image of the] Puruṣa;
thereafter, one should cause the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) to be offered with the five Brahma-mantras.
One should gaze upon the ghee with the mantra "ghṛtam īkṣe," bathe it with the mantra "ghṛtasnānam," and likewise [offer] curd with "dadhi krāviṇo adbhyaḥ.
One should swell the milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva," and offer honey with the mantra "tā madhūni. (4.248)
In this manner, one should perform the bathing of the image there in its midst;
thereafter, one should perform the bathing of the trident, as well as the two auspicious rites for the sacred thread.
It is a great sacred site, a great means of subjugation, a protection that destroys enemies;
it removes all diseases, is pure, brings prosperity, and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Having arrived at the temple, one should perform the *puṇyāha* rite there;
then, in due order, [one should install] the *liṅga*, the image, and the trident, along with the complete ritual of worship. (4.251)
First, one should perform the flower sacrifice (puṣpayāga) accompanied by the ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅga) on the new vehicle;
thereafter, one should perform the silent sacrifice (maunayāga), and immediately following that, the sacrifice to the deity (devayāga).
One should perform the *mṛgayāgata* [rite] immediately after the *gandhayāga*;
by performing it in the manner previously described for the *yāga*, all fruits shall be attained. (4-253)
One should cause the auspicious sacrifice of Caṇḍeśvara to be performed as prescribed;
one should then consecrate the jars situated at the sacrificial stake upon the primary liṅga.
Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Vikrānta, and Cāṇḍeśāna are the deities;
one should worship the pure deity Caṇḍa, who destroys all enemies. (4.255)
Having established the conclusion at the flagpole, one should avoid the area directly beneath the flagpole;
one should cause the offering of the bali-oblation to be performed from Brahmā up to Īśāna.
One should perform the dismissal of the pedestal (pīṭha) using the Astra-mantra along with the Śakti;
having placed it upon the offering pedestal (balipīṭha), one should worship it especially.
Having performed the washing of the feet, he should thereafter honor the preceptor with necklaces,
armlets, crowns, and golden sacred threads.
The patron should worship the Guru with perfumes, flowers, incense, and other offerings;
and at the conclusion of the Teacher's festival, he should perform an auspicious festival for the devotees. (4.259)
One should sequentially bind the protective thread (kautuka) upon the devotees and the images, surrounded by ornaments such as dancing, singing, and the like, as previously described. (4.260)
Accompanied by the sound of the Vedas both in front and behind,
and having performed the circumambulation of the village, he should then enter the temple.
O Lord, one should worship the Guru as before with garments, ornaments, garlands, and so forth, for the devotees seated in order within the house at the rear part.
Having performed three circumambulations, one should dismiss the deities of the junctions.
Thus, whoever should perform the festival of Śiva with supreme devotion— (4.263).
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage, he rejoices in the world of Śiva;
therefore, with every effort, one should celebrate the great festival of Śiva in this manner.
One should cause [the festival] to be performed according to the prescribed rules for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
The procedure for the Śiva-festival has been declared; now hear the procedure for expiation. (4.265)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the ritual for the festival of Śiva, in the Kriyāpāda of the Trisahasrasaṃhitā within the Makuta-tantra. 4.
Now begins the chapter on the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
"Prāya" is said to mean destruction, and "citta" is said to mean restoration; the restoration of what has been destroyed is traditionally known as *prāyaścitta*. (5.1)
I shall now declare the expiation beginning with the plowing and ending with the worship;
if there is a lapse in the time for worship, it becomes double at the two junctions of the day (saṃdhyā).
If one fails to perform the evening worship, one should offer a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra),
present milk-rice as an offering, and perform the worship of Śiva once again.
If the worship is omitted for one day, the bathing is performed with nine jars;
if it is omitted for two or three days, it is performed with twenty-five jars.
Having offered the oblation of rice cooked with jaggery (gulānna), one should worship auspiciously as before;
having performed a special worship, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
On the fourth day and the fifth day, accompanied by the days of worship,
there shall be the ritual bathing with fifty-nine jars in successive order.
Having established [the sequence] from six days up to ten days, there may be eighty-one *kumbhaka*s; from eleven days up to a fortnight, however, it may be devoid of worship. (5-7)
Having established the Śiva-fire there and performed the ablution with one hundred and eight [offerings],
and having performed the worship as before, the food offering (naivedya) should be double.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *śikhā-mantra*, one should present milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
However, in the event of a deficiency in worship, one should offer three hundred oblations of *kalāśas* at the end of the month.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra), one should present milk-rice;
if the worship has been omitted for two months, one should perform it in sequence with a thousand water-pots.
If the worship is omitted for six months, one should perform a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) there;
however, in the event of the omission of the bali offering or the sandhyā prayers, one should perform twice as much elsewhere.
In the case of two junctures (*dvisandhi*) where there is a loss of offerings (*balihāni*), however, it is double in another juncture;
but when there is a loss of offerings at three junctures (*trisaṃdhi*), one should perform a ritual ablution (*snāpana*) there.
If there is an interruption of the bali offerings starting from the second day up until the end of the month,
one should perform the rite for Śivāgni as before and conduct the ceremonial bathing with one hundred and eight [offerings].
But when the strength of the month has decreased by more than half, the preceptor should worship Śiva-Agni in due order,
having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Śiva-mantra.
One should perform the ceremonial bath with one hundred and eight jars;
one should conduct the single-day festival with two *bhāra*s of food offerings.
Upon touching a woman, a Śūdra, or even a Caṇḍāla,
one should perform a ritual bath and offer one hundred oblations with the twenty-five-fold Śiva-mantra.

One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there and worship with devotion; likewise, at the time of the procession of the offerings (*balibhramaṇa*), one should worship the image and the linga. (5.17)
If [the image] should become cracked, displaced, split, broken, or severed,
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) at that very spot or in the center of the temple.
Having performed the offering of the bali-oblation as before, he should circumambulate that place;
or else, having performed it as before, he should offer oblations a hundred times with the Śiva-mantra.

p. 143) Thereafter, the Guru should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times; having committed the act of approaching a forbidden woman, he should offer oblations with the Śiva-mantra one hundred times. (5-20)

There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; one should offer oblations a hundred times with the root mantra alone, and afterwards, the Guru should mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
At that time, however, when the lamp is extinguished, leave the offering of food (bali) there;
then, taking up the lamp once more, perform the remaining circumambulation. || 5-22 ||
If the food offering (*naivedya*) is omitted, [the penance is] double;
if the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*) is omitted, one hundred oblations (*āhuti*) should be made with the Heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*).
Now hear the rule for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) specifically regarding a festival (*utsava*).
Regarding the procedure for atonement for festivals:
if the prescribed substance is lacking at the proper time, one should multiply that amount threefold and offer it to Śiva. (5.25)
Likewise, if one half of the face is not seen when the nails, body hair, and so forth are visible, a calamity will arise in that kingdom; therefore, one should remove that object. (5.26)
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while recollecting the five Brahmans,
and having then performed the fire-oblation for peace (śāntihoma), one should mutter the Pāśupata-mantra and others.
By the power of all those mantras, through their transgression, one should remember each respective mantra and offer oblations and recite it one hundred times each. (5.28)
If the offering of food (naivedya) is placed at an improper time or even if it is small, famine arises upon the earth; the remainder is called *nirmālya*.
Having set aside that substance, one should later offer cooked food;
it should be placed upon the head of the linga or the image. || 5.30 ||
But one should worship [the deity] in that sequence, avoiding the flower on the head. (5.31) p. 144)
If, however, the ritual for the ablution is deficient, a great plague will break out;
having recited the Astra-mantra one hundred times, one should thereafter collect [the water] once it has been purified.
If the installed jars are broken, cracked, or fallen,
the wise practitioner should take another new one, install it, and fill it.
The Procedure for Expiation in the Case of a Festival:
Listen specifically to the procedure for expiation regarding a festival;
[it applies] when the sacrifice of the bull is omitted and when the hoisting of the banner is omitted. (5.34)
If it is devoid of the flagstaff, or lacks the staff and pedestal, or is indeed devoid of the flag and bell, or lacks its various auxiliary parts; || 5-35 ||
If it is devoid of a garland of *darbha* grass,
[and] if it is lacking the offering of sprouts, lacking the sacrifice with the weapon-mantra (*astrayāga*),
lacking the mantra, lacking the ritual action, or lacking the encircling boundary of *darbha* grass; || 5.37 ||

If the placement of the water-pot (kalaśa) is deficient, or if it is lacking the jar, or devoid of water; or if it is bereft of gems and gold, or lacking the sacrificial grass-bundle (kūrca) and the thread.
If the seat and the enclosing sticks are missing, and likewise if the cloth is missing, [the offering of] the food oblation and so forth [is rendered ineffective]. || 5.39 ||
When there is a mixture of substances that have been kept overnight with the linga and the image, [the following applies].
When a statue is being transported, when the husband is missing a limb, during a festival in that village, or when someone has died within the house-site; || 5-41 ||
During an eclipse, at night, when [the body] is consumed by fire, in a terrifying situation, and when deprived of the protective thread—[in these cases, one should perform the rite]. (5.42)
And in the case of a confusion of mantras or their being deficient, the teacher should receive the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
When such things as these arise, they cause harm to the village and its inhabitants; however, when the bull-sacrifice is omitted, the cattle perish—of this there is no doubt. (5.44)
Having performed the ceremonial bathing of the bull, one should provide it with fragrant flowers;
one should then offer it green gram (*mudga*) rice and [other] offerings.
Then, having performed the pacifying homa according to the ritual procedure, one should thereafter cause [the tree] to be planted.
If the sacrificial altar is devoid of its banner, it brings fear to the practitioner;
therefore, having performed a pacificatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma), one should again perform the re-consecration.
If the flagpole is deficient in its rope, broken, lost, or if it has fallen, or if it is devoid of its flagstaff... || 5-48 ||
Then, having performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should worship the devotees as well. || 5.49 ||
If [the image] falls down without its bell, there will be the destruction of children;
one should cause the proclamation of a "day of merit" (puṇyāha) there and recite the Mūlamantra a hundred times.
Having consecrated the bell with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), one should perform the re-consecration;
if the drum is struck improperly, there will be fear from a hostile army.
One should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) for Śambhu and beat the large drum (bherī);
likewise, when the time for proclamation arrives, or when the small drum (paṭaha) is broken or even fallen.
One should predict the destruction of crops upon the breaking of a hide;
having recollected the mantra of the deity's color, one should offer oblations and recite that same mantra.
Afterwards, having taken hold of another auspicious [disciple] according to the rite, one should strike him.
However, if the sacrificial hall is lacking, or if it is devoid of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the altar (*vedi*), [the rite should not be performed]. (5-54)
When these characteristic signs are present, the destruction of that village will occur;
for whoever should act without proper authority, his authority shall not be admitted upon entry. (5-55)
Having performed the pacifying oblation at the end, one should then carry out each respective rite;
however, if the altar is devoid of a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), there will undoubtedly be the destruction of the crops.
Having purified [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should recite the root mantra one hundred times;
having prepared the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the rite, one should install [the deities] there in the proper sequence.
If one places earthen jars in the middle of the sacrificial hall,
there will be fear from a foreign army in the kingdom, and the king will meet with invincibility.

In the sacrificial hall facing the east and so forth, according to the prescribed rite with other jars, one should perform the Punarutsava (re-enactment festival) again, beginning from that very day. (5.59)
And if [the site] is burnt by fire through negligence, one should perform the rites in sequence as before;
having proclaimed an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should recite the *hṛdaya-mantra* one hundred times.
When the *sṛksṛva* is lost, fever and death prevail among the people; a great disease spreads throughout that village where it dwells. (5–61)
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the Tryambaka mantra;
if the darbha garland is absent, a drought will prevail.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred times, one should apply a garland of *darbha* grass;
even when devoid of sacrificial materials, there will undoubtedly be rain through this alone. (5–63)
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra as well as the Mahāvyāhṛtis,
the wise man should perform the fire-sacrifice in that very place according to the previously mentioned procedure.
And when weapons have been lost, there will be fear from thieves;
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with the three-syllabled mantra a hundred times.
Having fashioned it with the proper characteristics, one should sprinkle it with the auspicious water of Śiva;
for if it is devoid of the eight auspicious signs, there will be the destruction of the people. (5-66)
One should install those [deities] in the sequence beginning with Īśāna, as before; even when the rite of sowing sprouts is omitted, one should proceed with the *pālikās*. (5–67)
Due to the outbreak of a great disease, there will undoubtedly be a destruction of the crops;
having offered a thousand oblations with the root mantra, one should worship the devotees.

Then she should perform the rite of offering the sprouts into the *pālikās*, according to the prescribed characteristics; provided that [the vessels] are not devoid of the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*) and are not lacking the encircling with thread (*sūtraveṣṭana*).
If [the vessel] is devoid of a lid and a kūrca-grass mat, and likewise devoid of a cloth,
and if it is devoid of food offerings (naivedya) and so forth, then certainly bad food is produced.
Having performed the oblation of the forms (mūrti-homa) at the end, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra;
there, one should perform the consecration of the sacrifice (yāgādhivāsana) according to the previously stated method.
If the installation of the water-pot (kumbha) is omitted, a state of poverty certainly arises;
therefore, having performed the fire-oblation for the image, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra.
And likewise when it is devoid of jewels and gold, when it is lacking the thread-wrapping, when it lacks the lid and the grass mat, and similarly when it is without cloth. || 5-73 ||
If the offering of food (naivedya) and other such items are omitted, famine will certainly arise;
therefore, having performed the fire-oblation for the image (mūrti-homa), one should offer oblations a hundred times with the root mantra.
If the sacrificial lamp is extinguished during a rite, or especially if there is negligence, the destruction of crops occurs and madness will certainly arise. (5.75)
Having recited the terrible mantra a hundred times, one should again offer a lamp;
furthermore, if the fire in the sacrificial pit is extinguished, a famine will arise.
Having removed the ashes and embers and having established the fire as before, one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks, sacrificial porridge, and parched grain using the root mantra. (5.77)
Having offered a hundred oblations for each [deity], one should offer the *vyāhṛti* at the end of the substances. (p.
148) If the *praṇītā* vessel moves or becomes diminished, fever and disease will arise. 5-78.
One should offer oblations with the Astra-mantra one hundred times, or half that number;
for if the mantra is deficient or the ritual is deficient, mental derangement arises.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the root mantra, one should perform the reconnection;
and with the prescribed substances and mantras, one should perform the fire sacrifice according to the rule.
If the darbha grass or the enclosing sticks are missing, the arising of suffering occurs;
having offered a hundred oblations with the mantra of Īśa, one should perform the re-establishment again.
When the sacrificial offerings are deficient and especially when they have fallen, the destruction of the crops is certain to occur. (5.82)
Having discarded that substance, one should take up a new substance, even if it is devoid of the marks of power, cracked, or fallen. (5.83)
If it breaks, the destruction of the performer will certainly occur;
having performed a propitiatory rite (*śānti*), one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra alone.
Having first prepared the *bali* offering characterized by the *liṅga*, one should subsequently perform the *bali* rite;
likewise, [this applies] when the trident-weapon has fallen, been broken, or even lost.
There shall be affliction for that village and its kingdom by enemies;
having performed the consecration when [the image] has fallen, one should cause a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa) to be performed. || 5.86 ||
One should offer oblations with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and recite the Śiva-mantra;
having offered the bali-offering at the remaining places, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion.
When the staff of the trident has been severed, one should cast it into a body of water;
then, taking up another staff, one should complete the remainder of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, one should take up the spear-weapon and place it according to the prescribed rite;
and in the case of a fracture in any other limb, one should perform the reattachment again.

The ritual immersion in water (*jalādhivāsana*), the time for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the piercing (*bhedana*), as well as the breaking, destruction, or even the falling of weapons (*āyudha*). (5.90)
A great pestilence will undoubtedly arise, destroying cattle and food;
however, by awakening with the mantra and reciting it one hundred and eight times, one should perform the fire oblation (homa).
That which is lost or broken must first be restored according to its defining characteristics;
for if it is devoid of the vessel for offerings, wealth and grain will perish. (5.92)
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *ghora* mantra, one should take up the nine vessels;
and when the *bali* is free from the *tāla* [rhythm], it will in every way become dear. (5.93)
One should offer oblations of the form-mantra and the root-mantra one hundred times each;
however, if the offering and the lamp are omitted, the destruction of prosperity will certainly occur.
Having offered one hundred oblations each for the five Brahmās and the six limbs,
and having lit twice as many lamps, one should perform the remaining rites of the bali offering.

If the time for the offering of the bali-oblation and the procession has passed, it is declared that the destruction of that village will occur; one should then recite the mantra of the [respective] caste a hundred times.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and performed the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) as before, if the festival lacks a vehicle, the king shall meet his death. (5.97)
Having recited the Varṇamantra one hundred times, the auspicious rite for placing the protective amulet (kautuka) should be performed;
furthermore, upon returning, one should not perform a circumambulation of the village.
If at that time there is strife or fear from thieves,
one should offer a hundred oblations of root-seeds and then enter the supreme abode.
If there is a confusion of substances used for worship between the *liṅga* and the *bimba*,
fear from a foreign army arises, as does disease among the king.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Āghora weapon-mantra, and having performed the ablution twenty-five times,
one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day and then recite the auspicious Pāśupata mantra.

At the time of the image-vehicle (pratimāyāna), when [the ritual] has fallen or when there is a deficiency of limbs, the destruction of the site, the king, and the presiding deities may occur in an instant. (5.102)
One should perform a ritual bathing there and then have the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited;
having then performed a *śānti* oblation, one should once again carry out the procession. (5.103)
If the head, arms, or feet are severed, one should abandon that [limb];
likewise, if the nails or fingers are split, one should abandon their ornaments.
O Maheśvara, when there is a break in the lotus-band or a fracture in the matted locks,
perform the rejoining once more and carry out the consecration there.
Likewise, if Śūdras perform initiations other than their own, or if they transgress the words of the Guru,
there is no doubt that those living in his village shall be expelled from their place.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Then, having performed the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should have the ceremonial bath (snapana) performed for the image and offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra.
If a mortal should die in a village during the interval of a festival, the corruption of the kingdom will arise; therefore, one must quickly abandon that corpse.
One should offer oblations a hundred times each for the *varṇamantra*, the *tathā* mantra, and the *astra* mantra;
if the sequence of the circumambulation is deficient, one should predict ignorance among the people.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra, one should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra a hundred times;
for if the lustration (nīrājana) is omitted, there will be danger from fire.
Having specifically recited the hundred-fold mantra of the root-prakṛti (*mūlaprakṛti*) a hundred times,
the wise one should then perform the ritual waving of incense (*nirājana*) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
If a palace is consumed by fire, there will be danger of hunger for the village dwellers;
having offered one hundred oblations of *sadyamantra*, one should bathe the auspicious *biṃlanta*.
If the commencement of war occurs when [the lunar mansion] is devoid [of its proper asterism], there will undoubtedly be the destruction of crops;
having offered one hundred oblations with the face turned upwards, one should then undertake the commencement of war.
And when the Śakṣā-sūtra is lacking, there is the destruction of all women;
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the seed-mantra of Mūlaprakṛti.
If the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) is omitted, the deities will become angry;
therefore, having recited the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred times, one should then perform the powder festival. (5.115)
One should subsequently cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed and then carry out the consecration (abhiṣecana).
If the lowering of the flag (dhvajāvarohaṇa) is omitted, that [omission] is equal to a great sin (mahāpātaka).
Having recited the *praṇava* one hundred times, he should afterwards cause him to descend;
for if the ritual bath is omitted, there will undoubtedly be drought.
If there is an excess of days, great suffering arises and the performer or the master perishes;
having recited the Puruṣa-sūkta one hundred times, one should have a ritual bath performed there.
Having offered one hundred oblations with the *varṇa-mantras*, one should then perform the ceremonial bathing;
on the following day, one should perform the rite at the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) as before.
Furthermore, the kingdom will become deficient and the villages will meet with destruction;
therefore, having performed the *diśāhoma*, one should then perform the *śāntihoma*.
[The previous portion is missing from the source text.
If the removal of the impurity (bandhu) is lacking, however, all the deities will be displeased. (5.122)
Having offered a hundred oblations with the root mantra, one should thereafter perform the ritual of dismissal (udvāsana).
If the Caṇḍayāga is omitted, there will be fear from the armies of enemy forces.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing of Śambhu and carry out the Caṇḍayāga;
otherwise, due to the fault of confusion in the Tantras, pestilence and disease arise.
Having offered one hundred oblations with the Varṇamantra while the fire is kindled, one should perform a recitation (japa) of that same number. || 5.125 ||
One should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara, who brings about all peace;
now listen to the rule for expiation regarding the failure to understand the true nature of reality.
Having touched one initiated into one's own caste, one should perform an ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*);
in the case of touching those belonging to intermediate castes, a bath alone is required. (5.127)

O Caṇḍāla, [the procedure for] bathing is declared to be twofold; one should mutter the root mantra a hundred times. If a foul odor should come with the wind, one should turn it away even at the tip of the nose. (5.129) p. 152)
Likewise, having touched cow dung, a wise man should quickly recite the five-syllable mantra;
even after eating the food of those of his own caste who are uninitiated, he may do so out of desire. (5.130)
One should mutter the Vyomavyāpin mantra;
during a meal of royal food, the wise man should mutter one hundred Śivamantras.
Having eaten the food of a Vaiśya, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times in due order;
but having eaten the food of a Śūdra out of desire, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
If he eats continuously for a month, he is then born as a Śūdra;
joined with the status of a Śūdra, he should always behave like a Śūdra. (5.133)
If sexual union with a Śūdra woman occurs, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Aghorāstra mantra;
upon touching a woman during her menses, one should bathe, perform a hundred oblations, and recite [the mantra] a hundred times.
Having recited the Varṇa-mantra one hundred times, one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara;
at the time of eating without a lamp, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times.
But having eaten at the time of the [deity's] vision, one should recite the heart-mantra according to one's ability;
by remembering the Lord of the Gods of gods, one becomes purified through bathing in ashes. (5.136)
One should avoid garlic, fish, meat, and other leavings;
however, if one should consume them through negligence, one should recite the mantra one hundred times. (5.137)
The remnants of the food of the eldest preceptor grant all accomplishments;
visible salt in the center, when consumed with water during the spring season, [yields the same]. (5.138)
By reciting the heart-mantra, all defects are destroyed;
having abandoned the sound "uccha" while eating, one should likewise utter the heart-mantra. (5.139)
Upon hearing of the devotion of those who have not been initiated, one should recite the *hṛn-mantra*. This is the procedure for expiation for sins;
now hear the procedure for expiation for minor sins (*pātaka*) and major sins (*mahāpātaka*).
Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing gold, transgressing the word of the guru, and killing a cow—these are the five great sins (pātakas). (5.141)
Then, having meditated upon the Lord as the Purifier in the house of the preceptor,
he should consume sacrificial porridge for a month or half a month while observing a vow of silence.
Having drunk water from the Supreme Lord, one should perform the ritual bath at the three junctions of the day;
having recited the hundred mantras of the [respective] classes, one should perform the gift of all one's possessions.
Standing in water reaching up to the neck, one should constantly recite the three-syllable mantra;
having meditated for three nights, one should cause [the disciple] to dwell [in that state] and worship the Guru as the deity.
Having constantly recited the name-mantra, one should meditate upon the mudrā of gnosis;
thus one is liberated from all sins and shall attain the southern direction.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in order the rules for impurity due to birth (sūtaka) and death (pretaka),
as well as the purification of the Brahmin in ten days and that of the Kṣatriya in twelve. (5.146)
A Vaiśya attains purity after a fortnight, and a Śūdra becomes pure after a month;
one who knows the truth and abides by his own duty shall conquer the ignorant man.
On the day it is proclaimed, both the knower and the ignorant are purified at that very moment;
for in the Ūrdhva-tantra, there is no ritual purification regarding birth or death.
Therefore, with every effort, one should initiate [the disciple] into the Ūrdhvaśaiva [tradition].
For those who have been initiated, there is indeed no impurity regarding birth or death.
The "Knowledge-Seal" (Jñānamudrā) is taught for the purpose of removing all defects;
having meditated upon it and recited it, and having worshipped it, one should always mutter the name-mantra.

By constantly reciting the name-mantra, one shall destroy all defects. I shall now describe, in due order, the procedure for the decay of trees and other such matters regarding the linga, as well as the rules for atonement.
If the *liṅga* is cracked, split, severed, or likewise broken, burnt, or decayed, one should discard it and install a renewed one. (5.151)
To pacify all defects, one should recite the hundredfold mantra;
there, one should perform the ritual ablution according to the extent of one's means.
Whether it has been moved or fallen, divided by the current of a river, uprooted by a lordly elephant, or even plundered by thieves or madmen; || 5.153 ||
Having installed the appropriate linga there, one should worship it auspiciously as before;
then, having bathed it with a thousand jars of water, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
One should apply the four-fold staff (*caturdaṇḍa*) to that which is worn out or broken by the currents of rivers;
the primary linga is invisible, while the new linga is as described before.
One should quickly install that auspicious [image], which brings about all prosperity, in its proper place;
having recited the heart-mantra one hundred times, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
But when the retinue is destroyed, one should perform [the rite] as before, starting from the feet;
having offered a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra, one should present milk-rice.
Its characteristic has already been established as having the nature of a mode;
it should be understood as being without characteristics, increasing the victory that is difficult for kings to conquer. (5.158)
The syllable "khaḍantu ḍam" is proclaimed for the purpose of uprooting faults;
one should then place it on the side of the great boundary as previously performed.
Having offered one hundred oblations with the *varṇa-mantra*, one should recite the *śiva-mantra* one hundred times;
if a *liṅga* is installed in an improper location, the king shall incur invincibility [by enemies]. (5.160)

Therefore, with every effort, one should [avoid] a linga situated at the side preceded by another linga, as well as a linga situated in the middle of a wall that has been installed by an enemy. (5.161)
It causes great suffering to the king and the kingdom, and it is an increase for the Rākṣasas;
yet, O Maheśvara, the Liṅga previously mentioned stands by its side. (5.162)
One should not move a *śivaliṅga*, whether it be poorly situated or well-situated; for the primary *liṅga* (the *mūlaliṅga*), there should be no movement. (5-163)
The shifting of another's linga brings prosperity to the king and the kingdom;
at that time, O Maheśvara, one should install the linga as previously described. (5.164)
The Rite for Averting Portents: Now, I shall describe the pacification of portents for the removal of defects, when discoloration occurs in the *liṅga* or when the image weeps. (5.165)
One should perform the final oblation with twenty-five [offerings] for the ceremonial bath;
one should offer one hundred oblations of Apāmārga wood according to the sequence of the castes.
One should perform a festival for three days, and the defect of color will perish;
likewise, in the event of the weeping of an image, one should first perform a fire-oblation (homa).
One should offer three thousand oblations with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and *audambarī* wood;
and with the fifth mantra, one should perform a single great festival.
One should perform a bath with a thousand jars and double the sacrificial oblation when a temple has fallen or been broken, or when a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa) laden with fruit [is damaged].

If a garland of lamps flickers out during the entry [of the deity], or if foul odors and the like arise, and such other [inauspicious signs] occur, there will be danger to the king and the kingdom. (5.170)
To pacify that defect, one should perform a fire oblation (homa) in the northeast;
one should offer a hundred oblations with fuel-sticks of the aśvattha tree while reciting the Varṇa-mantra.
One should perform a three-day festival and the worship of devotees during an earthquake, the burning of the quarters, or the appearance of portents. (5.172)
When two lunar mansions arise together at night in Indra’s bow (the rainbow), and there is the conjunction of the tail and the fish, the destruction of people will occur. (5.173)
To pacify those defects, one should perform ten thousand oblations (*homa*) with the *Tryambaka* mantra in a pavilion constructed in the southeast. (5.174)
The materials for the oblation are as previously described; the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be made of Plakṣa wood.
One should perform the pacification rite in the prescribed sequence for the removal of defects.
When an anthill is observed on a palace, a pavilion, or similar structures, or when it arises near a red maiden, or on a palace situated in honey; 5-176.
When the unchaste woman has thus entered the interior of the temple along with the *putga*,
one should lead her out to that spot and fill it with pure sand.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma).
One should construct an auspicious pavilion in the northeast, in front of the deity. (5.178)
There, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with apāmārga fuel-sticks a thousand times every day for seven days or three days, at the three junctions of the day.
Reciting the mantra *namo namo yad asya*, one should offer a hundred oblations of the Śiva-mantra, which pacifies all defects. (5.180)
One should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara with cakes twice the amount of the sacrificial oblation, and especially perform an ablution with ghee and milk according to one's capacity. (5-181)
One should place a cool-water jar above the head according to the prescribed rite,
and perform the consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) by means of the previously mentioned method.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Īśa-mantra, one should recite the root mantra a hundred times,
even if the mirror has become discolored, worn out, or fallen.
Whether it be broken or lacking luster, one should cast it into water or upon the ground;
then, having taken a new mirror, one should establish it with the *varṇamantra*.
One should worship Śambhu as before for the prosperity of the king and the kingdom;
he who is attended by the four Vedas in the four directions, beginning with the east. (5.185)

Just as one should arrange an extensive ablution according to one's means, so too should one perform it with the perfected five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). (5.186)
One should perform the consecration with the waters of coconuts, as well as the fruits of the jackfruit tree and others,
with turmeric, myrobalan, and so forth, and with pure foods.

Having purified [the site] with ashes, one should afterwards worship Dakṣiṇeśvara with pure substances; it is traditionally taught that at the end of the regular offerings of abundant oblations, the [final] rite should be performed twice.
Thus has been proclaimed this rite that brings peace and destroys all misfortunes;
wherever peace is performed, there wealth and grain increase. (5.189)
Longevity, health, good fortune, victory, and prosperity shall increase;
this expiation has been declared by me for the sake of the advancement of the king and the kingdom. (5.190)
This has been declared as expiation; now hear the rule for the ripening of the fruit.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Expiation," in the Kriyāpāda of the Makuta Tantra.
The Chapter on the Rite for the Ripening of the Fruit:
That man who, having seen the peak from afar, offers salutation, is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Rudra. (6.1)
He who, untiring, performs the circumambulation from afar,
reaches the highest goal, having accomplished his purpose and transcended all affliction.
Just as one offers salutations to the gods, so too should one who honors them perform circumambulation during festivals and at the time of making offerings. (6.3)
At every step, a person obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice; one rejoices in the Flower Vehicle with both land-flowers and water-flowers. (6.4)
O God, if a man honors the temple of the Lord, he alone becomes wealthy and glorious, and is honored both in this world and the next. (6.5)
Whatever merit one who practices yoga gains by giving ten thousand [gifts] to a maintainer of the sacred fires,
one shall obtain that same fruit simply by bathing in the water from my feet.
Whoever bathes the Lord of the gods with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with water infused with kuśa grass shall obtain the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
He who, endowed with devotion, stays for three nights in the place of his guru,
even if accompanied by various distractions, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Whoever should give a bell for incense, their fame shall spread upon the earth;
and whoever especially gives garments and ornaments, [their fame likewise spreads].
Endowed with various garments and adorned with various ornaments,
being honored in this world, he shall attain the state of Śiva.
If one should give even a piece of land the size of a cow’s ear to the eldest preceptor,
he shall become the lord of villages and a sole sovereign over the earth.
He who offers a lamp to the heart of the teacher even once at the time of the ritual offering (sakṛtāle) shall obtain full knowledge and a beautiful form in this world.
He upon whose ground an undertaking directed toward Śiva proceeds shall, therefore, always obtain the fruit of all gifts and sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
He who causes a temple to be built with iron, brick, stone, or other materials, dwells in a golden celestial chariot and is glorified in the world of Śiva. (6.14)
Having attained perfection in the land of the Guru according to the ritual through the path of injunctions,
he reaches the world of Śiva, being ever worshipped by the gods.
By dwelling near a temple of the gods, one attains the state of Arūpya;
likewise, having gone to the world of Śiva, one attains the station of Sāmīpya.
Having fully worshipped Dakṣiṇeśvara, the Lord of Gods, as prescribed in the Āgamas,
he became endowed with beauty and youth, and possessed of all enjoyments.
Having enjoyed pleasures in Śivapura, one shall become the sole sovereign of the earth;
likewise, those who give a vessel of black gram, or even gold or silver, [attain the same].
Having extracted [this] twenty-one times, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
[this is the merit of] serving those devoted to the guru and residing in the city of the Teacher.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures endowed with all objects of desire,
upon the exhaustion of his merit, he shall become a sole ruler of the earth.
By offering gold upon the image, one attains the supreme state;
having recited the mantra "yato vā ca" and meditated upon Sadāśiva.
Having gone to the area in front of Śiva, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
likewise, having built a pavilion, a hall, or a dwelling for enjoyments, [one attains the same].
Surrounded by many sons, he enjoyed his own immeasurable enjoyments,
having recognized the true nature of the seats and the Lord Dakṣiṇa.
One should worship for the sake of attaining all perfections; such a person shall dwell forever in my world.
Furthermore, he who would give up his life for the sake of Śiva [shall likewise attain this].
Sālokya, sāmīpya, and sārūpya are indeed accomplished;
having performed the worship with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one goes to the supreme state.
Therefore, one should always worship Śiva with every effort.
The procedure for the ripening of the fruit has been declared; now hear about the Kṛttikā-lamp rite. (6.26)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Ripening of Fruits," in the Kriyāpāda of the Makuta-tantra.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the Kṛttikā-lamp in the Makuṭa [Tantra].
In the month of Kārttika, during the constellation of Kṛttikā, one should perform the offering of lamps;
then, that most excellent lamp, situated within you, shall be ever-present in the light.
Therefore, having meditated upon Maheśvara as the lamp situated in the center of all,
and having adorned the temple of the deity with archways, one should worship him.
Having first performed the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should worship Dakṣiṇeśvara;
O Agni, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the Śūla-gate with the Triṣum mantra.
There, one should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed according to the desire of the patron;
and on the right side of the temple, the lamp-pillar should be erected as before.
It may be made of khadira wood, or campaka, or even tālīka;
or of tāla, bilva, bamboo, or the wood of the sacrificial bull.
One should place the vessel, filled up to its thirty-two ribs, upon the top of the temple, whether it be a full archway with its pillars or even just a single quarter-section.
Or half of that, or even half of that again; one should place either ghee or oil, combined with cotton seeds, along with a new cloth.
The exterior of the temple is adorned everywhere with rows of lamps;
and above the temple, either in a pavilion or at the gateway (gopura), [the same is done].
One should employ lamps on all the enclosures;
having recited the seed-syllable mantra, one should place it upon the lamp-staff. (7–9)
One should place lamps everywhere and illuminate them all around;
one should circumambulate either a village, a city, or even a temple.
One should adorn everything with lamps according to the requirements of devotional yoga;
with such specific qualities, one should perform the circumambulation of the village.
Thereafter, one should enter the sanctuary fully adorned with all ornaments;
one should offer abundant sacrificial oblations and cause cakes to be presented.
One should worship with offerings of fruit and flowers— accompanied by plantain fruits and joined with mangoes— as well as with portions of cooked rice.
One should perform the worship at night and cast the bali offering right there; having tied the protective amulet (pratisara) at night, one should worship the devotees as well. (7.14)
At dawn, the wise one should worship the immutable Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
who resides within the great mirror and is as auspicious as before.
Uttering the syllable-mantra of Tryambaka Mahārudra,
and having recited the three-syllabled mantra once, one should worship well with dance and song.
One should offer the bali-oblation at the village site, starting from Brahmā and ending with Īśāna;
one should perform the rite of powdering with the Hṛdaya mantra.
In a river, or a pond, or especially in the ocean,
one should perform the ritual bath with the trident (triśūla) amidst the fresh water.
Then, having returned again to that temple, one should subsequently perform the ritual bathing;
there, O son of Ganga, one should stand beside the deity accompanied by dancing and other such performances.
Combined with parched grain flour, mixed with the essence of *aṅkola*, joined with plantain fruit, and accompanied by mango fruit. (7.20)
One should offer everything with devotion, including *mātuluṅga* fruits and coconut fruits, while reciting the syllables and the mantra. (7.21)
Having offered abundant sacrificial oblations, one should worship the images and other sacred objects;
one should also cause garments and other gifts to be bestowed upon the devotees and attendants. || 7.22 ||
Thus has the ritual bathing been briefly described; now hear about that which follows.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Kṛttikā Lamp," in the Kriyāpāda of the Makuta-tantra. || 7 ||
Now follows the chapter on the ritual procedure for the consecration of the crown.
On the eighth and ninth days, on the fourteenth day, on the two festival days (parvan), at the transit of the sun, at the equinox, during an eclipse, and at both solstices— 8:1.

During initiation and the rites beginning with it up to the final consecration, as well as during sprinkling, festivals, at the conclusion of a sacrifice, under auspicious constellations, on festive occasions, and in the practice of mantra-siddhi; (8.2)
At the time of a king's consecration, on the three days following a king's birthday, during excessive rain or drought, in times of famine, or when there are ill omens. (8.3)
During an earthquake, in times of great disease, or when oppressed by enemies;
