on the day of Ārdrā, on a Saturday, and on the days of the king’s sons (Wednesday and Friday).
During the birth-stars of the three generations of the king's lineage, at the time of a king's death,
and on such occasions as these, one should cause an auspicious ceremonial bath to be performed.
The group of five, the group of nine, and likewise the group of twenty-five—these three have been declared as the first; now hear the three middle ones. (8.6)
First, forty-nine; then eighty-one;
and thereafter one hundred and eight—these are called the three middle [categories]. (8.7)
Two hundred increased by sixteen, then likewise five hundred,
and one thousand joined with eight— these would constitute the three highest [categories].
In front of the deity, one should place all [the items] in sequence upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
having made a single square in the center, it should be shaped like a lotus with a pericarp.
One should likewise draw a nine-square grid by means of four lines;
having drawn six lines, one should proceed sequentially facing east and facing north.
Having made twenty-five squares, one should then establish a triad;
the width should be the measure of a *tāla*, and twelve lines are to be laid out.
One should place twenty-five intermediate two-pada enclosures.
Having grasped the five words from that which is possessed of a pedestal, listen now to these forty-nine and eighty-one words. 8-13.
Having stepped out one square, [one should mark] eighty-one squares in sequence;
likewise, there is a sixteenth line with its tip pointing east and another with its tip pointing north.
As before, one should establish the day; likewise, with cow-dung water, one should place twenty-five [units] in the center and twelve in each direction.
Having made a nine-square grid in the corner, one should [place] one hundred and eight [units] for the purpose of Śiva;
likewise, twenty-five squares are assigned in due order to the cardinal and intermediate directions.

p. 164) In the middle, within the central array, one who knows the ritual procedure should draw a nine-square lotus; thus it should be made, and there will be two hundred and sixteen [squares]. (8-17)
The bathing (snapana) and the installation (sthāpana) have been declared; now hear of their materials:
diamond (vajra), emerald (marakata), lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya), and coral (pravālaka).
One should thus place pearls and the five gems into the pitcher;
however, in the event that gems are unavailable, one may use a diamond or even coral.
Likewise, in the absence of gems, gold [should be used]; and in the *vardhanī* vessel, gold alone [is placed].
Now listen to [the description of] the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). || 8-20 ||

The aforementioned five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as water for the feet (pādya) and the respectful offering (arghya), should be placed in their proper order as before; the best of installers should likewise set out milk, curd, and clarified butter.
Honey and sugarcane juice, as well as the jackfruit and the mango, the plantain and the coconut, mustard and likewise sesame; 8-22.
Bilva, mātuluṅga, two varieties of nāraṅga, yavanī, vāralā, jātī, powdered parched grain, and ashes. (8.23)
Sandalwood, a small chest, a water-pot, flowers, leaves, camphor, betel nuts, ivory, a girdle of muñja grass, and an elephant’s entrails. || 8-24 ||
Śamī, dūrvā grass, white arka, bilva, arjuna, campaka, śaṅkhapuṣpa, apāmārga, viṣṇukrāntī, and dhurttūra.
The *nandyāvarta*, the white lotus, the *punnāga*, the jasmine, the *pāṭali*, the *sahadevī*, the *śatapatrī*, the *lakṣmī*, and the land-lotus. (8.26)
Dhātakī, tulasī, karavīra, mallikā, kṛṣṇavallī, śatāvarī, gokṣūra, and kṛtāñjali. (8.27)
Mahādroṇa, Droṇa, Mahābhadra, Anemadhu, Dhātrī, Harītakī, Rudraparṇī, and Indravallikā. || 8-28 ||
Vyāghranakhī, mañjiṣṭhā, or the entire fresh wood [of the latter], along with fresh butter, Drāviḍa, takkola, and excellent pippalī. (8.29)
Atibalā, balā, along with priyaṅgu, loddhra, nāgakesara, jambūka, kapittha, aśvattha, and guggulu. (8.30)
Cumin, black cumin, saffron with oil, agallochum, and gorocana; || 8.31 ||
Śrīveṣṭaka, ginger, resin, long pepper, elephant pepper, agallochum, realgar, and red sandalwood. || 8.32 ||
Lavaṅga, the powder of rajanī, and the decoction from the end of the cleansing;
and the decoctions of udumbara, plakṣa, vaṭa, and jambu. (8.33)
Sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, apāmārga, and the substance for sprinkling—
these four kinds of substances are proclaimed as this [method of] bathing.
The bathing substances, such as fruit powder and medicinal herbs, are for wiping; likewise, one should prepare other powders from juices and waters. (8.35)
The five [substances] beginning with jewels and ending with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are placed in five jars;
thereafter, the nine [substances] ending with clarified butter (ājya), up to the twenty-five [finger-breadths].
One should place two jars each, starting from sandalwood and ending with grass;
this would thus be forty-nine, or likewise eighty-one.
These [mantras], ending with Rudraparṇī and concluding with the Mārjana, number one hundred and eight;
however, in the middle Śiva-vyūha, the [qualities] beginning with Adharma are located in the great directions.
O Maheśvara, one should place the Dharma and the other [elements] in the corner and establish them;
one should worship with perfumes and flowers and spread [the ground] with darbha grass.
In the center, one should place the Śiva-pitcher, joined with the Śiva-mantra;
it is to be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the syllable-mantra.
The Śiva-kumbha is said to be provided with thirty-two prasthas, or else sixteen; the vardhanī should be half of that. (8.41)
Equipped with the five jewels, provided with a tuft of hair, and wrapped in cloth,
one should sequentially place the *vardhanī* vessel to the north of the *śiva-kumbha*.
Having placed [the vessel] together with a tuft of grass and a cloth, along with a *vardhanī* adorned with gold,
one should establish it with the *praśānta-mudrā* and then form the *jñāna-mudrā*.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the seed-syllable mantra,
one should establish [the deity] within the water for the feet (pādya) and other substances, up to the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara).
Likewise, one should worship the Rudras from the offering of clarified butter (ājya) up to the ritual purification (mārjana);
each one should be worshipped individually, and each should be wrapped in a cloth.
Having pronounced one's own name and so forth, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
having established the sixteen [deities] and the two hundred [others], one should worship them in sequence as before.
All the substances have been described; the installation was performed as before.
That number and the secondary bath is remembered as the "Seven Holy Fords" (saptatīrtha).
Starting from the lowest of the low up to the highest of the high, it is endowed with the aforementioned substances; and the highest [offering] is likewise performed together with them.
In the highest [grade], it consists of sixteen [verses] plus two hundred; now hear about the middle [grade].
There is the highest-middle and indeed the highest-highest as well. (8.49)
O Maheśvara, this is the distinction regarding the installations and the substances:
having placed six threads on the right, they should be directed toward the east in a sequence of six.
The distance between steps is forgotten as being five tālas in measure;
having encircled the inner lotus, one should take eight steps.
Four methods have been taught, consisting of four gates and four feet;
having established twelve feet, each one consists of twenty-five.
Having made a nine-square grid in the center, one should establish it in the sequence as before.
I shall now describe the arrangement of five rows for the five enclosures.
In the first [mandala] are the seeds; in the second, the metals; in the third, the jewels; and in the fourth, the minerals. (8.54)
In the fifth [day], these auspicious five products of the cow (pañcagavya) [are offered] one hundred and eight times;
likewise, barley, millet, mung beans, sesame, and mustard seeds.
White rice, great rice, red rice,
as well as fragrant golden rice— these are known as the ten types of seed-grains.
In this manner, one should place [the substances] in thirty-two jars in the first enclosure;
as many as there may be, one should perform the secondary ablution (upasnāna).
One should worship forty-four water-pots and cause water to be offered while recollecting the root mantra. (8.58)
The first enclosure has been described; now hear of the second enclosure:
[it consists of] cāmīkara, likewise hema, and beyond that, śātakuṃbha.

One should place gold that is refined, heated, and mixed with natural gold from the Jāmbūnada river and other such sources, having recited the twenty-six Kālāgni mantras over it, using water alone for the placement.
There should be that same number of those waters within the jars;
[this applies] to fifty jars, and likewise to the two northern ones among them.
Having meditated upon the second enclosure with the Varṇamantra, the instructor has described the second enclosure;
now hear about the third enclosure.
The previously mentioned nine gems [should be placed] within the thirty pitchers; as many gems as there are, they should be inside the water within the pitchers. (8.63)
There should be sixty water-pots, which one should worship with Brahma-mantras; this is declared as the third enclosure. Now hear about the fourth enclosure.
Yellow orpiment, collyrium, realgar, saurāṣṭra, siktaka, and likewise red chalk. (8.65)
In thirty-four pitchers, together with the seven elements and the waters, there should be as many pitchers as there are [elements], with water inside those pitchers. (8.66)
Likewise, one should worship sixty-eight water-pots;
each of them should be honored with a mantra beginning with the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "Namaḥ."
Listen to the five products of the cow, the tips of *kuśa* grass, and the five coverings:
the aforementioned five products of the cow, *kuśa* water, and the five-footed verse. (8.68)
In this rite, there should be thirty-eight [substances] including the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth;
one should place the five products of the cow and the Brahma-aṅgas in sequence with the palms.
One should continue until these become equal, with water added to each one individually;
this should be applied to the substances placed therein, especially during the recitation of the Śatarudriya.
The preceptor should worship all the jars with the heart-mantra;
three hundred and eight recitations are declared to be the most excellent of the excellent.
O Maheśvara, having divided the twelfth thread at the front and likewise the northern thread into one hundred and twenty-one parts, one should establish the square there.
One should discard each individual thread situated within the [main] threads;
one should lay down the threads arranged in a circle, joined with thirty-six threads.
The wise one should lay out four gates situated in forty squares;
in the center, the square of Śiva should be taken, and there he should fashion nine squares.
Within each individual word, twenty-five jars are likewise prescribed;
thus, there are ten thousand jars in the tenfold enclosure.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in sequence the eight thousand verses concerning the seeker of Śiva.
Seeds indeed in the first [layer], and metals in the second.
In the third [vessel] are the jewels, and in the fourth, the elements in due order;
in the fifth are the five products of the cow, and in the sixth, water with fruit.
All fragrant herbs and the like are proclaimed in the seventh [chapter]; clay and the letter *bha* are in the eighth, and thereafter come the ochres (*kāṣāya*) and the letter *bha*. (8.78)
And in the tenth [vessel], listen to the sequence for the flower-water and the rest, one by one;
one should auspiciously place the five gems and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as before.
The five obstructions have thus been described; now hear about the sixth obstruction:
the plantain, the wood-apple, the *pūtana*, the citron, and the pomegranate. (8.80)
The coconut, the orange, and likewise the jackfruit—
these are the fruit-waters, and they are said to be eight in number.
One should place each of those [mantras] within water inside the jars;
likewise, there should be twenty-four jars and four archways (toraṇas).
One should worship each of those individually with the mantra "pavamāna" and with perfumes and other medicinal herbs; now hear about the sevenfold enclosure.
Uśīra, sandalwood, camphor, and indeed jāti; the śatapatra, the goddess Śrī, viṣṇukrānti, and śatāvarī. (8.84)

The eight medicinal herbs beginning with *gandha*, as well as one hundred and eight [other substances], should be known to be of that same number; this is especially for the preliminary bath (*upasnāna*).
It is said that there are thirty-two jars; one should perform one hundred [rites].
[One should also offer] the fruits of medicinal herbs, creepers, and trees.
And let the root of all that has been stated also be grasped;
the seventh enclosure has been described—now hear of the eighth enclosure.
At the root of *darbha* grass, on a mountain peak, at the place where a boar has tilled the earth,
at an anthill, on the tip of a bull's horn, by a river, or on a mountain summit— (8.88)
And having especially collected eight kinds of earth from the ocean, one should place them individually into the jars, numbering twenty-one.
Having filled the jar with water up to its brim, one hundred and forty [drops] are proclaimed as the measure. (8.90)
One should worship with the five mantras; now hear of the ninth enclosure:
the mango, the banyan, the jackfruit, the banyan, and likewise the udumbara.
One should place the Aśvattha, Citraka, Panasa, and Mathuka trees, as well as the Navacūrṇa tree, together with water. (8-92)
Having filled each one seventy-four times, as many as there may be, those waters are placed within the jars. (8–93)
There shall be forty-eight [squares], with one square enclosed;
one should worship them in sequence, as before, with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Now hear in sequence the flowers for the tenth enclosure:
the *arka*, the lotus, the *bilva*, the *nandyāvarta*, and the *pāṭalī*. (8–95)
Karavīra, Caṃpaka, and Nīlotpala—
these eight [are placed] in the seventy-eight pitchers in due order.
Having placed eight flowers, one should fill [the vessel] with pure water;
there should be that same number of [offerings], such as scents and flowers, in due order.
One should individually wrap the water-pots with a clean cloth;
over the ritual substances, one should recite the Śatarudriya, and within the water, one should invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas).
One should establish the ninefold [mantra] and display the eye-mudrā;
it begins with "namas" at the head, ends with "namaḥ," and has the seed-syllable in the middle.
One should not perform the ninefold ablution in this manner;
rather, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) upon the previously mentioned [deity], or on the right side, or subsequently on the liṅga, or on the vehicle and so forth.
One should place the pitcher containing the deity of the southeast upon a three-legged stand;
then, having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) of the pitcher, one should carry it again on the head or on the shoulder.
Then, having gone to the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), the knower of mantras, standing facing north, should bathe the God, the Lord of Gods, with the root mantra. (8.102)
Having installed the Vardhanī pitcher upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā) in its respective place with the mantra "Gaṇāmbike," one should proceed as before in due order.

Having bathed the Lord, the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, with bathing substances according to the rule and likewise with subsidiary baths, and having established him with the mantra, one should bathe him.
Holding the water-pot with the left hand, one should cause a stream of water to fall from the right hand, with a thickness equal to the tip of a cow's horn.
One should cause the consecration with water-pots to be performed separately, offering flowers for each;
and for all the ablutions, one should include turmeric powder in the mantra.
As before, one should fashion the deity with an ablution of pure water;
O gods, one should worship those deities installed in the jars in their respective places.
But if even seeds are not available, one should collect yava and nīvāra;
and in the absence of the aforementioned metals, [the vessel] should be joined with refined gold.
If even gems are not available, one should certainly take a pearl;
and if even metallic ores are not available, one should especially take yellow orpiment.
But if even grass is unavailable, one should take the root of *darbha*;
and if even trees are unavailable, one should collect the bark of the *aśvattha*.
But even if flowers are not available, one should gather mountain flowers;
for the mortal who performs such a great ceremonial bath for the God in this manner, [attains great merit].
He who acts like Śiva is eternally honored in the world of Śiva. The ninefold ceremonial bathing has been declared; now hear the characteristics of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā). || 8-112 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bathing," in the Kriyāpāda of the Makuṭa Tantra. || 8 ||
Now follows the chapter on the ritual for the consecration of the inner sanctum in the crown.
O Maheśvara, [the image] may have a height of nine tālas with a width of seven tālas,
or a height of five tālas with a width of three tālas.
Nine tālas for Brāhmaṇas, seven tālas for kings (Kṣatriyas), five tālas for Vaiśyas, and three tālas for Śūdras alone. (9-2)
Whether it be a *liṅga*, or an image, or even a mural painting on a wall—images made of stone increase longevity, prosperity, and nourishment. (9.3)
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in due order the installation of all the deities: those made of iron, those for all desired objects, those made of brick, and those arising from fire.
The previously described pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed as before;
it should be provided with four archways (toraṇas), and one should place the ritual jars (kalaśas) at its base.
One should place the Three Jewels at the eastern archway and worship them;
likewise, one should place silver in the southern direction and pearls in the west.
Having placed coral upon the northern [side], one should worship it at the arches;
one should especially worship [the faces] beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Sadyojāta.
However, in the center of that very same *kuṇḍa* as before, having performed the worship of Śiva as previously described, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) exactly as stated before.

p. 173) One should offer all substances individually in this manner a hundred times with the heart-mantra; at the end of that, however, one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the mantra beginning "yad asya. || 9-9 ||
Likewise, one should properly perform the fire-oblation with sacrificial fuel-sticks in the nine fires,
using *palāśa*, *śamī*, *plakṣa*, and *udumbara* wood.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with aśvattha, apāmārga, bilva, arka, and kundaka,
in their respective locations from the direction of Indra up to the direction of Īśāna.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should properly worship the preceptor as if he were a guru;
then, having performed his ablutions, the teacher should perform the installation in the morning.
In the center of the Great Net (mahājāla), one should worship the image of the consecrated form;
at the time of the preliminary water-consecration (jalādhivāsa), one should recite the seed-syllable mantra.
Having especially honored the teacher at the hour of Brahma, one should recite the declaration of an auspicious day, words of well-being, and all that signifies auspiciousness. (9.14)
With lutes, flutes, and clay drums, with conchs, kāhala trumpets, and musical instruments; with perfumes, the ritual of incense, and with peacock-feathered umbrellas and chowries.
At an auspicious moment, under a favorable constellation, and at a time according to the teacher’s wish,
one should circulate the mantra of the [respective] color, meditate upon it, and [worship] the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
At dawn, one should perform the installation, descending [from the pedestal] very slowly;
at the conclusion of that, having performed the ritual bathing, one should worship those respective deities.
Furthermore, one should have three types of beds, seats, and vehicles prepared;
at that time, one should worship all the deities with the Jñānamudrā.
Uttering that very form-meditation and that very mantra, and having then performed the placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) as before, one should worship the auspicious [deity]. (9.19)
One should divide half of the temple's area into seven parts;
the central portion is the Brahma-part, and the second is the divine (daivika) part.
At its end, the human [element] is to be known, and the piśāca [element] rests upon the earth.
Therein, situated in the middle, one should then place the mountain of the feet as established by the wise. (9.21)
One should place the jewels in the nine compartments according to the prescribed sequence:
the nine seed-syllables in the first [compartment] and the nine jewels in the second.
In the third [layer], one should place the elements and the Saṅgha; in the fourth, the metals.
Having thoroughly purified all substances, one should cause them to be deposited in the Brahma-position.
One should take the previously mentioned seed-syllable of all the deities into the center, along with collyrium, honey, sunlight, and realgar. (9.24)
One should properly install, according to the prescribed rule, yellow orpiment, a linga, black pigment, red ochre, and sarjaka, starting from Brahmā and ending with Īśāna.
One should place the eight metals in their proper order: gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, bell-metal, and brass.
But if even seeds are not available, rice is recommended there; and if even mineral ores are not available, yellow orpiment is recommended. (9.27)
In the absence of even metals, gold is recommended there;
one should place that [gold] in nine compartments with the *devasumantreṇa* mantra.

One should cause perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps to be offered; one should have the declaration of an auspicious day recited there and sprinkle the area with consecrated water using mantras. (9.29)
The Vajracakra should be in the east, and the Ūrdhvacakra in the south; the Kālacakra in the west, and the Mukticakraka in the north. (9-30)
In the southeast is that called Vidruma, while in the southwest is Bhūtacakraka;
in the northwest there should be Nīlacakra, and in the northeast Śūlacakraka.
One should worship the deity individually and honor the surrounding circle of the wheel;
however, in the Sakala form, that very form is considered to be Śakti herself.
That which abides in that form is both partless and yet consists of all parts;
thus, everything is proclaimed to be a mixture of the partless and the whole. (9.33)
The installation of the deities has been explained; that very goddess is now established.
The characteristics of the installation have been proclaimed; now hear about the *pavitrārohaṇa* (the rite of offering the sacred thread). || 9-34 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Consecration of the Womb," in the Kriyāpāda of the Makuta Tantra. 9.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the investiture of the sacred thread upon the crown.

The wise practitioner should perform the preliminary worship (pūrvapūjā) for half of the [required] success, and the full worship (pūrṇā) for the sake of those seeking fulfillment; in all auspicious rites, one should cause the full worship to be performed.
At dawn, having invited the deity for the sake of attaining all prosperity,
one should then perform the rite of the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) with the fullness of Śiva.
In the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, or especially in Śrāvaṇa, or again in the dark fortnight of Nabhasya or the month of Āśvayuja. (10.3)
The second and so forth, the fourth and so forth, or likewise the sixth and so forth;
specifically, [the sequence] beginning with the second and ending with the fourth, or beginning with the sixth. (10.4)

One should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) beginning on the eighth lunar day, ending on the tenth, or thereafter ending on the twelfth, or ending on the fourteenth. (10.5)
One should perform it for seven days, five days, or even three days,
on the seventh lunar day, the thirteenth, under the asterism Revatī, or in the month called Kārttika.
One should have the *pavitraka* performed under the asterisms of Mṛgaśīrṣa and Rohiṇī;
one should fill nine jars with pure, purified water. (10.7)
Filling twelve *prasthas*, or half of that, or even a quarter,
one should wrap it with threads and enclose it with a clean cloth.
Having deposited the five jewels— or, in the absence of jewels, gold—
one should first secure the thread prepared by a daughter of the twice-born.
Alternatively, one should wash the image fashioned by others with a mixture of ash and water;
first, one should prepare a triple-thread, and that too should be made threefold.
In this manner, one should have an auspicious purifier (pavitra) made with nine threads;
there, the deities of the nine threads are the powers (śaktis), beginning with Vāmā.
The sacred thread (*pavitraka*) for the temple should have a length equal to the height of the *liṅga*. In this case, a sacred thread with a length of one cubit is auspicious. (10–12)
The wise one should increase the *pavitraka* ninefold by means of threads;
thus it is said that there are three types: nine, sixteen, and twenty.
Twenty-five, thirty-two, and thirty-six are the three middling [stages];
fifty, seventy, and ninety are the three superior [stages]. (10–14)
O Maheśvara, one should collect even a single one of these as a purifier;
one should have that purifier fashioned with the *yuvā suvāsāḥ* mantra. (10.15)
Among those, there are ten knots; for each of the ten, there are presiding deities.
(For the sake of purifying that *pavitra*), the wise practitioner should fashion the knots with nine, seven, or eight [strands], as previously described. (10–16)
The world-protectors and the deities named Granthi;
for the sake of purifying that sacred thread, one should let it remain overnight.
Having strewn a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains, flowers, and other offerings, and having covered it over with a cloth along with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. || 10-18 ||
Having placed darbha grass upon it according to the Śiva-mantra,
and having covered it with a cloth, one should fumigate it with incense while holding it to the head and reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should place the *pavitra* in the center, anointed with all fragrant substances;
one should arrange ashes, sandalwood, and powdered earth in the western direction. (10.20)
Water and likewise the tooth-stick and other items should be placed on the northern side;
these one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having provided an upper covering and placed darbha grass above it,
the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), preceded by the planting of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), should be performed.
One should perform the ablution according to one's ability, especially in the fire of Śiva;
having performed the special worship and having prostrated before Śiva, [one should proceed]. (10.23)
Having prepared incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should present milk-rice (pāyasa).
There, having worshipped the Lord of Gods and meditated upon the deity of the Tāṇḍava dance, [one should proceed].
Having covered them with perfumes according to the rule, having carefully covered them with flowers,
and having covered the deities with *darbha* grass, the wise man should encircle them with threads.
One should worship [the deity], provided with incense and lamps, by means of the syllable-mantra:
"The gifts, religious duties, and vows performed by me... (10.26).
O Lord, by this worship, may all my mantras, ritual actions, and the instruments such as the intellect become complete for me. (10.27)
Having paid homage to the temple of the deity with devotion and affection, one should fetch earth, ashes, a tooth-stick, and so forth, along with three or four threads. (10.28)
O Maheśvara, one should collect earth from the previously mentioned places;
likewise, one should collect ash, as well as a tooth-stick made of palāśa wood, according to the previous procedure.
Alternatively, it may be made from the wood of a sacrificial tree, measuring seven spans in circumference by the little finger and twelve finger-breadths in length.
Having offered oblations into the fire and absorbed it [into oneself], one should worship the sacred *liṅga* with its mantra;
furthermore, there should be abundant food offerings (*naivedya*), especially those of five colors. (10.31)
Having offered oblations into the Śiva-fire with the Varṇamantra, one should finally worship the fire;
the ritual substances are not to be offered into the heart, but rather the Vyāhṛtis are to be offered thereafter.
Hṛdaśakti is to be offered as oblation; Jyotiḥśakti transcends the qualities (guṇas); then there are Jñānaśakti, Jayāśakti, and the power known as Yogānandā. (10.33)

The distinctions based on the nature of their substrates are traditionally taught as ninefold; the various divisions beginning with "name" have been fully explained, so now hear in order about the doors.
For all [castes], the southern direction is declared to be the best according to the sequence of colors;
O Maheśvara, the eastern gate is likewise praised for the Brāhmaṇas.
The southern gate is for the Kṣatriyas, likewise the northern for the Vaiśyas, and the western gate for the Śūdras; such is the distinction, O Maheśvara. (10.36)
For all castes as well, the southern gate is the most excellent;
one should perform the rites with the five Brahmans and the six ancillaries as previously described.
One should avoid sleep at night while engaged in dance and song;
having bathed according to the rules at dawn, one should consecrate one's body with the ritual gestures (*sakalīkṛta-vigraha*).
One should discard the sprinkled flowers after they have become impure;
then, having performed the worship as before, one should [re-install] the Lord of Gods together with his pedestal.
Having offered oblations with the Tryambaka mantra, one should worship the fire at the conclusion;
then, having placed the sacred thread (pavitra) into the fire, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (pariṣeka).
One should offer the purifying thread (pavitraka) to all the Āvaraṇa deities with the Heart mantra, and one should likewise cause the purifying thread to be given to the other deities as well. 10.41.
The preceptor should cause that *pavitraka* to be given to these [other] preceptors, to their devotees, to the disciples, and to the attendants. (10.41)
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, especially with incense and lamps,
and having presented abundant sacrificial food, one should cause milk-rice (pāyasa) to be offered.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should provide food for the sages from beginning to end;
thereafter, one should cause all manner of gifts to be bestowed upon the people according to their merit.
Then, one should worship the preceptor with garments, ornaments, and other offerings;
likewise, one should worship the Śaivas, such as the Ūrdhvaśaivas and others, as well as all others, with devotion. (10.44)
There, one should perform a special gift for the yogins according to one's own capacity;
thereafter, having taken up the bathing water, one should do so before the God of gods.
"May these gifts of ghee be complete for me.
Having thus made this petition to the deity and having then concluded the religious observance (niyama), [he should proceed].
"Having completely severed the waters of the noose, you ought to attain liberation.
Having thus informed the God, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground.
At the conclusion of the observance for one who has lived according to the rules, there is the descent of the thread;
having descended it, one should discard the sacred threads and the flowers.
Having performed worship as before, one should offer abundant sacrificial oblations;
then, facing the south, one should worship Naṭeśvara.
One should cause garments and other articles to be given to the devotees and attendants;
one should collect the materials required for the sacrifice from the preceptor and the deity.
One should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the Varṇamantra,
and one auspicious oblation with the mantra "yad asya" (RV 10.87.24).
Having performed an embrace with the fire, one should contemplate its dancing form;
this is declared to be the Pavitrāropaṇa. Now hear the sequence of yoga and meditation.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Investiture of the Pavitra," in the Kriyāpāda of the Makuṭatantra. || 10 ||
Now, in the *Makuṭa*, the chapter on the procedure for yoga-meditation.

Restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and postures (āsana), followed by breath control (prāṇāyāma), then withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), and finally absorption (samādhi). || 11-1 ||
First, Yama is proclaimed; likewise, the second is Niyama.
The third is said to be Āsana, and after that, Prāṇāyāma.
Pratyāhāra is the fifth, and dhyāna is indeed said to be the sixth;
dhāraṇā is declared the seventh, and samādhi is remembered as the eighth.
This should be known as the eightfold means for yogins to accomplish yoga:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession. (11.4)
Yama has been declared to be fivefold; now hear about Niyama:
therein are purity, contentment, austerity, and self-study. (11.5)
And the observance of devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna) is remembered as the fivefold restraint (niyama):
Gomukha, Svastika, Padma, and Ardhacandraka. || 11-6 ||
The heroic posture (vīrāsana) is declared to be the yogic seat; thus, the sixfold system of postures is explained in sequence.
Prāṇāyāma has been described previously; now hear the method for pratyāhāra.
To whatever extent the activity of the senses regarding their objects remains established in its place, to that same extent it has become steady; this is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra). || 11-8 ||
Just as the nature of meditation is to be conceived within its supports, so too is meditation; now hear from me about concentration (dhāraṇā), which is of a different kind from that. || 11-9 ||
The support (ādhāra) is said to be dhāraṇā, while that which is supported (ādheya) is samādhi.
Dhāraṇā is declared to be of two kinds; now hear the sequence for dhyāna itself.
(181) The support and the supported, volition, the flow, and the nature of meditation;
the upper and the lower, the lowermost, the void above, and the stainless void below. || 11-11 ||
O Maheśvara, I shall specifically explain the sequence of the support for yoga—the samādhi which is entirely empty, formless, and the cause of the mind. (11–12)
Four finger-breadths below the navel is the circle of fire;
it has the color of a kadamba flower, possesses eight petals, and is triangular.
This is declared to be the root support; the second is rooted in the navel, shaped like a coiled serpent and consisting of eight circles.
The great channel called Kuṇḍalī is said to be the solar orb;
it is located in the heart, at the root of the throat, at the root of the palate, or in the forehead. (11–15)
Having visualized them at the locations of the crown of the head and so forth, one should meditate upon the lotuses as before.
O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in detail the characteristics of the heart-lotus.
At the navel is that stalk; likewise, it extends upward with its opening above.
Like the flower of a plantain tree, it has eight petals and a pericarp.
The characteristic of the support has been declared; now hear about that which is supported, by the application of which one is indeed consecrated through meditative absorption. (11-18)
Iḍā and Piṅgalā are on either side of the neck of the lute, while Suṣumnā is situated in the middle; therein, in its center, is likewise a subtle channel.
The individual soul (jīva), joined with the vital breath (prāṇa), moves within those [channels];
established in the foundational centers (ādhāras), it indeed moves at that time. || 11-20 ||
The "conjoined" (saṃyukta) is declared to be yoga; one should take recourse in that conjunction.
With fire conjoined at the mūlādhāra, one who is thus conjoined should practice yoga. (11-21)
Through the practice of yoga, that yogi shall attain the world of fire;
by meditating on the sun above that, he shall attain the world of the sun.
Having meditated upon the moon, one shall attain the world of the moon above it;
by constantly dancing within the heart, one is glorified in the world of Śiva. (11.23)
Having meditated on the Nāda, one should then abide at the root of the throat;
one should remember Rudra at the root of the palate, and by the supreme will, [remember] the Root of Rudra.

One should contemplate the supreme sound (parāvāk) as extending from the feet to the top of the head by means of its pervasive radiance, reaching as far as the Lord (Īśvara) within the space between the eyebrows.
Having meditated on Maheśvara in the center, there shall be a dance upon the head;
having meditated in the middle of the heart-lotus, one should recollect the *bindu* and *nāda*. (11.26)
One should visualize a lamp-shape measuring four finger-breadths;
Maheśvara is in the center, while Nṛtta is above the head—having thus meditated. (11.27)
Aṇimā, mahimā, garimā, laghimā, as well as prāpti, prākāmya, īśitva, and vaśitva—these are the eight siddhis. || 11-28 ||
Because one attains minuteness (aṇimā) through this, it is designated as "aṇimā. || 11-29 ||
Or likewise, having gone a thousand [steps], because one obtains one's own shadow at the point where the distinction of the root-syllables occurs, one should cause [the disciple] to enter there.
Having made one's pride as swift as thought, one is honored by those who dwell in that place;
because one is thus perfectly honored, for that reason one should overcome that [pride]. (11.31)
Having reached all substances, this is proclaimed as attainment (prāpti), due to the entry of the vital breaths into bodies at will. (11.32)
The attainment of the abodes of the Sun and other deities is declared to be their mastery (*aiśvarya*);
however, that which is *vaśitva* (the power of subjugation) is established as being within those very same abodes.
Through the power of union with Śiva, that state is known as "Śivatva";
moreover, the yogi specifically attains the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*. (11.34)
(183) O Maheśvara, I shall now describe in sequence the fourfold [liberation] beginning with *sālokya*. *Sālokya* is defined as the attainment of residence in the same world;
*sāmīpya* is declared to be that which is situated in the immediate proximity of the Lord. (11.36)
The attainment of that very form is renowned as *sārūpya* (conformity);
through knowledge, *sāyujya* (union) itself is said to occur, just as water merges with water.
These qualities arise for those who have exerted themselves in the practice of yoga;
therefore, having undertaken yoga, which excludes all suffering, [one should persevere]. (11.38)
Having constantly practiced meditation through yoga, one should attain absorption in that [reality] through knowledge;
by means of knowledge, while reciting the supreme *haṃsa* mantra, one attains one's own true nature. (11.39)
Within the bodies of living beings resides the Haṃsa, who is Sadāśiva;
the Haṃsa alone is the supreme dance, and the Haṃsa alone possesses the Śakti.
The *haṃsa* alone is the supreme speech; the *haṃsa* alone is the Vedic [truth].
The *haṃsa* alone is the supreme Rudra; the *haṃsa* alone is that which is higher than the highest.
The *haṃsa* situated in the midst of all the gods is indeed Maheśvara;
the *haṃsa* alone is the immutable (*kūṭastha*). There is no doubt about this—thus it is established. (11.42)
From Earth up to Śiva, there are the phonemes beginning with 'a';
however, mantras devoid of the *mātrās* are not seen anywhere at all.
The swan, the light that is unswerving, situated in the middle of the body—
having resorted to the south-facing direction, one should form the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā).
One should always practice meditative concentration while recollecting the *haṃsa* mantra—the stainless, crystal-like, divine form that is beyond compare. (11.45)
In the region of the navel is the supreme Haṃsa, whose essential nature is the Jñānamudrā.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Characteristics of Yoga," in the Yogapāda of the *Makuṭa-tantra*. 11.
Now, in the *Makuṭa*, the chapter on the procedure for the characteristics of the preceptor (*ācārya*):
"I shall declare the characteristics of the preceptor; listen thus, O Maheśvara!
One born in the lineage of the Upper Śaivas (Ūrdhvaśaiva) who possesses wealth and is accompanied by a guru is known as a preceptor. (12.1)
He knows the true meaning of the Śiva scriptures, is proficient in the science of knowledge,
possesses all limbs in their entirety, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
Whether he has a topknot, is shaven-headed, or specifically has matted hair;
whether he is a householder or a student, or one who practices the materialistic form of celibacy (bhautika-brahmacārin). || 12-3 ||
One who delights in the single tantra, from ritual action up to gnosis, being pure, skilled in ritual action and conduct, and endowed with truthfulness and the gathering of all [virtues]. || 12-4 ||
An ācārya is one who is undoubtedly proficient in this great treatise; one should designate as an ācārya even one who knows the essential principles only slightly. (12.5)

Those who have not studied the scriptures, those lacking the auxiliary sciences, the unworthy, those who have fallen from their status, atheists, those with crooked limbs, those with deformed eyes, and those devoid of knowledge— [these should be avoided].

Those who perform improper acts toward others, children, those who go to the wives of others, as well as renunciants, and likewise those whose minds are fixed on food other than [the prescribed] alms; (12.7)
Those who habitually slander others, those who are merciless, and those who are excessively argumentative;
likewise, those who are too tall, too short, too stout, or too thin. (12.8)
Those with protruding teeth, deformed nails, and misshapen feet,
who were restless and distinguished by their aged and decrepit forms.
Those who are devoid of strength, the wicked, those who lack Vedic conduct,
those who behave excessively, and those who are deficient in limbs— these should always be avoided.
They never perform excessive delusion, having completely renounced it;
thus the characteristics of the teacher have been declared. Now hear the procedure for the upper wheel (ūrdhvacakra).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Characteristics of the Preceptor," in the Kriyāpāda of the *Makuṭa*.
